0.title: The LORD Fights for His People: The Book of Joshua
0.overview:
The book of Joshua opens with a death and a charge. Moses, the servant of the LORD, is dead — and the man who could split the sea, who spoke with God face to face, who carried a stiff-necked people through forty years of wilderness, lies buried in an unmarked grave on the far side of the Jordan. And God says to Joshua, 'Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise' (1:2). The law could lead Israel to the edge of the land, but the law could not bring them in. Moses must die; another must take them across. And the name of that other is Yeshua — Joshua — the very name that, centuries later, the angel would give to a child born in Bethlehem: 'You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people' (Matt. 1:21). The whole book is a shadow cast forward by the cross. What Moses (the law) could not accomplish, Jesus (grace) does. He brings us into the rest.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Old Testament and the first of the so-called Former Prophets in the Hebrew canon. It records the conquest of Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and the covenant renewals that bracket the nation's entry into its inheritance. The driving theological claim of the book is announced in its title and proven on every page: the LORD fights for his people. Israel does not earn the land; God gives it. The walls of Jericho do not fall by siege engines but by trumpets and a shout, so that no flesh may boast. As Calvin observed, the conquest is a prolonged sermon on the faithfulness of God to his promise to Abraham — the down payment on a redemption that reaches its consummation in Christ.

Modern readers stumble over the violence of the conquest — the herem, the devotion of cities to destruction. We must not soften it dishonestly, nor must we read it as a charter for human aggression. It is, rather, a localized, time-bound, divinely commanded judgment upon a civilization whose iniquity had, in God's patient reckoning, finally become full (Gen. 15:16). The Canaanite cult burned infants to Molech. The conquest is an eruption of final judgment into history — a sober preview of the day when the King of kings returns with a sword from his mouth (Rev. 19). And astonishingly, in the middle of this judgment stands Rahab the Canaanite prostitute, saved by a scarlet cord, grafted into the line of the Messiah. Judgment and mercy meet, as they always meet, at the place of the blood.

Read Joshua, then, not as ancient military history but as gospel. Hear in 'Be strong and courageous' the voice that says 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (Heb. 13:5). See in the Jordan your baptism, in the ark your Christ going before, in the cities of refuge your only hiding place, and in the rest that Israel entered the deeper rest that 'remains for the people of God' (Heb. 4:9). The God who was faithful to Israel — of whom it could be said, 'Not one word of all the good promises had failed' (21:45) — is the God who keeps every promise to you in his Son.

1.title: The Commissioning of Joshua
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,<sup>2</sup>"Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.<sup>4</sup>From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory.<sup>5</sup>No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.<sup>7</sup>Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.<sup>8</sup>This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.<sup>9</sup>Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua commanded the officers of the people,<sup>11</sup>"Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"<sup>12</sup>And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,<sup>13</sup>"Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.'<sup>14</sup>Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them,<sup>15</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.<sup>17</sup>Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!<sup>18</sup>Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
1.overview:
The book begins where the gospel begins: with a death. 'Moses my servant is dead.' The mediator of the old covenant, the man who spoke with God as a friend, is gone, and the work is unfinished. That is the law's limitation set out as a story. Moses can bring a people to the threshold; he cannot bring them in. The charge passes to a man whose name is Yeshua, the LORD saves — and the letter to the Hebrews, having watched him lead the nation over the river, says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not later have spoken of another day (Heb. 4:8). He gets them into the land. He does not get them into the rest.

One imperative dominates the chapter. Three times God says be strong and courageous (vv. 6, 7, 9), and at the end the people say it back to Joshua (v. 18). Each time the ground of the courage is outside the man. Never 'be strong because you are capable' — always 'be strong, for you shall cause this people to inherit,' and 'be strong, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.' Courage here is commanded rather than felt, and it rests on an outcome that has already been decided.

The middle command is the one nobody expects. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is to keep a book: to have it in his mouth, meditate on it day and night, and turn from it neither to the right hand nor to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a plan is drawn or a sword is issued, the campaign is located in the soul of one man who reads.

The chapter ends in logistics and in loyalty. Provisions are packed, a deadline is set, and the tribes who already hold land east of the Jordan are told to leave it and fight for their brothers until everyone is home. Nobody in this book enters his rest alone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens on a grave. Moses is dead, and God's first word to his successor is not consolation but a marching order: arise, go over this Jordan (vv. 1-2). The land is spoken of as already handed over — I have given, past tense, before a foot has touched it (v. 3) — and its borders are sketched on a scale Israel will never occupy in Joshua's lifetime (v. 4). Then the promise everything else rests on: I will not leave you or forsake you (v. 5). Three times the command comes, and each has a different anchor: be strong, for you shall cause this people to inherit (v. 6); be strong and very courageous, and keep the Book (vv. 7-8); and at the last, have I not commanded you, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace arrives before duty and grounds it. The land is given in verse 3 and fought for from chapter 6 onwards, which is the pattern of the whole Bible: God announces the accomplished gift and then calls his people to walk into it. Israel does not fight to earn Canaan; they fight because it is already theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The middle command is the surprising one. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is not to storm a wall but to keep a book — to meditate on it day and night and not turn from it to the right hand or to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a single battle plan is drawn, the campaign is located in the soul of the man who reads.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant.'

The book is hinged on a grave. The greatest figure in Israel's history is gone — the man who stood in the sea-bed, who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend, who carried a whole nation on his back for forty years — and the work is not finished.

See how little time is allowed to pass. There is no interregnum, no committee, no anxious pause while the nation wonders what happens now. Moses dies and God speaks. There is no power vacuum in the kingdom of God, because the King does not die.

Read the two titles side by side, because the writer has put them there on purpose. Moses is the servant of the LORD, the highest description any man is given in the Old Testament. Joshua is Moses' assistant — the Hebrew word is used of the man who waits at table and carries his master's things.

That had been Joshua's job for decades. He held up Moses' arms on the hill while the battle went on below (Ex. 17:12). He stayed behind in the tent of meeting after Moses had gone back to the camp (Ex. 33:11). He stood with Caleb against ten frightened men and a nation ready to stone him (Num. 14:6-10). None of it made him famous. All of it made him ready.

His name matters more than the chapter says out loud. Joshua is Yeshua, the LORD saves — the name that would be given to a carpenter's son in Nazareth. The letter to the Hebrews makes the connection and then makes the limitation: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Heb. 4:8). This man will get them into the land. He will not get them into the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.'

God says it himself: Moses my servant is dead. The grief is not denied and not hurried. But the next word is arise, and it is the right word to a man who has been sitting down for thirty days of mourning.

There is a kind of loss that persuades a person the story has stopped. It has not. God's answer to a funeral, here, is a river and a date.

Then the tense in verse 3, which is the engine of the entire book. Not I will give you but I have given to you — before a single Israelite has crossed the water, the land is deeded over. Every battle in the next eleven chapters is fought on ground that already belongs to them.

That is the shape of the Christian life and not merely an Old Testament curiosity. Nobody fights sin in order to become a child of God; the fighting is what a child of God does about territory the Father has already put in his name.

Yet the gift has to be walked on. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread — the promise is title deed, and the foot is possession. Faith is the foot set down on the promise. A man may own a field for years and never once walk it, and there is a way of holding the promises of God that amounts to exactly that.

verseByVerse.quote: From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.'

The borders are drawn wide — south to the desert, north to Lebanon, east to the Euphrates, west to the Mediterranean. These are the boundaries God swore to Abraham (Gen. 15:18), and they are enormous.

They were never occupied. Chapter 13 opens with God telling an old man that very much land remains, and the fullest extent was reached only briefly, centuries later. The book is honest about the gap between what was promised and what was held, and the gap is not a failure in the promise; it is a signpost. Paul says the promise to Abraham was never really about a strip of coastline but that he should be heir of the world (Rom. 4:13), and the last chapters of the Bible show what that finally means.

Then verse 5, which is the bedrock the whole chapter is quarried out of: I will not leave you or forsake you.

It is worded with care. Not no one will attack you, but no man shall be able to stand before you. Not I will make it easy, but I will be with you. The promise is presence, not exemption.

The letter to the Hebrews lifts this sentence out of a general's commissioning and hands it to ordinary Christians worried about money, and the Greek piles up negatives in a way English cannot quite carry: he will never, never leave you; he will never, no never forsake you. The conclusion drawn is a matter of nerve — so we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear (Heb. 13:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.'

The first of three, and the first thing to see is that it is an imperative. Courage here is not a temperament some men are born with and others are not. It is commanded, which means it must be available to whoever is commanded to have it.

What makes it available is the clause attached to it. Joshua is not told to attempt the conquest and hope. He is told he shall cause this people to inherit, because God swore it to their fathers. The outcome is settled before the courage is required, and the courage is simply the appropriate response to a settled outcome.

Turn that over slowly, because most fear works the other way round. We wait to see how a thing will turn out and take our courage from the evidence. God reverses it: here is how it turns out, now be strong.

The oath reaches back through Moses to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — four hundred years and more. God's covenant memory does not shorten with time, and his word does not expire with the generation that first heard it. Joshua leads as the trustee of a promise much older than himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.'

The second command raises the temperature — very courageous — and then attaches it to something nobody expects. Not the walls of Jericho. The law.

The hardest thing asked of this man is to keep a book, and the reason is in the middle clause: do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left. Both directions are named because there are two ways off a road, and a leader in a long campaign will be pressed to take either — the shortcut on one side, the compromise on the other. Straight on is the harder walk.

'This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.'

Three organs are named, and the order is instructive: the mouth, then the mind, then the hands. The book is to be spoken, chewed over, and done.

The word for meditate is hagah, and it does not mean an empty mind. It is a low muttering, the noise of a man reading half-aloud to himself, the same word used of a lion over its prey and of the blessed man in Psalm 1. Meditation in the Bible is not emptying but gnawing.

A word about the prosperity, since the sentence is often quoted badly. The success promised is the success of this specific commission — getting a people into a land God had sworn to give them. It is not a formula for turning devotions into money. What the verse does teach, and teaches at the worst possible moment for it, is that the campaign will be won or lost long before the army forms up, in the quiet of one man's reading.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.'

The third time, and it opens with a question that lands like a hand on the shoulder: have I not commanded you? Joshua is not being encouraged. He is being reminded that he has orders.

This puts fear in an uncomfortable light. If courage is commanded, then settled fear is not merely a weakness of the nerves; it is a way of not taking God at his word. That should be said carefully — Scripture is full of frightened people who are handled gently, and God does not shout at the trembling. But it does mean that fear is answerable to something, and that a believer is allowed to argue with his own dread rather than obey it.

Then the ground, for the third time in nine verses: the LORD your God is with you. And the last two words are the best in the chapter. Not wherever I send you, which would cover obedient errands only, but wherever you go — including the places Joshua would choose badly, the valley at Ai after a bad decision, the day he believed the Gibeonites without asking.

The repetition is not God running out of things to say. It is a promise being hammered until it lodges. He knows what is in this man; he says it three times because it will need to be remembered three hundred.

The whole chapter narrows to those five words, and the New Testament does not improve on them so much as give them a face. A child is born and called Immanuel, God with us; and the last thing the risen Christ says on a hillside, to men about to be scattered across the world, is that he is with them always, to the end of the age (Matt. 1:23; 28:20). The promise made to one soldier at a river has turned out to be the standing arrangement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Charge to the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God said in private, Joshua says in public within a day. The officers go through the camp with an order about food and a deadline: provisions ready, the Jordan crossed in three days (vv. 10-11). Then he turns to the two and a half tribes who already have their land east of the river and holds them to a promise: wives, children and cattle stay, and every fighting man crosses over armed ahead of his brothers (vv. 12-14) — and stays there until the LORD gives rest to the brothers as he has to them (v. 15). The chapter closes with the people's pledge, their prayer that God would be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and the words of God given back to him by the men he commands (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: No tribe rests while its brothers are still fighting. The men of Reuben and Gad have their inheritance in hand and are sent to war for somebody else's, which is plainly what Paul means by bearing one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2).
verseByVerse.examples: The last sentence of the chapter is the people saying to Joshua exactly what God said to Joshua: only be strong and courageous (v. 18). Courage in this chapter is not generated. It is handed down from God to a leader and passed along from a people back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"'

The word spoken in private becomes an order in public, and the gap between them is nothing at all. God speaks; Joshua turns and mobilises the camp. Obedience that waits for better feelings has already begun to be disobedience.

The order itself is wonderfully unspiritual: prepare your provisions. Pack food. Faith in this book does not sit still waiting for God to do everything; it gets the bread ready for the journey it believes God will provide.

Both halves of the sentence are true at once and neither cancels the other. God has given the land, and the people are to pack lunches. Divine sovereignty and human effort are not rivals sharing out the work between them; the certainty of the outcome is what makes the preparation confident rather than anxious.

There is also a quiet change of era in that instruction. These are people who have eaten manna every morning for forty years and have never had to think about supplies. The manna will stop within a month of this order (5:12). God's provision does not become less; it stops being miraculous and starts being a harvest, which is how he feeds nearly everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.' Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you... Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you."'

Two and a half tribes had asked for the land east of the river and been granted it, on one condition (Num. 32). Joshua now collects on the condition, and the phrase he uses is remember the word.

Look at what is actually being asked. These men already have their inheritance. Their farms are allocated, their families are safe, their cattle are grazing. They are told to leave all of it and cross a river to fight a seven-year war for land that not one of them will ever own.

Verse 15 sets the term of service, and it is not a number of years: until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you. They go home when everyone else is home.

Here is the principle, and it is one the church needs about as badly as Israel did: my inheritance does not excuse me from my brother's battle. It is entirely possible to be settled, provided for, and spiritually comfortable while people you are bound to are still fighting for their lives, and this chapter treats that arrangement as a debt rather than a blessing. Paul says it in four words — bear one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2) — and this is what it looks like with boots on.

Something greater than Reuben is faintly visible here. One who was at rest, at home, and in possession of everything crossed over armed into a war he had no need to fight, for the sake of an inheritance that would belong to his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses! Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!"'

The pledge is total, and the sentence that matters most is the last one. Their loyalty to Joshua is real, but it is conditioned on something they cannot give him: only may the LORD your God be with you.

They have understood the arrangement exactly. Joshua's authority is borrowed. They will follow him not because he is impressive but because they believe God's hand is on him, and their one anxiety about the new leadership is not competence but presence.

'Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous.'

The clause about death is severe and it is not decoration. In a covenant nation crossing into a war, rebellion against God's appointed leader was rebellion against God, and the penalty says how seriously the arrangement was meant. It is one of the places where the Old Testament feels a long way from a Sunday morning, and the distance is real; the mediator now is not a man with an army but a Son with a cross, and the stakes have gone up rather than down.

Then the last four words of the chapter, and they are the same four God used. Only be strong and courageous. God said it to Joshua three times; now the people say it back to him.

That is how courage travels. It begins in the mouth of God, is spoken over one frightened man at a riverbank, and comes back to him out of the mouths of the people he is supposed to be leading. The LORD who will not leave or forsake gives his own words away, and they go round the camp all day and come home to him at evening, undiminished.

1.theology:
Grace before duty. The land is given in verse 3, past tense, before a foot has touched it; the fighting begins five chapters later. Israel does not battle in order to earn Canaan but because Canaan is already theirs. That order is never reversed anywhere in Scripture, and it is the whole difference between obedience and bargaining.

The sufficiency of God's presence. 'I will not leave you or forsake you' (v. 5) and 'the LORD your God is with you wherever you go' (v. 9) are the foundation of the book. What is promised is presence, not exemption — not that no one will attack, but that no one will stand. Hebrews lifts the sentence straight out of a soldier's commissioning and gives it to Christians anxious about money (Heb. 13:5-6), and it finds its face in Immanuel and in the last words of the risen Christ (Matt. 1:23; 28:20).

The Word as the source of strength. Meditation is commanded before strategy (v. 8), and the Hebrew hagah is not an emptied mind but a low muttering, the noise of a man reading half-aloud — the word used of the blessed man in Psalm 1. The promised 'good success' is the success of this commission, getting a people into a land God swore to give them, and not a formula for turning devotions into money.

No one rests alone. The eastern tribes hold their inheritance already and are sent to war for somebody else's, until the LORD gives rest to their brothers as he has to them (v. 15). Being settled is not a discharge from a brother's battle. It is the Old Testament in its plainest form of what Paul means by bearing one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2).
1.examples:
Then: A nation stood at a river with its leader newly buried, forty years of wilderness behind it and walled cities ahead. They had no army to match Canaan's, no experience of siege warfare, and no successor of Moses' stature — only a sentence spoken over them: I have given you the land. Everything that followed depended on whether that sentence was treated as a fact.

Now: The cure prescribed for fear here is not a change of circumstances, and God never offers Joshua one. It is a presence and a book. When the props go — a person dies, a job ends, a diagnosis lands — the promise held out is not that the river will be easier to cross but that the same God will be on both banks. Ask what you have actually been waiting for before you will be at peace. If the answer is a change in the facts, this chapter is offering something else, and calling it better.

2.title: Rahab and the Spies
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land."<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."<sup>4</sup>But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.<sup>5</sup>And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them."<sup>6</sup>But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof.<sup>7</sup>So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.<sup>8</sup>Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof<sup>9</sup>and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.<sup>10</sup>For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.<sup>11</sup>And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.<sup>12</sup>Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign<sup>13</sup>that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death."<sup>14</sup>And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! 2.overview:
The conquest of Canaan opens with a conversion, and the convert is a Canaanite prostitute. Two spies cross the Jordan and end up in the one house in Jericho where somebody is ready to believe. Rahab's trade and her nationality both marked her for destruction under the coming judgment, and she ends up named in the roll of faith (Heb. 11:31), held up by James as the pattern of a faith that acts (James 2:25), and written into the genealogy of Jesus between Salmon and Boaz (Matt. 1:5) — which makes her David's great-great-grandmother.

Her confession on the roof is the summit of the chapter: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (v. 11). She has no Scripture, no temple and no covenant. She has two items of news off the trade routes — a sea dried up forty years ago and two Amorite kings destroyed last season — and out of them she has arrived almost word for word at what Moses told Israel to lay to heart (Deut. 4:39).

One line in that same verse is usually misquoted, and it repays getting right. It is often said that Jericho melted in terror while Rahab melted in faith. She says our hearts melted. She was as frightened as everybody else in the city; what distinguished her was not steadier nerves but what she did with the same terror. Her neighbours locked the gate. She went upstairs and asked for mercy.

The chapter ends with a scouting report containing no military intelligence at all: truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands (v. 24). Set it beside the report the previous generation brought back from the same country, and the difference is not the walls but the men.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Spies Sheltered and Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua sends two men, quietly, to look at Jericho, and they end up lodging in the house of a prostitute called Rahab (v. 1). Word reaches the king within hours and his messengers arrive at her door with a direct demand: bring out the men (vv. 2-3). She lies to them, sends the search party off towards the Jordan fords, and the city gate is shut behind them (vv. 4-5, 7) — while the two spies lie flat on her roof under stalks of drying flax that she had laid out and moved before anyone knocked (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is out of sequence on purpose. The narrator tells us afterwards that she had already hidden them, which means the decision was made before the soldiers arrived. Rahab is not improvising under pressure; she had chosen a side while there was still time to choose the other one.
verseByVerse.examples: Her lie is the honest difficulty in the chapter and it should not be smoothed over. The New Testament twice commends her (Heb. 11:31; James 2:25) and commends the sheltering, never the deception; the older Reformed reading is that God accepted the imperfect service of a believer days old without endorsing every part of it. What is beyond dispute is the direction she moved: away from her king, towards a God she had only heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.'

Two men, sent secretly. The last time Israel sent spies into this country there were twelve of them and the report was made in public, and it cost the nation forty years (Num. 13). Joshua was one of the two who came back from that expedition telling the truth. He has learned something about how many people need to hear a scouting report.

Where they end up is the surprise. The narrator says it flatly, without euphemism and without a sneer: the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab.

There were practical reasons. A house where strangers came and went at night attracted no attention, and a house built into the city wall had a window on the outside. But the practical explanation runs out quickly, because of all the doors in Jericho, these two men walked through the only one behind which somebody was ready to believe.

Scripture never tidies her up. Both New Testament writers who mention her keep the word: Rahab the prostitute (Heb. 11:31; James 2:25). The genealogy of Jesus does the same, naming her without explanation between Salmon and Boaz (Matt. 1:5) — which makes this woman the great-great-grandmother of David and a direct ancestor of Christ. The conquest of Canaan opens not with a battle but with a conversion, and the convert is the least likely person in the city.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land." Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land." Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."'

The intelligence is good and it is fast. The spies have been in the city a matter of hours and the king already knows the house. Jericho is a frightened city watching its own gates, and frightened cities are observant.

The demand is issued directly to Rahab, and it puts her in an impossible position within a single sentence. Her king has sent men to her door. Handing over two foreigners costs her nothing and is what any loyal citizen would do. Refusing is treason, and treason inside a walled city under siege conditions has one penalty.

Weigh what she is being asked to weigh. On one side: her city, her king, her neighbours, her livelihood, and the roof over her family's heads. On the other: a rumour about a God she has never seen, whose people are camped across the river and have not yet won a single battle on this side of it.

Everyone in Jericho had the same information. The whole city had heard about the Red Sea. What separates Rahab from her king is not that she knew more; it is what she did in the ten seconds after the knock.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them." But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof. So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them... But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof.'

Read verse 6 carefully, because the narrator has deliberately told it out of order. He mentions the hiding after the interview at the door, and the verb is a pluperfect: she had brought them up, she had laid the flax in order.

So the decision was not made under interrogation. It was made earlier, when there was still time to make the other one. By the time the king's men were at the door, Rahab was not choosing sides; she was covering a choice already made. Faith that survives a crisis is nearly always faith that settled the question before the crisis arrived.

The flax is a domestic detail with weight in it. Stalks were spread on flat roofs to dry before being worked into linen; it was ordinary household work in progress, and she moved two grown men in under it without the soldiers seeing. She had thought about the roof.

'And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them."'

Then she lies, in detail, with a false direction and a note of urgency to get them moving. This is the honest difficulty of the chapter and it should not be hurried past.

What Scripture does with it is precise. Hebrews commends her faith and specifies what the faith did: she had given a friendly welcome to the spies (Heb. 11:31). James commends her works and specifies the same two: she received the messengers and sent them out another way (James 2:25). Neither commends the lie. The older Reformed reading, and it still seems the right one, is that God accepted the genuine service of a believer a few days old without approving every part of how she rendered it — which is a mercy the rest of us live on.

What is not in doubt is the direction. A woman with everything to lose put herself between the government and two enemy soldiers because she had concluded that their God was the real one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Confession on the Roof
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the spies can sleep, Rahab comes up to the roof and says the most remarkable thing anyone says in this book. She knows the LORD has given them the land, and that the country is melting (v. 9); she recites the evidence, the drying of the Red Sea forty years earlier and the recent destruction of Sihon and Og (v. 10); and she draws the conclusion — the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (v. 11). Then she asks for mercy, by oath, for her father, mother, brothers and sisters (vv. 12-13), and the spies pledge their own lives as the price of hers (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: She has no Scripture, no covenant, no priest and no temple. She has a rumour off the trade routes, forty years old at one end and a few months old at the other, and out of it she has reached a conclusion that half of Israel had failed to reach in the wilderness. Faith comes by hearing, and this is what it sounds like when the hearing is all there is.
verseByVerse.examples: The word she asks for in verse 12 is hesed — covenant kindness, the loyal love God shows his own people. A Canaanite asks a foreign God for the one thing he gives only to family, and the spies swear it to her: our life for yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you."'

She cannot wait until morning. The men are lying down to sleep and she climbs the stairs to say this.

Take the first three words on their own: I know. Not I suspect, not I have heard it said. And what she claims to know is precisely what God had said to Joshua a chapter earlier — that the land has been given. A Canaanite on a roof in Jericho and the LORD on the far bank of the Jordan are using the same sentence.

She also uses the covenant name. Not your god or the god of the Hebrews, which is how everyone else in the region speaks, but the LORD, the name given to Moses at the bush.

Her reading of the political situation is more accurate than her king's, and she gives the reason without flattering the men in front of her. It is not the Israelite army that has frightened the country; there is no army worth the name, only a nation of shepherds who have been walking in circles for forty years. What has fallen on Jericho is the fear of you, and behind that stands a promise made at the Red Sea that terror and dread would fall on the inhabitants of Canaan (Ex. 15:16). She is watching a song come true from the wrong side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction. And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction. And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath."'

Here is her evidence, and there are only two items on the list. One is forty years old and happened five hundred miles away. The other is recent and local. That is the whole of her theological library: two pieces of news carried up the trade routes by men who had no interest in converting anybody.

Now read the middle clause slowly, because it is regularly misquoted. It is usually said that Jericho melted in terror while Rahab melted in faith. The verse will not carry it. She says our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man. She is inside that description, not outside it.

She was as frightened as everybody else, and that settles what faith is and is not. Faith here is not a steadier nervous system or a braver temperament; it is what one melted heart did with its melting. Every other person in that city took the same terror and locked the gate. She took it upstairs and asked for mercy.

Then the summit of the chapter, and one of the great confessions in the Old Testament: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.

That is not a compliment paid to a strong local deity. It is a denial that there is anybody else, sky or soil, and it is almost word for word what Moses had told Israel to know and lay to heart (Deut. 4:39). She has never read Deuteronomy. Nobody taught her. She heard two stories about what God did to water and to kings, and arrived where the covenant nation was still being argued into.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death." And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death."'

Confession turns immediately into petition, which is the order faith always runs in. She has said who God is; now she asks him for something, and what she asks for is her family's lives.

The word behind deal kindly is hesed, and it is one of the great words of the Old Testament: loyal love, the settled kindness of someone who has bound himself by covenant. It is what God shows Israel. Rahab asks a foreign God for the thing he gives to family, and she asks it as a Canaanite with no claim on him whatever.

See how wide the request is. Father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all who belong to them. Days-old faith and her first instinct is to get everyone she is related to under the same roof as herself. Salvation in this chapter is never a private arrangement.

'And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."'

The oath is startling. Two Israelite soldiers put their own lives up as the security for a Canaanite prostitute's — if she dies, they die. There is no reason on earth why either man should have offered that.

A woman with no standing asked for mercy and was answered with a life laid down as the price of hers. She had heard two rumours and believed them, and it was enough to bring her inside a covenant she was born outside of. The whole gospel is in that room, some centuries early, and neither of the men saying it had any idea what they were prefiguring.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She lets them down the outside of the wall on a rope, because her house is built into the wall itself (v. 15), and gives them sound advice about where to hide and for how long (v. 16). The spies then set the terms of the rescue (vv. 17-20): the scarlet cord tied in the window, the whole family gathered inside, and a line drawn at the threshold — anyone who steps into the street carries his own blood on his own head (v. 19). Rahab agrees without asking for a single change, and verse 21 records that she tied the cord in the window that night.
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are precise, and precision is mercy here rather than meanness. There is one sign, one house, and one condition: be inside. Judgment is coming to that city, and the only question that will matter on the day is which side of a doorway a person is standing on.
verseByVerse.examples: The Hebrew word for the cord is tiqvah, from a root meaning to twist a rope — and the same word is the ordinary Hebrew for hope. What hung in that window for the next several weeks was, quite literally, a line of hope, and everyone in the house could see it from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall. And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall. And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."'

The detail about the wall is given because the story needs it twice — once now, for the escape, and once later, when that wall comes down.

Living in the wall was not a fashionable address. It was where the poor and the disreputable were housed, in the cavity between the outer and inner walls, and it tells you exactly where Rahab stood in Jericho's social order. The place that made her marginal is the place that makes her useful to God.

Her advice is worth attention because it is not pious. She does not tell the spies that God will protect them. She tells them to run the wrong way — into the hills, not towards the Jordan where the search has gone — and to sit still for three days until the patrols give up.

Faith in this chapter has a working head on it. She has calculated how long a search party stays out and where they will not look. Trusting God has never meant declining to think, and the newest believer in the story is the one giving competent operational advice to professionals.

verseByVerse.quote: The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household. Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head. But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household."'

The terms are three, and they are exact. A cord in the window. Everyone she wants saved, inside her house. And no one steps out.

The cord is the same rope she has just used to lower them down the wall. It is not a special object fetched for the purpose; it is the working equipment of the escape, left hanging where anyone could see it.

The Hebrew for it is tiqvah. The root means to twist strands into a line, and from that comes the ordinary Hebrew word for hope — a cord stretched out towards something still ahead. What hung in that window for the next several weeks was a line of hope, in the plainest sense the language allows.

'"Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head."'

The line is drawn at the doorway, and both sides of it are spelled out. Inside, the spies carry the responsibility. Outside, a man carries his own.

The pattern here is the Passover, and the parallel is structural rather than merely a matter of colour. On that night the sign went on the doorframe, the family was gathered indoors, the instruction was that no one should go out until morning, and the judgment passed over the marked house (Ex. 12:22-23). Every element recurs here. The text does not call the cord blood and it makes no comment on the Passover; what it gives is the shape, and the shape is unmistakable.

Salvation in this arrangement has an address. There is one house, one sign, and one requirement, which is to be inside. Grace is free and it is not vague, and a man who preferred the street was not less loved on the day the walls came down. He was simply not in the house.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.'

She asks for no amendment. Not one clause is negotiated, which is remarkable given that she is agreeing to hand her entire family's survival to two foreign soldiers on the strength of their word.

Then the last sentence of the verse, which is the point of the whole scene: she tied the cord in the window. That night. Not on the morning the trumpets started, not when the dust of an approaching army appeared on the road — immediately, while the spies were still climbing the hills.

Consider what the next few weeks were like. Jericho carries on. The market opens, the gate opens, the king's men patrol, and in a window in the wall there is a red rope that everybody can see and nobody understands. She has to leave it there. She has to persuade a household of relations, who have almost certainly told her she has lost her mind, to come indoors and stay indoors.

That is the position of every believer between the promise and its keeping: living under a sign in a city that is carrying on as normal, on the word of someone who has gone away and said he will come back.

Rahab of Jericho, whose name was a byword in her own street, hung a rope in a window on the strength of a God she had heard about twice, and it held. The wall she lived in fell flat and she walked out of it alive, and Israel's genealogies, which had no reason on earth to keep her, wrote her name into the line that runs to Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies do exactly what a Canaanite convert told them to do: into the hills, three days, until the search is called off (v. 22). Then they cross back and report to Joshua (v. 23), and the report is one sentence long and contains no military intelligence whatever: truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands, and all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Set that beside the report the last generation brought back from the same country — we are not able, the people are too strong, we seemed like grasshoppers (Num. 13:31-33). Same land, same walls, same giants. The difference is not the intelligence but the men carrying it.

verseByVerse.quote: They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing. Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing. Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.'

The spies do exactly what she told them. Two men on a mission from the leader of Israel take their operational orders from a Canaanite prostitute and are preserved by them.

The pursuers search all along the road to the Jordan and find nothing, which is the narrator noting quietly that her lie worked. He does not comment further, and neither should we; the chapter is not offering a rule about speech, it is telling us that the men got out.

They report all that had happened to them. That phrase is doing more work than it looks. What happened to them was not reconnaissance; the only thing recorded from three days inside enemy territory is a conversation on a roof. And this is why, when the city falls, Joshua knows the name of one household and sends the same two men to bring them out (6:22-25). The report saved her family a second time.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."'

The whole intelligence report is one sentence, and there is not a single military fact in it. No estimate of the walls, no count of the garrison, no assessment of the gate. Just a verdict about who owns the country and what the country is feeling.

It is also, word for word, what two other people in this story have already said. God said it to Joshua: I have given to you (1:3). Rahab said it on the roof: I know that the LORD has given you the land (2:9). Now the spies say it. The same sentence has travelled from God to a Canaanite to Israel's scouts, and nobody has changed a word of it.

Set the report beside the one from forty years earlier, because the writer means us to. Ten men came back from this same country saying: we are not able to go up, the people are stronger than we are, there are giants there, and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:31-33).

Same land. Same fortifications. The giants had not moved. What changed was not the size of the walls but the direction the men were looking, and a generation had died in the desert learning that lesson.

The LORD who dried a sea forty years before the news reached Jericho had been working on that city ever since, without an army, without a preacher, and without one word of written Scripture in it. By the time Israel arrived, the walls were still standing and the hearts behind them had already gone. He had a woman in that town before he had a soldier on that side of the river.

2.theology:
Grace reaching outside the covenant. Rahab has no claim of any kind. She is the wrong nationality, in the wrong trade, in a city under sentence, and she says out loud what God had said to Joshua, in almost his own words. Israel's own scouts end up quoting her. If the conquest were a story about a deserving nation dispossessing an undeserving one, this chapter would be unwritable — which is why it stands where it does, at the front.

A faith that acts, and a faith that is afraid. Rahab is the rare figure cited by Hebrews for faith (11:31) and by James for works (2:25), and both specify the same actions: she welcomed the messengers and sent them out another way. Neither commends the lie. And verse 11 keeps her honest company for everyone who has ever been frightened: her heart melted with the rest of the city. Faith here is not the absence of fear but what a melted heart does next.

The cord, the house, and the line at the door. The text never calls the scarlet cord blood and never mentions the Passover, so the connection should be made the way the text makes it — structurally. A marked house, a family gathered inside, an instruction that no one go out, a judgment passing over (Ex. 12:22-23): every element recurs. The Hebrew word for the cord is tiqvah, from a root meaning to twist a line, and it is also the ordinary word for hope. Salvation here has an address, and the only question on the day is which side of a doorway a person is standing on.

The conquest is God's before it is Israel's. No Israelite preached in Jericho, and no army had yet crossed the river. God had been working on that city for forty years with nothing but a rumour, and by the time the spies arrived the walls were still standing and the hearts behind them had already gone.
2.examples:
Then: A woman in a doomed city heard what God had done at a sea she had never seen, believed it, hid two enemy soldiers on her roof, and hung a red rope in her window. Then she lived under it for weeks, in a town going about its business, arguing her relatives indoors on the word of two men who had gone away and promised to come back.

Now: That is the position of every Christian between the promise and its keeping — living under a sign, in a world carrying on as normal, on the word of someone who has left and said he will return. Rahab's evidence was two pieces of news about what God had done in history; ours is a tomb that did not stay shut. Ask what you are actually waiting for before you will commit. She had less information than anyone reading this, and she tied the cord that night.

3.title: Crossing the Jordan
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.<sup>2</sup>At the end of three days the officers went through the camp<sup>3</sup>and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it.<sup>4</sup>Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."<sup>5</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you."<sup>6</sup>And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.<sup>8</sup>And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'"<sup>9</sup>And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan.<sup>12</sup>Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man.<sup>13</sup>And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."<sup>14</sup>So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people,<sup>15</sup>and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest),<sup>16</sup>the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.<sup>17</sup>Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
3.overview:
Forty years earlier an older generation walked out of Egypt through the Red Sea on dry ground. Now their children walk into Canaan through the Jordan on dry ground. The two crossings bracket the wilderness, and between them they say one thing: the God who brings people out is the God who brings them in.

The difference between the two is where the miracle sits. At the sea, the water divided and then Israel walked in. At the Jordan the water goes on flowing until the priests' feet are in it (v. 13), and the river is in spring flood at the time (v. 15) — the one season of the year when it cannot be waded. God removed every other explanation before he acted.

At the centre of it is the ark, going in front at half a mile's distance, with a reason attached that is the tenderest line in the chapter: for you have not passed this way before (v. 4). Nobody in the column knew the road. They were not asked to know it; they were asked to keep something in sight and walk after it.

The chapter ends with the priests standing in the middle of the riverbed and refusing to move until all the nation has crossed (v. 17). The throne of God goes down into the place where the water would be and stays there until the last straggler is over.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel breaks camp at Shittim, comes down to the Jordan and spends a night on the bank looking at the flood (v. 1). The order that goes through the camp is about direction: when the ark moves, follow it, and keep half a mile back, for you have not passed this way before (vv. 3-4). Joshua adds one instruction of his own before anything happens — consecrate yourselves, because tomorrow the LORD will do wonders (v. 5) — and then tells the priests to shoulder the ark and walk in front of the nation (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason given for following the ark is not that the ark is powerful but that the people are ignorant: you have not passed this way before. They were not asked to know the route. They were asked to keep something in sight.
verseByVerse.examples: The half-mile gap is the detail nobody would invent. It kept the ark visible to every person in a column of that size, and it kept everyone out of reach of it. Both are the point: near enough to follow, far enough to fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over. At the end of three days the officers went through the camp and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it. Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.'

They camp on the bank and spend a night looking at it. Nothing happens for a day. Whatever faith this generation had, it had to survive an evening within sight of a river it could not cross, in a camp full of children who had never seen God do anything on this scale.

'"As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it. Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."'

The instruction is simple and the reason attached to it is the tender thing in the chapter: for you have not passed this way before. Nobody in that column knew the road. There was no map of the riverbed, no memory of the country, no veteran to ask.

They are not told to work it out. They are told to keep something in sight and walk after it.

The distance is about half a mile, and it does two jobs at once. A gap that size keeps the ark visible to every family in a column of that length — the person at the back can see where God is going. And it keeps everyone well out of arm's reach of it. Near enough to follow, far enough to fear, which is the working arrangement of the whole Christian life.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.'

Before the river, a wash. Consecration meant the ordinary business of cleaning up and setting apart — garments washed, households put in order, a night spent deliberately rather than casually. It is startling as a piece of military preparation: the night before the crossing is given to holiness rather than to logistics.

Look at the tense Joshua uses. Not the LORD may do wonders but tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you. He puts a date on it in front of the whole nation, which is either faith or a career-ending mistake, and there is no indication he thought it a risk.

Then the priests pick up the ark and walk to the front. Stop there a moment. The ark normally lived behind a curtain in the middle of the camp, screened from every eye. Now the most protected object in Israel is carried out to the head of the column, towards the water, first.

God does not send his people anywhere he has not gone. The order of march in this chapter is the order of the gospel: the presence goes in front, and the people follow into ground nobody has walked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Living God Among You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Joshua that this day will begin his public exaltation, so that Israel may know that the God who was with Moses is with him (v. 7), and gives him the order for the priests: walk to the brink and then stand still in the river (v. 8). Joshua calls the people to hear before they see (v. 9), promises that the living God among them will without fail drive out seven named nations (v. 10), and names the one going in front as the Lord of all the earth (v. 11). Twelve men are appointed, one per tribe (v. 12), and the promise is made exact: when the soles of the priests' feet rest in the water, the Jordan will be cut off and stand in one heap (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The title in verses 11 and 13 settles the question the whole book raises. If the LORD is a local god of the desert, then the conquest is one tribe's land-grab. If he is the Lord of all the earth, Canaan was never anyone's but his, and he is disposing of his own property.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 is the difference from the Red Sea, stated in advance. There the water parted and then Israel walked in. Here the water parts when the feet are already in it. The promise is given first and the path appears second, and between the two there is a step that has to be taken in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'" And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God." And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites. Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan. Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man. And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you."'

The purpose clause is the important part. The exaltation is not for Joshua's benefit; it is so that they may know. A nation that had followed Moses through one body of water now has to learn to follow somebody else, and God gives them the evidence before he asks for the trust.

'"And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'"'

The order to the priests is not to cross. It is to walk into a flooding river and then stop. Standing still in a riverbed in spate, holding a gold box, while a nation files past behind you, is a harder assignment than running across.

'"Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you... Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan."'

Two titles are given, and neither is decoration. The living God is set against the gods of the country they are entering, who are carved and carried and cannot do anything — a contrast Isaiah will spend whole chapters on later. And the Lord of all the earth answers the question the conquest raises. If Israel's God is a regional deity, this is one tribe taking another tribe's land. If he owns the earth, then Canaan was never anyone else's to begin with, and he is disposing of his own property.

'"And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD... shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing."'

Here is the difference from the Red Sea, and it is stated in advance so that nobody can miss it. At the sea, Moses stretched out his hand, the water divided, and then Israel walked in. At the Jordan the water goes on flowing until there are feet in it.

The promise comes first and the path comes second, and between them is a step taken with nothing under it but a sentence. That is not a special demand made of priests. It is the ordinary shape of obedience: the evidence usually arrives after the foot goes down, and not before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The Waters Stood in a Heap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nation sets out, the priests reach the water, and the narrator drops in the sentence that makes the whole thing impossible: the Jordan is over its banks, because it is harvest time (vv. 14-15). Their feet are dipped in the brink, and sixteen miles upstream at a town called Adam the river stands and rises in a heap while everything below drains away to the Dead Sea (v. 16). The chapter ends with the priests standing on dry ground in the middle of the riverbed, not moving, until the whole nation has crossed (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is dated to the worst possible week of the year. Snowmelt off Hermon puts the Jordan over its banks every spring, and God brings his people to it then rather than in the autumn, when a child could have waded it.
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the picture the chapter is built to leave. The ark does not cross and wait on the far bank. It goes down into the riverbed and stays there, in the place where the water would be, until every last person is over.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people, and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest), the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.
