Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'...and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest).'

The narrator waits until this moment to mention the river's condition, and he puts it in brackets, which is the driest way of saying something enormous. It is spring. The snow is coming off Hermon. The Jordan is over its banks.

God brought them to the river in the one season of the year when it could not be waded. Six months later a child could have crossed it. The timing is not bad luck; it is the removal of every other explanation.

'the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.'

The geography is exact enough to check. The water stopped at a town sixteen miles upstream and piled up there; everything below that point ran on down to the Dead Sea and left the bed dry. This is not a story about a river politely dividing at the point of crossing. It is a story with a place name in it.

The phrase rose up in a heap is quoted, not coined. It is the line from the song Moses sang at the Red Sea (Ex. 15:8), and the generation crossing here had learned that song from parents who died in the desert. Their fathers sang about it. They walked on it.

'Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.'

Everything in the chapter has been building to this one sentence, and it repays being seen rather than summarised. The ark does not go across and wait on the far side. It goes down into the middle of the riverbed, into the place where the water would be, and stays.

It stays until all the nation has finished passing over. Not most. Not the strong ones and the quick ones. The priests hold that ground while the last of the flock straggles by — the old, the pregnant, the children, the man with the lame leg who has been at the back of this column since Egypt.

The throne of God went down into the riverbed and would not come up until everyone was across. Centuries later another Priest went down into the flood that this river only pictures, and stood in it, and did not come out until every last one the Father had given him was safely on the other side. Of those whom you gave me, he said, I have lost not one (John 18:9).

3.theology:
The presence goes first. The ark leads, and the reason given is the people's ignorance rather than their weakness: you have not passed this way before (v. 4). God never asks a people to know the route. He asks them to follow something they can see, into country nobody has walked.

The step before the sight. The promise is exact and it is conditional on a movement: when the soles of the priests' feet rest in the waters, the Jordan shall be cut off (v. 13). Had they waited on the bank for the river to open first, they would still be there. This is not a special rule for priests; it is the ordinary shape of obedience, where the evidence tends to arrive after the foot goes down.

The Lord of all the earth. The title is given twice at the crossing (vv. 11, 13) and it carries the moral weight of the whole conquest. A regional god handing one tribe another tribe's land is theft with a religious label. The Lord of all the earth disposing of his own property is something else entirely, and Joshua names it before a single Canaanite city falls.

The ark in the riverbed. The last verse of the chapter is the picture: the priests stand firm in the middle of the flood until all the nation has finished passing over (v. 17). They do not move for the strong or the quick; they hold the ground until the slowest child is across. A greater Priest went down into the flood this river only pictures and stayed in it on the same terms — of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (John 18:9).
3.examples:
Then: A nation stood on a bank in the barley harvest, looking at a river over its banks, with no boats and no bridge, and were told to follow a gold box into it. The men carrying the box had to get their feet wet before anything happened.

Now: Most of what God asks of a Christian is asked at that same spot, and the honest difficulty is not doubt about God's power but the order of events. We would like the river opened and then to walk. Consider what you are currently waiting for before you will obey — the finances to be clear, the outcome to be certain, the fear to lift. This chapter says the water moved when there were feet in it, and not one moment sooner.

4.title: The Twelve Memorial Stones
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man,<sup>3</sup>and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"<sup>4</sup>Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe.<sup>5</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel,<sup>6</sup>that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?'<sup>7</sup>then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever."<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste.<sup>11</sup>And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them.<sup>13</sup>About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho.<sup>14</sup>On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>16</sup>"Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan."<sup>17</sup>So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."<sup>18</sup>And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.<sup>19</sup>The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho.<sup>20</sup>And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.<sup>21</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?'<sup>22</sup>then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.'<sup>23</sup>For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over,<sup>24</sup>so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
4.overview:
The crossing is finished and God is not. Before a single soldier moves on Jericho, he stops the campaign to have a monument built: twelve stones lifted out of the middle of the riverbed, from the exact spot where the priests had stood, and carried to that night's camp. The first thing Israel does in the promised land is remember the last thing God did.

The reason is given twice, and both times it is a child. When your children ask in time to come, What do those stones mean? (vv. 6, 21). The stones teach nobody anything on their own; they provoke a question, and a parent answers it. God supplies the question and the answer in advance, and the faith of the next generation is put in the hands of ordinary adults who were there, talking to children who were not.

There are two sets of stones. The visible twelve go up at Gilgal where the whole camp walks past them daily. The other twelve Joshua sets up in the riverbed itself, where the flood covers them within the hour, and the narrator's aside is written by a man who knows they are invisible and knows they are there: they are there to this day (v. 9).

The chapter ends by naming the point of all of it, and it faces two ways: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and that Israel may fear the LORD forever (v. 24). One monument, a witness outward and worship inward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Twelve Stones Out of the Riverbed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nation is across and God speaks before anyone marches: take twelve men, one per tribe, and twelve stones out of the middle of the Jordan, from the exact spot where the priests' feet had stood (vv. 1-3). The stones are to be carried out and laid down at that night's camp, because a question is coming — when your children ask in time to come, what do those stones mean? (v. 6) — and the answer is supplied in advance (v. 7). The people obey (v. 8), and then a second set is mentioned: Joshua set up twelve stones in the riverbed itself, where the priests had stood (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The battle waits while a monument is built. Jericho is a few miles away and the first order after the miracle is not to advance but to remember, because God knows exactly how long a nation keeps a wonder without help.
verseByVerse.examples: The stones are quarried from one particular place: where the ark stood and the water did not come. Israel did not gather rocks from the bank. They carried out of the riverbed the ground that had been dry only because God was standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, "Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man, and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, "Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man, and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"'

The nation is across, the enemy city is five miles off, and God's first instruction is about rocks.

Nothing in the military situation calls for a pause. What calls for it is the human memory, and God is under no illusion about how it works. A wonder like this one will be vivid for a month, argued about for a year, and gone in a generation unless something is done about it, so the first act of Israel in the promised land is to build a monument.

Look at where the stones come from. Not the bank, which would have been easier, but from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly — out of the middle of the riverbed, from the patch of ground that was dry for one reason only.

Twelve men are named, one for each tribe, and each carries his own stone on his own shoulder. The memorial could have been built by a work party in an hour. Instead every tribe in Israel has a man with a wet stone on his back, and nobody in the nation can look at that heap later and say it was somebody else's deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe. And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever." And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there. And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"...that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD."'

The purpose of the monument is stated, and it is not commemoration. It is a conversation that has not happened yet.

God is anticipating a child at Gilgal, some years from now, who was not born when this happened, playing near a pile of stones and asking his father what they are for. The entire arrangement exists for that moment. The stones do not teach anybody anything; they provoke a question, and a parent answers it.

So God has arranged for the faith of the next generation to be carried by ordinary adults who were there, talking to children who were not. He gives them the question in advance and he gives them the answer with it, so that nobody can plead that he was not ready. Moses had made the same provision in the same words — when your son asks you in time to come, What is the meaning of the testimonies? (Deut. 6:20).

'And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.'

Then a second set of stones, and this one nobody will ever see again. Joshua plants twelve in the riverbed itself, at the spot where the ark had stood, and within the hour the flood closes over them.

They are useless as a monument. No child will ask about them; no traveller will point them out. Twelve stones stand under a running river with nobody but God to look at them, and the narrator's aside — they are there to this day — is written by a man who knows they are invisible and knows they are there.

Not every witness to what God has done is public. Most of the evidence in most Christian lives is submerged: prayers answered that nobody else heard about, sins killed that nobody knew were alive, a marriage still standing for reasons that were never explained to anyone. The water goes back over it and it is still there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests hold their position in the riverbed until everything is finished, and the people cross in haste (v. 10). Only when the last of them is over does the ark come up behind them (v. 11). The eastern tribes cross armed at the head of the column, as they promised in chapter 1 — about forty thousand men (vv. 12-13). Verse 14 records the promise of 3:7 coming true: that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel. Then the priests are called up out of the river, and the moment the soles of their feet touch dry land the Jordan comes back and runs over its banks as before (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Read the order of march twice. God's presence goes in FRONT into the water (3:6) and comes out LAST behind the people (v. 11). The same ark that led them in stayed to see them out, so that at no point in the crossing was anybody the last one in the river.
verseByVerse.examples: The timing in verse 18 is the proof. The flood returns not gradually but at the instant the priests' soles clear the bed — not an ebb that happened to coincide with a crossing, but a thing that started and stopped on command.

verseByVerse.quote: For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste. And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people. The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho. On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people... The people passed over in haste. And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people.'

Two small phrases are doing quiet work here.

The first is in haste. They did not stroll. There were walls of water standing in a heap somewhere upstream and every family in Israel was walking across a riverbed as fast as it could carry the children. The event was glorious and it was also frightening, and the writer lets both stand.

The second is the order in verse 11. The ark went into the water first, ahead of everyone (3:6), and it comes out last, behind everyone. The presence of God led them in and then stood between them and the river until the last of them was clear. Nobody in that nation was ever the last one in the water.

'The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho.'

The promise made in chapter 1 is kept in chapter 4. Forty thousand men from the tribes who already had their land walk past their own farms and cross a river to fight for somebody else's. It cost them years.

'On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.'

What God said he would begin (3:7) he did. And the verb is the one to notice: the LORD exalted Joshua. He did not exalt himself, campaign for it, or manage his reputation. He carried out an instruction about a river and God did the rest, which is the arrangement Peter describes when he tells frightened church leaders to humble themselves under God's mighty hand so that he may exalt them at the proper time (1 Pet. 5:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan." So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan." And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD said to Joshua, "Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan." So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."'

Follow the chain of command. God speaks to Joshua; Joshua repeats it to the priests, in almost the same words, adding nothing. It is a small picture of what leadership in this book actually is.

'And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.'

The timing settles the question. The river does not subside back over hours. The instant the soles of the last men clear the bed, the water is back and over the banks.

It began when feet went in (3:15) and it ended when feet came out. Anyone downstream that afternoon watching the Jordan run dry and then, hours later, come back in a wall, was watching something switched on and off. Whatever else it was, it was not the river having a quiet week.

Then look at what the returning flood does to the way home. Behind them is a river in spate that no one is crossing back over. The wilderness is now unreachable. Every complaint about Egypt, every proposal to go back, every option but forward has just been closed by God himself — and he waited to close it until every last one of them was safely on the other side.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — What Do These Stones Mean?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel comes up out of the river on the tenth day of the first month and camps at Gilgal, on Jericho's eastern border, and there the stones are set up (vv. 19-20). Joshua puts the children's question a second time and gives the answer again, and this time he adds something: they are to be told about the Jordan and the Red Sea, the river their parents crossed and the sea their grandparents crossed (vv. 21-23). Verse 24 gives the purpose of all of it, and it looks in two directions at once — outward, that all the peoples of the earth may know the hand of the LORD is mighty, and inward, that Israel may fear the LORD forever.
verseByVerse.theology: The date is not decoration. The tenth day of the first month is the day Israel was told to take the Passover lamb into the house in Egypt (Ex. 12:3), forty years earlier to the day. They enter the land on the anniversary of the night they were bought out of it, and they will keep the Passover four days later (5:10).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 keeps the whole event from turning inward. The Jordan was dried for Israel and it was dried so that the nations would hear about it — which is exactly what had already happened to one household in Jericho two chapters earlier, on much older news (2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.'

The date is given, and it is not a filing detail.

The tenth day of the first month is the day Israel was told, in Egypt, to take a lamb into the house and keep it until the fourteenth (Ex. 12:3). That was the beginning of the exodus: a lamb chosen, four days before the blood went on the doorframes.

Forty years later to the day, the same nation walks into the land. The exit and the entrance share an anniversary. And four days after this, on the fourteenth, they will keep the Passover in Canaan for the first time (5:10) — so the calendar of their slavery becomes the calendar of their inheritance, without a single date being changed.

They camp at Gilgal, on Jericho's doorstep, and the stones go up there. Not on a hilltop and not at a shrine, but in the middle of the camp, where the washing is done and the children play and everyone walks past them a dozen times a day.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?' then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.' For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?' then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground. For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over.'"'

The question comes round a second time, and Joshua adds something to the answer he gave in verse 7. Now the Red Sea is in it.

Watch the pronouns, because they carry the whole point. The Jordan was dried up for you; the Red Sea was dried up for us. Joshua is one of two men alive who was at both. He stands in front of a nation of people who were not born when the sea opened and he puts the two events in one sentence, so that no child grows up thinking God did something for his grandparents and something else, unrelated, for him.

That is how a family teaches faith: not by handing on a doctrine but by handing on a story with the child's own name in it. The people who came out and the people who came in are one people, and the God who did the one did the other.

'"...so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."'

The last verse turns the monument outward before it turns it inward.

First: that all the peoples of the earth may know. The river was not dried up simply to get Israel across; there were shorter ways to do that. It was dried up so that the news would travel, which is exactly what had already happened in Jericho, where a woman had heard about the Red Sea from strangers and staked her family on it (2:10).

Second: that you may fear the LORD your God forever. The right response to a memorial is not nostalgia. Twelve stones in a camp are not there to make anyone wistful about the good old days at the river; they are there to produce awe, permanently.

The hand that stopped a flooded river at a town sixteen miles upstream, and held it, and let it go again at the exact second the last priest stepped out, is mighty. He arranged the whole thing so that a child not yet born would ask a question, and so that a stranger in a foreign country would hear the story and be saved by it. Two rivers, forty years apart, and one hand over both.

4.theology:
Memory is commanded, not assumed. God halts a military campaign to build a heap of stones, because he knows how long a nation keeps a wonder without help. The instinct runs through the whole Bible and lands on a table in an upper room: do this in remembrance of me (1 Cor. 11:24-25). Christian memory is not nostalgia; it is a discipline with physical objects attached — water, bread, wine, stones.

Faith is handed on in conversations. The arrangement here puts the next generation's faith in the hands of parents answering questions. Moses had made the identical provision in identical words (Deut. 6:20), and the psalmist describes the chain running four generations deep so that children not yet born would set their hope in God (Ps. 78:4-7). Faith is always one silent generation from disappearing.

One work, two waters. Joshua deliberately puts the Red Sea and the Jordan in the same sentence when he tells the children what happened (v. 23), and he changes the pronoun as he goes: dried up for you, dried up for us. The God who brings people out of slavery and the God who brings them into the inheritance are not two Gods with two projects. The date makes the same point — they enter the land on the anniversary of the day the Passover lamb was chosen in Egypt (v. 19; Ex. 12:3).

Salvation aimed at the nations. The stated purpose reaches further than Israel: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty (v. 24). This is not a private deliverance with a religious souvenir. It is a public act meant to travel — and it had already travelled, into a house in Jericho, where a woman heard about the Red Sea and believed (2:10).
4.examples:
Then: Twelve men carried wet stones on their shoulders out of a riverbed and built a heap in the middle of a camp, where children would play round it and eventually ask what it was for. That question, and the answer given to it beside a cooking fire, was how the story survived.

Now: The question still has to be answered by somebody who was there. Consider what your own children, or the younger believers around you, actually know about what God has done — not the doctrine, which they may have in good order, but the deeds: what he did at the cross, and what he has done in your house. Most Christians have a Gilgal they have never described to anyone. The stones are no use standing in silence.

5.title: Circumcision, Passover, and the Commander of the LORD's Army
5.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.<sup>4</sup>And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised.<sup>6</sup>For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>7</sup>So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.<sup>8</sup>When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.<sup>10</sup>While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho.<sup>11</sup>And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.<sup>12</sup>And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.<sup>13</sup>When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"<sup>14</sup>And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?"<sup>15</sup>And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
5.overview:
Israel is in the land, and God's first command is not a battle plan but a knife. Every fighting man is to be circumcised — because the covenant sign had lapsed for forty years, and a whole generation had grown up belonging to God by promise while carrying nothing in their bodies to say so (vv. 2-7).

What that costs is easy to miss and Israel could not have missed it. Jericho is five miles away, and an army recovering from circumcision cannot fight; their own family history says exactly what happens next, because Simeon and Levi destroyed Shechem on the third day, when its men were sore (Gen. 34:25). So verse 1 is placed where it is on purpose: at the very week Israel becomes helpless, every king in Canaan loses his nerve. God empties the enemy of courage on the same morning he empties his own army of strength.

Then the reproach of Egypt is rolled away and the place is named Gilgal, from the verb to roll (v. 9). Israel keeps the Passover in the land for the first time (v. 10), eats grain from fields it never planted (v. 11), and the next morning the manna is not there (v. 12). Forty years end in one sentence — and the order of it is the kindness: they eat the new food first, and the old supply stops the day after.

The chapter ends outside the walls with a man holding a drawn sword. Joshua asks whether he is friend or enemy and is told No — neither. God has not come to take sides; he has come to take command. And no orders about Jericho are given here at all. They wait until the general is face down with his shoes off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Knife Before the Battle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of Canaan hear about the Jordan and their hearts melt (v. 1) — the same words Rahab used two chapters earlier. Then God's first command in the land, and it is not a battle plan: make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time (v. 2). The reason is given at length (vv. 4-7): every man who came out of Egypt had died in the wilderness, and their sons, born on the way, had never received the covenant sign at all. The whole nation is circumcised and then lies still in the camp until it can walk again (v. 8), and God gives the place its name: today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The sign of the covenant had lapsed for forty years. A generation grew up belonging to God by promise and carrying nothing in their bodies to say so, and the first thing God does with them in the land is put the mark back on.
verseByVerse.examples: The timing of verse 1 is the providence in the chapter. Canaan's kings are paralysed at precisely the week Israel is least able to fight anybody. God empties the enemy of nerve on the same day he empties his own army of strength.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.'

The wording is not new. It is Rahab's, word for word, from her roof three chapters ago: their hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man (2:11). What she reported about her own city has now happened to every king in the country.

Israel has not fought anybody. There has been no battle, no siege, no demonstration of arms — only a river that behaved oddly for an afternoon, and the news travelling faster than the army.

Now hold this verse against what God commands in the next one, because the two belong together. Within days Israel will circumcise every fighting man in the nation and lie helpless in the camp. The one week in which Israel could have been wiped out by a determined attack is the exact week in which no king in Canaan can bring himself to move.

God empties the enemy of nerve on the same morning he empties his own army of strength. That is not luck and it is not tidy timing; it is how this book says the conquest was won.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time." So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth. And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt. Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised. For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey. So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time." So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.'

God's first order inside the promised land is for a knife, not a sword.

Flint, not metal, and Israel had metal. Circumcision was done with a stone blade because that is how it had always been done, back to Abraham; the same word appears when Zipporah takes a flint and circumcises her son on the road (Ex. 4:25). This is deliberately the old rite, performed the old way.

'And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness... For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD.'

The explanation is long and the writer takes his time over it, because it is a painful piece of history. For forty years the covenant sign was not administered. A whole generation grew up belonging to God by promise and carrying nothing in their bodies to say so.

The text does not soften why. Their fathers had not obeyed, God swore they would not see the land, and the sign lapsed with them. Israel spent four decades in a kind of covenant suspension — still fed with manna every morning, still led by the pillar, and unmarked.

Then think about what this order actually costs, standing where they are standing. Jericho is five miles away. Every fighting man in the nation is about to be put out of action for days.

Israel knew exactly what that meant, because it is in their own family history. When Shechem's men were circumcised, Simeon and Levi came in on the third day, when they were sore, and killed every male in the city (Gen. 34:25). That is the precedent. God is telling this army to do to itself, in sight of an enemy stronghold, the very thing that once left a whole town defenceless.

That settles what the conquest is going to rest on. Not readiness. God will have a people marked as his before he has a people fit to fight, and if that leaves them lying in a field within sight of a walled city for three days, he is apparently content with the arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.'

They stay put until they are healed. It is one of the quietest sentences in the book and one of the most exposed: an entire army lying still in enemy country, waiting to be able to walk.

Then God speaks, and what he says is about shame rather than strength. Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.

The reproach of Egypt is the whole weight of what they had been. Slaves. A people whose God had, on the evidence, brought them out into a desert and left them there for forty years to die, which is precisely the taunt Moses had twice warned God the Egyptians would make (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16). Every year in the wilderness had made the sneer look more reasonable.

The place is named Gilgal, from a verb meaning to roll. The picture is of a weight the size of a millstone rolled off a nation, and it is done in one day, and it is done by God — I have rolled it away. Israel did not answer the taunt. They were not required to.

Whether the writer of the Gospels had this in mind when he described a stone rolled back from a tomb is not something the text argues, and it should not be pressed. But the pattern is the same in both places, and it is the pattern of everything God does about shame: the people concerned are lying still, unable to do anything at all, and the weight is moved from outside by somebody else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Passover, and the Last Morning of Manna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four days after crossing, on the fourteenth of the month, Israel keeps the Passover on the plains of Jericho (v. 10) — the first one ever kept inside the land. The next day they eat the produce of the country, unleavened cakes and parched grain from fields they never planted (v. 11). And then one sentence closes forty years: the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land, and there was no longer manna for the people of Israel (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The order in verse 12 is exact and it is kind. They eat the new food first, and the old supply stops the morning after. God did not withdraw the manna and then tell them to trust him for a harvest; the harvest was in their hands before the miracle ended.
verseByVerse.examples: For forty years every Israelite woke up and found breakfast on the ground. Then one morning there was nothing there, and nothing was wrong. The provision had not failed; it had changed form, because the promise it was covering had arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho. And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain. And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho.'

Count the days. They came up out of the Jordan on the tenth (4:19), the day the lamb was chosen in Egypt. Now it is the fourteenth, the night the lamb was killed. The first four days of Israel's life in the promised land follow the Passover calendar exactly, and this is the first Passover ever kept inside the land.

Forty years of these meals had been eaten in tents in a desert, remembering a rescue and waiting for a country. This one is eaten in the country, in sight of the first city they will have to take.

'And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.'

Parched grain is the plainest food in the Bible: heads of new barley held over a fire until the husks burn off, then eaten in the hand. Nothing about it is a feast. What makes it remarkable is whose field it came out of — grain they did not sow, in a land they had owned for less than a week, exactly as Moses had promised them: houses they did not build, vineyards they did not plant (Deut. 6:10-11).

'And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.'

One sentence ends forty years. Every adult in that camp had woken up every morning of his life and found breakfast lying on the ground. Then one morning there was nothing there.

Read the order carefully, because it is the mercy in the verse. They eat the produce first, and the manna stops the day after. God did not withdraw the old provision and then invite them to trust him for a harvest. The harvest was in their hands before the miracle ended.

Hold onto that when a form of God's care that a person has leaned on for years comes to a stop — a job, a health, a person, a season of unusual nearness in prayer. The manna ending was not the withdrawal of God's kindness. It was the arrival of what the manna had been standing in for.

It was always standing in for something. Jesus, arguing with a crowd who wanted the bread trick repeated, said their fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and died, and that he himself was the bread that came down from heaven, which a man may eat and live for ever (John 6:49-51). The manna stopped at Gilgal because the land had come. It stopped for good because the true bread had.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — The Commander of the LORD's Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua is out looking at Jericho when he sees a man with a drawn sword and challenges him: are you for us, or for our adversaries (v. 13)? The answer is a refusal of the question — No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD — and Joshua goes face down on the ground and asks for orders (v. 14). What he is given is not a battle plan but an instruction about his shoes: take off your sandals, the place where you are standing is holy (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua offers two options and is told neither. God does not join sides in this book; he takes command of it. The question a person brings to God about a conflict is almost always whether God is with him, and it is almost always the wrong way round.
verseByVerse.examples: No orders for Jericho are given here. They come in the next chapter. This encounter exists to settle who is in charge before anything is planned, and it ends with the commanding general of Israel lying in the dirt with his shoes off.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?" And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"'

Joshua is doing what a commander does the night before an assault: walking the ground, looking at the walls. And a man is standing there with his sword already out of the scabbard.

See that Joshua walks up to him. A drawn sword and an unknown man in the dark outside an enemy city, and Israel's general goes over and challenges him. Then he asks the only question a soldier can think to ask: whose side are you on?

It is a completely reasonable question and it is the wrong one, and the answer says so in a single syllable.

'And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come."'

No. Not I am for you, and not I am for them. Joshua has offered two options and been told that neither applies.

God does not enlist. He commands. The question that this man's answer refuses is the question most of us bring to God about anything difficult — is he on my side in this argument, this decision, this dispute — and the refusal is not unkind. It is a promotion of the whole subject. The right question was never whether God had joined Israel's war. It was whether Israel had joined his.

'And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?"'

Joshua's response tells us who this is. He worships, and he is not stopped. That is the decisive detail: elsewhere in Scripture, when a man falls at the feet of an angel, the angel will not have it — you must not do that; worship God (Rev. 22:8-9). This one receives it.

'And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.'

Then the sentence that removes all doubt, because Israel had heard it before. It is what was said out of a burning bush to a shepherd on the far side of a desert, in almost the same words (Ex. 3:5). The same voice that commissioned Moses is standing outside Jericho.

The ground is not holy because of the soil. It is a field on the edge of a Canaanite city and there is nothing sacred about it. It is holy because of who is standing on it, which is the only thing that has ever made any ground holy.

No orders are given at all. The chapter ends without a single instruction about Jericho; those come in the morning. This entire encounter exists to settle one question before any planning begins, and it is settled with the commanding general of Israel lying in the dirt with his shoes in his hand.

The Captain of the LORD's host came to Jericho with his sword already drawn, and he did not come to be recruited. He came to take the field. Every wall in the country was already his, and the man he was speaking to would not swing a sword for seven days.

5.theology:
Consecration before conquest. The order of this chapter is the argument of the book. Circumcision, then Passover, then worship on holy ground, and only then a battle. God will have a people marked as his before he has a people fit to fight, and he is willing to leave them lying in a field within sight of a walled city for three days to get it. The conquest never rested on Israel's readiness.

The reproach rolled away. The taunt of Egypt was that this God had brought a nation out into a desert to die — the exact sneer Moses twice warned God about (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16) — and forty years of wandering had made it look reasonable. It is removed in a day, by God, while the people concerned are lying still and unable to walk. Israel never answered the accusation. They were not asked to.

When the manna stops. The provision that had defined a generation ends the morning after the first harvest is eaten (v. 12), and nothing is wrong. God does not withdraw an old kindness and then ask for trust about a new one; the grain was in their hands before the miracle ceased. And the manna was always standing in for something — your fathers ate the manna and died, Jesus told a crowd who wanted it repeated, and then offered himself as the bread from heaven that a man may eat and live for ever (John 6:49-51).

He does not take sides. Joshua's question assumes two armies and asks which one this man belongs to. The answer is No. The commander of the LORD's army accepts worship, which an angel refuses (Rev. 22:8-9), and repeats the words spoken from the burning bush (Ex. 3:5) — and he gives no instructions at all. The encounter exists to settle who is in charge, which is the question every believer gets the wrong way round: not whether God is on our side, but whether we have joined his.
5.examples:
Then: An army in enemy country put down its swords, picked up flint knives, and made itself unable to fight for three days, five miles from a walled city. Then it ate a memorial meal, watched forty years of miraculous breakfast come to an end, and its general finished the week lying face down in a field with his shoes off.

Now: The question Joshua asked is the one nearly everybody brings to God in a conflict, and it repays catching yourself at it. Are you for me in this — this argument, this church split, this decision I have already made? The answer given outside Jericho was a flat No, followed by an invitation to ask a better question: what does my lord say to his servant? Nothing was planned until that had been sorted out.

6.title: The Fall of Jericho
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.<sup>3</sup>You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days.<sup>4</sup>Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.<sup>5</sup>And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."<sup>8</sup>And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them.<sup>9</sup>The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>10</sup>But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout."<sup>11</sup>So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>14</sup>And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.<sup>15</sup>On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times.<sup>16</sup>And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.<sup>17</sup>And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.<sup>18</sup>But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it.<sup>19</sup>But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city.<sup>21</sup>Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.<sup>22</sup>But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her."<sup>23</sup>So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.<sup>26</sup>Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates."<sup>27</sup>So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
6.overview:
Jericho was a fortress and Israel was given a plan with no military content in it at all: walk round the city once a day for six days, and on the seventh walk round seven times, blow, and shout. No ladders, no ram, no tunnel, no assault on the gate. The one thing this method guarantees is that when the wall comes down, nobody will be able to explain how — which is not a side effect but the object of the exercise (1 Cor. 1:27-29).

The horns repay identifying. They are rams' horns, yobel, the jubilee trumpet blown in the fiftieth year to announce that debts were cancelled and slaves went home (Lev. 25:9-10). What went round Jericho for seven days was not the sound of an army arriving but the sound Israel associated with release — and inside the city there was one woman with a red rope in her window for whom that is precisely what it turned out to mean.

Most of the week is disposed of in seven words: so they did for six days (v. 14). Nothing improved as it went on. The wall stood exactly where it had stood, the defenders grew less frightened, and the only order was to come back tomorrow. That is the part of this chapter most Christians actually live in; the seventh day gets preached, and the six days are where the years go.

Then the wall falls flat, the city is devoted to destruction, and one household walks out alive. The hardest question in the book is asked by verse 21 and it is faced squarely in the commentary on verses 17-19 rather than managed. What can be said here is that the writer sets the judgment and the rescue side by side on purpose, and gives the last word to a Canaanite prostitute who is still living in Israel when he writes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Plan No General Would Write
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jericho is sealed, inside and outside, and nobody is going in or out (v. 1). God's first word about it is in the past tense: I have given Jericho into your hand, king and fighting men included (v. 2). Then the instructions, which no military academy would pass: walk round the city once a day for six days, seven priests with seven rams' horns going ahead of the ark (vv. 3-4), and on the seventh day walk round seven times, blow, and shout — and the wall will fall down flat (v. 5). Joshua relays it exactly as given, with no additions and no siege equipment (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The victory is announced before the first step is taken, which is the grammar of this whole book: God gives, and faith walks into what has been given. What is asked of Israel at Jericho is not strength, courage or tactics. It is a week of doing something that cannot possibly work.
verseByVerse.examples: The horns are rams' horns, and the Hebrew word behind them, yobel, is the jubilee trumpet — the sound blown on the Day of Atonement in the fiftieth year to announce that debts were cancelled and slaves went free (Lev. 25:9). Jericho does not fall to a war-trumpet. It falls to the noise that means release.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in. And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in. And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor."'

Two sentences, and they describe the same city from two sides.

From the ground, Jericho is sealed. The phrase is emphatic and slightly odd — shut up inside and outside — and it means total lockdown: the gates barred, nobody trading, nobody farming, the whole population inside the walls waiting. That is a city doing the only sensible thing available to it.

From heaven, it is already handed over. See, I have given. Past tense, as at 1:3, before a single Israelite has moved. And God specifies what is included in the transfer: the king, and the mighty men of valour. The best troops in the city are listed on the delivery note.

The two verses are not in tension; the second is a comment on the first. Everything Jericho has done to protect itself is real and competent, and it is being described as a completed transaction in somebody else's favour. Walls keep out armies. They have never once kept out God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days. Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets. And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days. Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets."'

Here is the plan, and no army in history has been given one like it. Walk round. Do it again tomorrow. And the day after. Bring no ladders, dig no tunnels, build no ramp, and do not attempt the gate.

The one thing this strategy guarantees is that when the city falls, nobody will be able to explain how. That is not a side effect; it is the object. Paul, writing about God's habit of choosing what looks foolish in order to shame the wise, says the reason in so many words: so that no human being might boast in the presence of God (1 Cor. 1:27-29). Jericho is that sentence acted out over a week.

Count the sevens: seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, seven circuits on the last one. The number that runs through the whole Bible for completion is stamped over every part of this, which is the writer's way of saying that nothing here is improvised.

Look at what the priests are carrying, because the detail is easy to skate over. These are not war trumpets. The Hebrew is yobel — the ram's horn of the jubilee, the instrument blown on the Day of Atonement in the fiftieth year to announce that debts were cancelled, land went back to its families, and slaves went home (Lev. 25:9-10).

So the sound that goes round Jericho for seven days is not the sound of an army coming. It is the sound Israel associated with release. A city under sentence hears, for a week, the noise that means somebody somewhere is being set free — and inside that city there is a woman with a red rope in her window for whom that is exactly what it means.

'"And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."'

The outcome is told in advance, in detail, including the manner: not breached but flattened, so that every man walks in straight ahead of himself rather than funnelling through a gap. God describes the ruin of the wall before the first lap.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD." And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD." And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."'

Joshua passes the order on and changes nothing.

That is more remarkable than it looks. He is a professional soldier who has been fighting since Rephidim, and he has just been handed a plan with no military content whatsoever. There is no record of a question, no suggestion of a contingency, no quiet arrangement of a battering ram at the back of the column in case the walking does not work.

It helps to remember what happened at the end of the last chapter. A man with a drawn sword told him that the ground he was on was holy, and Joshua took his shoes off. A general who has been face down in a field is not in a hurry to improve on the instructions.

The shape of the column matters: armed men first, then priests with horns, then the ark, then the rear guard. The soldiers are at the front and the back, and the ark is in the middle, which is exactly where it was in the riverbed. The presence of God is not out of harm's way behind the lines. It is in the centre of the formation, going round a hostile city at walking pace, in full view of the walls, thirteen times over a week.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The procession forms up in the order given: armed men, then the seven trumpets, then the ark, then a rear guard, with the horns sounding continually (vv. 8-9). And one extra command from Joshua that is not in God's instructions — total silence. Not a shout, not a word out of any mouth, until the day he says (v. 10). Then they walk round once and go back to camp for the night (v. 11). The same the next day (vv. 12-13). And verse 14 disposes of most of the week in seven words: so they did for six days.
verseByVerse.theology: Six days of obedience with no result whatever. The wall is exactly as high on Friday evening as it was on Sunday morning, and the only instruction is to come back tomorrow and do it again.
verseByVerse.examples: The silence is the hardest part of the order and it is Joshua's own addition. An army marching in front of a hostile city, in range of everything the defenders can shout down at them, and not one man is permitted to answer back for six days.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them. The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually. But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout." So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them. The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.'

The horns do not stop. That phrase — the trumpets blew continually — is repeated so often in this chapter that the reader begins to hear it. A whole week of noise going round a city that cannot see the point of it.

'But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout."'

Then the order that is not in God's instructions at all. Joshua adds it himself, and it is the hardest part of the week: absolute silence. Not a shout, not a war cry, not a word out of anybody's mouth.

Consider what that costs. Thousands of men walking in slow single file within earshot of a wall lined with defenders, who have nothing to do all day but look down at them. Whatever was being shouted from those ramparts — and something was — not one Israelite was permitted to answer it. For six days.

There is a discipline there that most of us have never attempted. The instinct when mocked is to reply, and the reply always feels like strength. Israel was ordered to walk past the insult with a closed mouth, on the grounds that the answer was coming on a day God had chosen and not before.

'So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.'

Day one ends with nothing. One circuit, no wall, no battle, and everyone goes back to bed. It is the flattest sentence in the chapter and it is doing real work: this is what obedience looked like on the first evening, and it looked like a wasted day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually. And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually... And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.'

The writer repeats the whole formation again, word for word, for day two — and then disposes of days three, four, five and six in seven words: so they did for six days.

Do not read past that too quickly, because those four words cover most of the week. Four more mornings of getting up early. Four more circuits. Four more evenings of walking back into camp past the same wall, standing exactly where it stood on Monday.

Nothing about the situation improved as the week went on. If anything it got worse: by Thursday the defenders had stopped being frightened of this and started finding it funny. Israel had no way of explaining what they were doing, because the explanation was a sentence from God and nothing else.

This is the part of the chapter most Christians actually live in. The dramatic seventh day gets preached; the six days are where the years go — praying for the same person, turning up to the same duty, keeping the same promise, and seeing the wall unchanged. Six days of obedience with no visible result is not failure. It is what the seventh day is made of.

It should be said plainly that Israel did not know it was the sixth day. They knew there would be a seventh; they did not know what the seventh would bring, because no wall had ever done what this one was about to do. They walked on the word alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Wall Fell Down Flat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seventh day they are up at dawn and go round seven times (v. 15). At the seventh circuit Joshua finally releases them — shout, for the LORD has given you the city (v. 16) — and sets the terms: the city devoted to destruction, Rahab and everyone in her house excepted, and nothing whatever taken as plunder (vv. 17-19). Then the shout, and the wall goes down flat, and the people climb in over it at every point (v. 20), and verse 21 records what happened inside without a word of softening.
verseByVerse.theology: The order of Joshua's sentence in verse 16 is the point of the chapter. Not shout, and the LORD will give you the city, but shout, FOR the LORD has given. The shout is not a technique that brings the wall down. It is an answer to something already decided.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 plants a warning in the middle of a victory: keep away from the devoted things, or you will make the camp of Israel itself a thing devoted to destruction. Somebody in the crowd hearing that is already thinking about a Babylonian cloak, and the whole of chapter 7 comes out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times. And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times.'

Up at first light, because there is a lot of walking to do. Seven circuits of a city, on foot, in armour, in the Jordan valley — this is most of a day's work before anything happens.

Six circuits pass. The seventh begins, and there is no reason on the ground to think this one is different from the twelve that came before it.

'And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city."'

The silence of six days ends in one word, and the reason attached to it is the theology of the entire chapter. Read the two halves in order.

Not shout, and the LORD will give you the city. That would make the shout a technique, a noise loud enough to do something to masonry, and Israel a people who bring walls down by volume.

What Joshua actually says is shout, FOR the LORD has given you the city. The gift comes first, in the perfect tense, exactly as in verse 2 and exactly as at 1:3. The shout is not the cause of anything. It is the response of people who have been told that a thing is already settled and are finally allowed to say so out loud.

Every act of Christian obedience has that grammar or it has none. We do not praise in order to be accepted; we praise because we have been. The shout comes after the giving, and it comes on the day God names.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it. But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent."'

This is the hardest thing in the book, and it should be met head on rather than hurried past.

The word is herem, usually translated devoted to destruction. It means something handed over to God entirely, taken permanently out of ordinary use. Jericho is the first city in the land, the firstfruits of the conquest, and like every firstfruit it belongs to God rather than to the people. Nobody profits from this one. That is why no plunder may be taken.

Verse 21, four verses later, states what that meant on the ground without any softening at all: men and women, young and old. Children died at Jericho. Any treatment of this passage that does not say so plainly is not worth reading.

What the Bible itself puts around this, taken in order:

First, the timing was announced four hundred years in advance, and the reason given was mercy. God told Abraham his descendants would not receive this land for four generations, because the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Gen. 15:16). The delay was deliberate. Judgment came late, not early, and it came to a culture that by then was burning its own children in fire to Molech — which is the practice Scripture names, again and again, as the reason (Lev. 18:21-25; Deut. 12:31).

Second, and decisively, Israel is told at length that none of this is about their being better. Not because of your righteousness, says Moses, twice in two verses, for you are a stubborn people (Deut. 9:4-6). The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants for what they do, and Israel is warned in the same breath that it will vomit them out too if they do the same things (Lev. 18:26-28). That warning was kept. Seven centuries later the same God brought the same judgment on Jerusalem through Babylon, and the prophets said so in advance and at length.
