Third, the ban was never about ancestry, and this chapter is the proof. A Canaanite household walks out of Jericho alive. Not because of nationality, which was against her, or morality, which was against her, but because she believed a report about God and acted on it. The door out of the judgment was open, and one household went through it.

Fourth, this was a specific, dated, geographically limited command, and Scripture never treats it as a template. No prophet urges Israel to repeat it elsewhere; no apostle applies it to the church. The New Testament is explicit that the weapons of the Christian war are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4), and anyone who has ever used Joshua to justify violence has had to ignore the entire New Testament to do it.

Does all that close the question? No. Verse 21 still says young and old, and no argument set out above makes that easy, and it should not be made to feel easy. What can be said is that the God who did this is the same God who, in the same book, took a prostitute out of the condemned city and put her name in the family tree of his own Son — and that anyone comfortable with the New Testament's doctrine of a final judgment has already accepted the principle, and is only objecting to seeing it happen in daylight, on a Tuesday, at an address.

'"But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it."'

Then a warning, dropped into the middle of the greatest victory Israel has ever had: take any of it, and the ban falls on you. Somebody in that crowd is listening to this and thinking about what he can see from where he is standing. The whole of the next chapter comes out of this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city. Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city.'

A week of walking, and one sentence.

The detail that matters is flat. The wall does not crack, or breach, or come down at the gate. It drops where it stands, all the way round, so that the army does not have to storm anything — every man simply walks up over the rubble in front of him, and the entire circumference becomes the way in at the same moment.

There is no fighting recorded at the wall, because there was no wall to fight for. Jericho's one advantage, the thing that made it worth living behind, ceased to exist between one breath and the next.

The letter to the Hebrews puts this on its list of what faith has done, and words it carefully: by faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days (Heb. 11:30). Not by shouting. By faith — and faith, in that verse, is thirteen laps of a city by people who had no idea what walking was supposed to achieve.

'Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.'

The verse is written flatly and it is meant to be read that way. Nothing is celebrated here and nothing is described in detail; the writer states what was done and stops.

The city that had shut itself up inside and outside got exactly what it had chosen. It had heard, for forty years, what this God had done at a sea. It had heard, for six days, the jubilee horn going round its own walls. Every soul in it had the same information a woman in the wall had, and one household acted on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — Rahab Brought Out, and the City Cursed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While the city burns, the two spies are sent to keep a promise made on a roof, and they bring out Rahab, her father, her mother, her brothers and everyone belonging to her (vv. 22-23). The city is burned and the metal goes into the treasury (v. 24), and verse 25 records, with something like wonder, that she has lived in Israel to this day. Joshua then lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, at the cost of his firstborn and his youngest (v. 26), and the chapter ends where chapter 1 began: the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: One household walked out of that city alive, and it was the household of a Canaanite prostitute who had believed a rumour. The exception is not a footnote to the judgment; it is the writer's comment on it.
verseByVerse.examples: The curse of verse 26 was not rhetorical. Five hundred years later, in the reign of Ahab, a man named Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho and buried his eldest son at the foundation and his youngest at the gates, and the historian records it as the word of the LORD spoken by Joshua coming true (1 Kings 16:34).

verseByVerse.quote: But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her." So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel. And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD. But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her."'

The city is coming down and Joshua stops to keep somebody else's promise.

He was not there when it was made. Two soldiers, on their own initiative, on a roof, swore their lives away to a foreign woman — and their commander now treats that oath as binding on the whole nation in the middle of a battle. The two men who swore it are the two men sent to honour it.

'So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.'

Every name she asked for on the roof is here: father, mother, brothers, and all who belonged to her. The list she recited in the dark, weeks earlier, is read back as a manifest of survivors.

The last clause is honest about the awkwardness. They are put outside the camp. Not immediately assimilated, not instantly at home — a Canaanite family in a holding position at the edge of Israel, ceremonially unclean, alive but not yet belonging. Grace got them out of the fire before it got them a tent.

'But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.'

Outside the camp is not where the story ends. She has lived in Israel to this day — written by a man who could still point to her family, generations later, living inside the nation.

The narrator keeps calling her the prostitute right to the last line, and it is not cruelty. It is the writer refusing to tidy up the person grace actually saved. Matthew does the same thing centuries later, putting her in the genealogy of Jesus without explanation (Matt. 1:5), between Salmon and Boaz, so that the Redeemer of Israel has a Canaanite in his family tree and the record says out loud what she used to be.

The wall she lived in fell flat that morning. Everything she had ever belonged to was on fire. And the God who levelled that city walked one household out of it because a woman with nothing to offer had heard a rumour about him and believed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates." So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates."'

Jericho is to stay down. Not as a strategic decision but as a monument: the firstfruits city is left in ruins so that anybody travelling that road sees what the beginning of the conquest looked like.

The curse was not rhetoric. Around five hundred years later, in the reign of Ahab, a man called Hiel of Bethel rebuilt the city, and the historian records the price in one grim sentence: he laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun (1 Kings 16:34).

'So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.'

The chapter closes on the promise it started from. God had said at the beginning, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you (1:5), and had said he would begin to exalt him (3:7). Both sentences are now signed off in a single line.

See what the fame is attached to. Joshua had done nothing a soldier would put on a record. He had walked round a city thirteen times and told his men to shout. His reputation is entirely the visible edge of somebody else's presence.

The Commander with the drawn sword said he had come, and then took a fortified city without Israel drawing a blade. He did it slowly, in daylight, to the sound of the trumpet of jubilee, and the only thing he carried out of the ruin was a household that had believed him. The LORD was with Joshua — and centuries later a greater Joshua would walk out of a sealed place of death, having brought down a wall no army had ever touched, with the same jubilee sounding over him and a great multitude coming out behind him that no one could number.

6.theology:
The gift comes before the shout. Twice the city is handed over in the perfect tense before anything happens — I have given Jericho into your hand (v. 2) — and Joshua's command at the climax keeps the same order: shout, FOR the LORD has given you the city (v. 16). The shout is not a technique that brings masonry down. It is the answer of people who have been told a thing is settled and are finally allowed to say so. Every act of Christian obedience has that grammar or it has none.

The six days. Hebrews puts Jericho on its list of what faith has done and words it precisely: the walls fell after they had been encircled for seven days (Heb. 11:30). The faith commended is not the shout on the last morning but the walking on the first six, when nothing whatever happened and there was no way to explain what they were doing. Obedience without visible result is not a failure of faith; it is most of what faith consists of.

The ban, faced honestly. Verse 21 says men and women, young and old, and no treatment worth reading softens it. What Scripture puts around it: four hundred years of stated forbearance, because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet complete (Gen. 15:16); an explicit denial that Israel deserved better, repeated twice in two verses (Deut. 9:4-6), with the warning that the same land would vomit Israel out for the same practices (Lev. 18:26-28) — a warning kept, in 586 BC; and Rahab, who proves the ban was never about ancestry, since the door out was open and one household went through it. It was also a dated, local command that no prophet or apostle ever treats as a template, and the New Testament says plainly that the weapons of this war are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4). None of that closes the question, and it is dishonest to pretend otherwise.

Judgment and mercy in the same morning. The writer sets them side by side without comment: a city devoted to destruction, and a household walked out of it by two young men keeping an oath sworn on a roof. She is called the prostitute in the same sentence that says she has lived in Israel to this day (v. 25), and Matthew keeps the name and the description when he writes her into the family of Jesus (Matt. 1:5). Grace in this chapter is not a softening of the judgment. It is a door held open in the middle of it.
6.examples:
Then: An army was told to defeat a fortress by walking. For six days nothing happened, and they were forbidden to answer anything shouted down at them from the walls. On the seventh they walked seven times, shouted once, and the wall dropped flat where it stood, and the only thing carried out of the ruins was one family who had believed a rumour about God.

Now: The six days are the test, not the seventh. Name the thing you have been obeying God about with nothing to show for it — the prayer, the marriage, the person you keep turning up for, the sin you keep refusing. The wall is the same height it was a year ago and the instruction has not changed. Israel did not know which day was the sixth. They only knew who had told them to keep walking.

7.title: Achan's Sin and the Defeat at Ai
7.text: <sup>1</sup>But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai.<sup>3</sup>And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few."<sup>4</sup>So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai,<sup>5</sup>and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.<sup>6</sup>Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads.<sup>7</sup>And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!<sup>8</sup>O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies!<sup>9</sup>For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"<sup>10</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?<sup>11</sup>Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings.<sup>12</sup>Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.<sup>13</sup>Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you."<sup>14</sup>In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man.<sup>15</sup>And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"<sup>16</sup>So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken.<sup>17</sup>And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken.<sup>18</sup>And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.<sup>19</sup>Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me."<sup>20</sup>And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did:<sup>21</sup>when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."<sup>22</sup>So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.<sup>23</sup>And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.<sup>26</sup>And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
7.overview:
The chapter turns on its first word: but. Jericho has fallen and Joshua's fame fills the land, and then one man reaches into a burning city and takes a coat, and God is angry with a nation that does not know it has done anything.

Verse 1 states the offence in a way that offends a modern reader on purpose: the people of Israel broke faith, for Achan took. One man acted and the nation is charged. Scripture is consistent about this and the whole gospel depends on it — nobody who rejects the principle here can keep it at 1 Corinthians 15:22, where in Adam all die and in Christ all are made alive.

What follows is a competent military decision made without a word of prayer (vv. 2-3), thirty-six dead men who had nothing to do with the sin, and the terror that had been fighting on Israel's side changing ends: the hearts of the people melted and became as water (v. 5), which is what this book has twice said about Canaanites. Then Joshua on his face all day, praying a prayer that is largely the complaint he had once opposed at Kadesh, until he arrives at the only argument that matters — what will you do for your great name? (v. 9).

God's answer begins Get up, and the detection walks toward Achan in four slow public stages that are also four invitations to stand up. His confession is the oldest sequence in the Bible: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. And the chapter ends in a valley named Trouble, which a prophet would later hand back to Israel as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens on a single word of contrast: but. Israel broke faith over the devoted things — and the sentence names one man, Achan, while charging the whole nation, and says the anger of the LORD burned against Israel (v. 1). Nobody in the camp knows it. Scouts are sent to Ai and come back with a confident recommendation: small town, few defenders, send two or three thousand and do not tire the army (vv. 2-3). Three thousand go, and run (v. 4). Thirty-six men are killed on the slope, and the hearts of the people melt and become as water (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no prayer anywhere in verses 2-3. At Jericho every move came from God; here the plan is a sensible estimate of the odds made by competent men who did not think to ask. Yesterday's victory had become this morning's assumption.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase at the end of verse 5 has been used twice already in this book, both times about Canaanites — hearts melting, no spirit left (2:11; 5:1). It has changed sides. The terror that had been doing Israel's work for them is now inside their own camp.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.'

One word turns the book over: but. The last chapter ended with Joshua's fame filling the land. This one begins with God angry.

Read the grammar of the verse slowly, because it is doing something deliberate. The subject of the sentence is the people of Israel, and the subject of the crime is Achan. One man reached into a burning city and took a coat, and the nation is charged with it.

That offends a modern reader immediately, and it should be met rather than smoothed over. We think of ourselves as separate units who are responsible for our own actions and nobody else's. Scripture consistently does not. A family, a church, a nation is treated as a body, and what one member does gets into all of it — which is precisely why the whole Bible can turn on two men, so that in Adam all die and in Christ all are made alive (1 Cor. 15:22).

You cannot object to the principle here and keep it there. If a nation could not be implicated in one man's sin, no one could be saved by one man's obedience.

Note also that the writer gives Achan's full pedigree — son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah — three generations, before anything else about him. He is not an anonymous thief. He is somebody's son and somebody's grandson, from the tribe of Judah, and every one of those names will matter before the chapter is finished.

Nobody knows. Israel wakes up the next morning under the anger of God, and the whole camp is entirely unaware of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai. And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few." So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai, and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai... "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai. And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few."'

The reconnaissance is competent and the recommendation is sound. Ai is a small place, the garrison is thin, and there is no sense marching an entire nation uphill for it. Any staff officer would have written the same report.

What is missing is the whole of chapter 6. Nobody asks God anything.

At Jericho, every detail came from outside — how many days, how many circuits, when to blow, when to shout, when to keep silent. Here the plan is assembled by men looking at a hill and doing arithmetic. It is not rebellion. It is something more ordinary and far more common: a victory so complete that praying about the next one felt unnecessary.

The phrase for they are few is the giveaway. Israel has started counting the enemy. The week before, the size of the opposition had been the least relevant fact on the field.

'So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai, and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.'

Thirty-six men. It is a small number for a battle and an enormous number for this book, because until now Israel has not lost a single soldier. Somebody had to carry that news back into thirty-six houses.

They died for a sin they did not commit and never heard about. That is the ugliest fact in the chapter and the writer does not soften it: this is what hidden sin does, and it does not do it to the person who committed it.

Then the last sentence, and it is a quotation. Their hearts melted and became as water is what Rahab said about her own city (2:11) and what happened to the kings of Canaan when they heard about the Jordan (5:1). Israel has caught the enemy's condition. The terror that had been fighting on their side has changed ends.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua tears his clothes and lies face down before the ark until evening, with dust on his head and the elders beside him (v. 6). What comes out of him is not a polished prayer: why did you bring us over the Jordan at all, and would that we had been content to stay on the other side (v. 7). He has no idea what to say about a defeat (v. 8). And then the argument he ends on, which is the best thing in the prayer: the Canaanites will hear, and surround us, and cut off our name — and what will you do for your great name? (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The complaint in verse 7 is almost word for word the complaint of the wilderness generation that Joshua himself had opposed forty years earlier (Num. 14:2-3). Under enough pressure, a man of faith can find himself saying the thing he once stood against, and Scripture records it without excusing it or condemning him for it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 is how Moses prayed at Sinai and at Kadesh — not we deserve better but what will this do to your reputation (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16). It is the one argument in prayer that has nothing to do with the merits of the person praying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads. And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan! O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies! For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads.'

He is there all day. Clothes torn, face in the dirt, dust on his head, in front of the ark — the posture of a funeral, held from morning to evening.

'And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!"'

This is not a good prayer and Scripture prints it anyway.

Listen to what he actually says: you brought us over here to destroy us, and we should have stayed where we were. Those are almost exactly the words of the wilderness generation at Kadesh — why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword? Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt? (Num. 14:2-3). Joshua had stood up in front of that crowd and contradicted them, and nearly been stoned for it.

Forty years later, one bad afternoon, and the man who opposed the complaint is making it. There is no comment from the narrator and no rebuke from God about this part. It is simply what came out of him.

'"For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"'

Then the prayer turns, and the last question is the only real argument in it.

Joshua does not say Israel deserves better; he has just watched thirty-six men die and has no idea why. He says: your reputation is attached to this. It is exactly how Moses prayed when God offered to destroy the nation and start again — not a word about Israel's merits, only why should the Egyptians say... (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16).

That is the one plea in prayer that does not depend on the person making it. A believer with nothing to say for himself can still say: your name is on this, and I am asking for your sake and not mine.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's first word is not comfort: Get up! Why have you fallen on your face? (v. 10). The diagnosis follows in four verbs — they have taken, stolen, lied, and hidden (v. 11) — and then the sentence that empties the conquest of everything it has been resting on: I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you (v. 12). The remedy is consecration and a process: tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, man by man (vv. 13-14), and whoever is taken is to be burned with all that he has (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God has been the whole argument of the book since 1:5. Verse 12 says it can be withdrawn, and names the condition. Sin in the camp does not merely displease God; it removes the one thing Israel had going for it.
verseByVerse.examples: The lot moves slowly and it moves in public, and the slowness is a mercy. Achan watched it come to Judah, then to the Zerahites, then to his grandfather's household, then to the men of his own family. He had four separate opportunities to stand up before it reached him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings. Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you. Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you." In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man. And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?"'

God's first word to a man who has been praying all day is to stop.

That deserves attention, because prayer is not usually the thing that needs interrupting. But there is a kind of praying that is a substitute for obedience — agonising before God about a situation he has already told us how to fix, or has been trying to. Joshua is asking why God has abandoned Israel. God's answer is that nobody has abandoned anybody, and there is a man in the camp with stolen property under his tent.

'"Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings."'

Four verbs, and they are a descent. Taken is the act. Stolen names what kind of act it was. Lied is what had to happen next, because Achan has been walking around the camp for days behaving normally. And put them among their own belongings is the settled state: the thing is in the tent now, and life has arranged itself around it.

'"Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies... I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you."'

This is the most frightening sentence in the book. Everything since chapter 1 has rested on one promise: I will be with you. Here God says it is conditional, and states the condition.

He does not say Israel will be forgiven when they feel worse about it. He says the devoted thing has to go. There is no route round the object itself, and a great deal of religious distress is the attempt to find one — genuine grief, genuine prayer, genuine resolve, and the thing still under the floor of the tent.

'"In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes... And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man."'

The detection is deliberately slow: tribe, then clan, then household, then individual. God knew the name on the first day. He could have said it to Joshua in a sentence.

Instead the lot walks toward Achan in four public stages, over a morning, in front of everybody. Four times he watches it come nearer, and four times he could have stood up. The machinery that exposes him is also, right up to the last moment, an invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — I Saw, I Coveted, I Took, I Hid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lot narrows exactly as God said: Judah, then Zerah, then Zabdi, then Achan (vv. 16-18). Joshua's words to him are gentler than anyone would expect — my son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel — and he asks for the truth (v. 19). Achan gives it, and the confession is a sequence: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid (vv. 20-21). The list of what he took is short: a cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty.
verseByVerse.theology: The four verbs are the oldest sequence in the Bible. Eve saw that the tree was good, took of its fruit, and the two of them hid themselves among the trees (Gen. 3:6-8). James describes the same descent as a pregnancy: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin grown up brings forth death (James 1:15).
verseByVerse.examples: Shinar is not a neutral place name. It is the plain where Babel was built (Gen. 11:2) and it is Scripture's shorthand for Babylon. On the first week of the conquest, a man of Judah looked at a Babylonian coat and wanted it enough to bury it under his tent.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken. And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken. And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken. Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me." And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken... and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.'

The pedigree from verse 1 is read out again, in full, in public. Every name that was mentioned privately to the reader is now spoken over the man in front of the nation.

The tribe is Judah. The royal tribe, the one Jacob had blessed with the sceptre, the tribe the Messiah would come from. The first recorded sin in the promised land is committed by a man of the line that produces the King.

'Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me."'

Joshua's first two words are the surprise of the chapter. My son. He is speaking to a man who has cost thirty-six lives and is about to be executed, and he addresses him the way a father would.

Then the framing he gives to confession: telling the truth is described as giving glory to God. Not as clearing the record, or making things easier, or getting it off his chest. To confess is to agree with God about what happened, which is a way of honouring him — and it means the last useful thing Achan can do in his life is available to him.

'And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."'

Four more verbs, and every one of us has used them in that order. I saw. I coveted. I took. I hid.

It is the oldest sequence in the Bible. Eve saw that the tree was good, and took of its fruit, and then the two of them hid themselves among the trees of the garden (Gen. 3:6-8). It is David on a roof. It is James's description of how sin gestates: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin fully grown brings forth death (James 1:15).

Now look at the inventory, because it is pitifully small. A coat. Five pounds of silver. A bar of gold he could hold in one hand. For that, thirty-six men are dead and his own family is finished.

The coat came from Shinar. That is the plain where men once said come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower (Gen. 11:2-4); it is the Bible's name for Babylon. In the first week of the conquest, a man of Judah smuggled a piece of Babylon into the camp of God and buried it under the place where he slept.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messengers run and find everything exactly where he said, and the goods are spread out before the LORD (vv. 22-23). Then Achan, the silver, the cloak, the gold, his sons and daughters, his animals and his tent are taken up to a valley (v. 24). Joshua says why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today, and the sentence is carried out (v. 25). A great heap of stones is raised over the place, the anger of the LORD turns away, and the valley is named Achor, which means trouble (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: A second heap of stones is now standing in the land. One at Gilgal marks a river that opened; this one marks a man who took what was not his. The writer puts the same words on both — to this day — and lets the reader feel the pair of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Hosea, seven centuries later, takes the name of this valley and does something extraordinary with it. Describing how God will win back an unfaithful people, he promises to give her the Valley of Achor as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15). The place where judgment fell is the place named as the way back in.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath. And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD. And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor. And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones. And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath. And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD.'

They run. And what was buried in the dark under a man's bed is dug up, carried across the camp, and spread out on the ground in the open, in front of everybody, before God.

That is what happens to everything eventually. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known (Luke 12:2). The only question about any concealed thing is whether it is brought into the light by confession or by exposure.

'And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.'

The list is long and it is meant to be. Everything he owned, everything he took, and everyone he loved goes up that valley with him.

The death of his children is the second hard thing in this book, and it should not be managed. Two things can honestly be said and neither closes the matter. The goods were buried under the family tent, in a dwelling shared by a household, which makes it difficult to believe that nobody knew — and Israel's own law forbids putting children to death for their fathers' sins (Deut. 24:16), which means the reader who finds this troubling is standing on ground the Old Testament itself provides. The text records what happened and does not explain it. Neither will this commentary.

'And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones... And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger.'

Another heap of stones. There are two monuments in the land now: one at Gilgal where a river opened, and this one, where a man is buried under the rocks. The writer says to this day about both.

The valley is named Achor — trouble — and the name is the last word of the chapter. It ought to be the last word about Achan, and it is not, because of what a prophet did with it seven centuries later.

Hosea is describing how God intends to win back a nation that has committed spiritual adultery against him. He says he will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her, and give her back her vineyards, and then this: and the Valley of Achor as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

The valley of trouble is issued as a doorway. God takes the name of the worst place in Israel's early history — a heap of stones over a thief, the site of a nation's shame — and hands it back as the entrance to the future. That is not sentiment; it is what he does. Centuries later he took the instrument of a criminal's execution and made it the sign under which the world is saved.

7.theology:
Sin is never private. Thirty-six men died for something they never did and never heard about. That is the chapter's flat claim, and it is the reason God treats a body as a body: a church, a family, a nation is not a collection of separate units whose choices stay inside them. The doctrine that offends here is the same doctrine that saves at Romans 5 — one man's act reaching everybody who belongs to him.

Yesterday's victory is not today's permission. Nobody in verses 2-3 does anything wicked. They take good advice from competent scouts and count the enemy, which they had not troubled to do at Jericho because the numbers were irrelevant there. Presumption in this chapter is not arrogance; it is the quiet assumption that God's involvement can be inferred from the last time.

The condition on the promise. Everything since 1:5 has rested on I will be with you. Verse 12 attaches a condition to it: I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you. And no amount of prayer substitutes — God interrupts a day-long intercession with Get up, because the problem is not in heaven but under a tent. There is no route round the object itself.

The Valley of Trouble as a door of hope. Achor is where a thief was buried under stones and a nation's shame was written into a place name. Seven centuries later Hosea, describing how God will win back an unfaithful people, promises to give her the Valley of Achor as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15). God has a way of taking the name of the worst thing that ever happened somewhere and issuing it as an entrance — which is precisely what he later did with a Roman cross.
7.examples:
Then: A man watched a city burn, saw a Babylonian coat and some silver in the rubble, and buried them under the floor of his tent. Nothing happened to him for days. Thirty-six other men were killed in a battle he was not in, an army ran downhill from a town it should have taken, and a nation went to bed frightened, and none of them knew why.

Now: The four verbs are the ones to check yourself against, because they run in order and each one is small. I saw. I coveted. I took. I hid. Most people reading this are somewhere in that sequence about something, and the chapter's counsel is not to feel worse but to dig the thing up — God interrupted a whole day of anguished prayer to say so. And Joshua's word to the man who had cost him everything was my son, and the confession he asked for was described as giving glory to God.

8.title: Ai Defeated and Covenant Renewal at Mount Ebal
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.<sup>2</sup>And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready.<sup>5</sup>And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them.<sup>6</sup>And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them.<sup>7</sup>Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand.<sup>8</sup>And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.<sup>10</sup>Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.<sup>11</sup>And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai.<sup>12</sup>He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city.<sup>13</sup>So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness.<sup>16</sup>So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city.<sup>17</sup>Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.<sup>19</sup>And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire.<sup>20</sup>So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.<sup>21</sup>And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.<sup>22</sup>And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped.<sup>23</sup>But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.<sup>24</sup>When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword.<sup>25</sup>And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai.<sup>26</sup>But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.<sup>27</sup>Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua.<sup>28</sup>So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day.<sup>29</sup>And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.<sup>30</sup>At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,<sup>31</sup>just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings.<sup>32</sup>And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.<sup>33</sup>And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.<sup>35</sup>There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
8.overview:
God speaks first, before Joshua asks, and gives back the words of the original commission unaltered: do not fear and do not be dismayed (v. 1; cf. 1:9). There is no probation and no reduced terms. Two things are corrected without a word of reproach — take the whole army this time, and the plunder of this city may be kept.

That permission is startling one week after a man was executed for taking plunder. The difference was never the goods, and it was never that wealth is unclean. Jericho was the firstfruits and belonged wholly to God; Ai is given away. What changed was what God said.

Ai falls to an ambush — a night march, a concealed force, a staged retreat — and God is the one who ordered it (v. 2). Jericho fell to a shout and no tactics at all. Both victories are entirely his, which means neither chapter can be made into a rule about whether faith waits or works. And the bait in the trap is Israel's own humiliation: the plan depends on Ai believing that Israel will run, because Israel ran last time.

Then the campaign stops, and the nation marches twenty miles north into unconquered country to build an altar on Mount Ebal, write the law on stones, and hear every word of it read aloud — women, children and foreigners standing in the valley with everyone else. The first structure Israel builds in the promised land is not a fort. It is an altar, on the mountain of the curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Same Words, After the Failure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks first, and what he says is what he said at the beginning: do not fear and do not be dismayed (v. 1; cf. 1:9). The commission is renewed word for word to a man who has spent a day face down in the dust. Two things are then corrected. Take all the fighting men, not a detachment of three thousand. And the spoil of this city, unlike Jericho's, may be kept (v. 2) — along with an instruction no one expected in this book: lay an ambush.
verseByVerse.theology: The words of chapter 1 are given back unaltered. God does not re-commission a chastened man on reduced terms or with a warning attached; the sentence he had used before the failure is the sentence he uses after it.
verseByVerse.examples: The plunder of Ai is handed to Israel freely — the very kind of thing Achan died for taking a week earlier. The difference was never the value of the goods. It was the word of God, which had said no at Jericho and says yes here.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land. And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land."'

The first thing to notice is that God speaks first. Joshua has not asked. After Achan, after thirty-six funerals, after a day face down in the dirt, God opens the conversation.

What he says is what he said at the start. Do not fear and do not be dismayed is verbatim from the original commission (1:9). Not a reduced version, not a probation, not let us see how you get on this time. The same sentence, given back whole.

Sit with that if you have ever failed at something that mattered. God's word to a man who has just presided over a disaster is the word he used before the disaster happened. The promise was never resting on Joshua's record, so Joshua's record has not altered it.

Two corrections are folded in without a syllable of reproach. Take all the fighting men — last time three thousand went, because the scouts had done the arithmetic. And I have given into your hand, the perfect tense again, exactly as at Jericho.

'"And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."'

Then a permission that ought to stop the reader cold. Take the plunder.

A week ago a man was executed, with his household, for taking a coat and some silver from a captured city. Now the same nation is told to help itself to the contents of the next one.

The difference was never the goods. It was never that wealth is dirty and poverty is holy. Jericho was the firstfruits and belonged wholly to God; Ai is given away. The only thing that changed between the two cities is what God said, and Achan died because he decided that a command about property was a suggestion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua takes thirty thousand men and sends them out at night to lie in ambush west of the city, with orders to stay close and stay ready (vv. 3-4). The main force will advance, be beaten, and run — because the men of Ai will say they are fleeing from us, just as before (vv. 5-6). When the city is empty the ambush is to take it and burn it (vv. 7-8). The trap is laid overnight (v. 9), the army musters at dawn and camps north of Ai with a ravine between (vv. 10-11), a further five thousand are positioned to the west (v. 12), and Joshua spends the night in the valley (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Jericho fell to a shout and no tactics at all. Ai falls to reconnaissance, a night march, a concealed force and a feigned retreat, and God is the one who says lay an ambush. Both victories are entirely his. What changes is the instrument, and nothing in this book lets a reader turn either method into a rule.
verseByVerse.examples: The bait is Israel's own humiliation. The plan works precisely because Ai has beaten them once and will believe it is happening again — just as before. The defeat that shamed the nation a chapter ago is the thing God uses to take the city.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night. And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready. And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them. And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them. Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand. And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you." So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready. And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them."'

Read that plan beside the one at Jericho, because the contrast is the point.

At Jericho there were no tactics whatsoever. Walk round. Blow. Shout. Here there is a night march, a concealed force, a decoy, a feigned retreat, a signal, and a coordinated turn. It is a competent piece of soldiering that any staff college would recognise.

God is the one who ordered it. Lay an ambush against the city came out of the mouth of the LORD in verse 2. This is not Joshua reverting to human wisdom after the miracle ran out; the ambush is as much a divine instruction as the trumpets were.

Neither chapter, then, can be turned into a rule. Christians tend to divide into those who think faith means waiting for God to act and those who think faith means competent effort, and each side has a favourite chapter of Joshua. God wrote both. The question is never which method is spiritual; it is what he has actually said.

Look also at the bait. The plan depends entirely on Ai believing that Israel will run, because Israel ran last time — they are fleeing from us, just as before. The worst day in the nation's short history is the hinge of the strategy. God takes the shame of chapter 7 and uses it as the lure that empties the city.

'So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.'

The last clause is small and it says a good deal. The commander does not withdraw to a tent to wait. He sleeps in the camp with the men who will be doing the running in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai. And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai. He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai. And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai.'

Up early again. It is the fourth time the writer has mentioned it, and by now it is a portrait rather than a detail: this is a man who does not lie in bed on the morning of an obedience.

The deployment is careful and it is meant to be seen. Israel camps in plain view on the north side, across a ravine, where the whole city can look down and count them. The visible army is the part of the plan that is supposed to be visible.

'He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.'

A second detachment goes west, between Ai and Bethel — which also blocks the road down which Bethel's men would come to help. Nothing here is improvised.

Once more the sentence about where Joshua slept: in the valley. Not on the ridge with the elders, and not behind the lines. The low ground between two armies, on the night before a battle in which he personally is the decoy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king of Ai sees the army and hurries out early, and the narrator adds the sentence the whole plan rests on: he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city (v. 14). Israel pretends to be beaten and runs for the wilderness (v. 15), and every fighting man in Ai and Bethel goes after them, leaving the city open (vv. 16-17). Then God tells Joshua to stretch out his javelin, the hidden force rises, takes the city and sets it alight (vv. 18-19). The men of Ai look back and see the smoke, and the army they were chasing turns round (vv. 20-21). Caught between the two, not one escapes, and the king is taken alive (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Their confidence was built on a real memory. Ai had beaten Israel, and the men running out of the gates that morning were reasoning from evidence. Presumption is rarely irrational; it is usually a sound argument from a previous week.
verseByVerse.examples: The outstretched javelin is the gesture Moses made with his staff over the sea and with his hands at Rephidim (Ex. 14:16; 17:11). It does nothing mechanically. It is a man standing in plain view with his arm up, so that nobody watching can mistake whose victory this is.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city. And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness. So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city. Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.'

He hurried. That one verb carries the whole of what is about to happen to him.

His confidence is not irrational. He has beaten these people once, in living memory, with this same army. He watched them run. Everything he believes about the morning is drawn from evidence, and it is all true, and it is about to kill him.

That is what presumption usually looks like from the inside. Not arrogance and not stupidity, but a sound argument from last week — which is precisely the error Israel made in chapter 7 when the scouts counted the defenders and did not think to ask God. The king of Ai is now making Israel's mistake, and it is the reason Israel will win.

'And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness. So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them... Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.'

Israel runs, and does it convincingly, because they have had recent practice at running from this town for real.

Then the sentence that seals it: they left the city open. The gates that had been shut against Israel a week ago now stand wide, with nobody behind them, because every man in the place is out on the hillside chasing a defeat that is not happening.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city. And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire. So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers. And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai. And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped. But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.'

The gesture does nothing mechanically. A raised spear kills nobody at that distance and moves no troops on its own.

What it does is put a man in plain sight with his arm in the air for the length of a battle, which is exactly what Moses did with his staff over the sea and with his hands on the hill at Rephidim (Ex. 14:16; 17:11-12). The victory is about to be won by five thousand hidden men and a well-timed turn, and God arranges for one visible sign that this is his doing and not theirs.

'And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire.'

They had been lying still since before dawn. Now they run, take an empty town, and light it — and the fire is the signal as well as the destruction.

'So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.'

The moment the pursuers turn round is the moment they understand everything at once: the retreat was staged, the city is gone, and there is nowhere to run because the road home is on fire.

The writer says they had no power to flee this way or that. An army caught between the men it was chasing and the men who took its houses is not defeated by superior force; it is defeated by having believed something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–29 — A King on a Tree, Taken Down by Sunset
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The killing is total and the number is given: twelve thousand, the whole population (vv. 24-25). Joshua does not lower his arm until it is finished (v. 26), the spoil is taken this time by command (v. 27), and the city is burned to a mound that is still there when the book is written (v. 28). Then the king of Ai is hanged on a tree, taken down at sunset, and buried under a great heap of stones at the city gate (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 29 is written to the letter of the law. A body was not to remain on a tree overnight, because a hanged man is cursed by God and would defile the land (Deut. 21:22-23). Israel executes a Canaanite king and then observes, to the hour, a commandment about how to handle the cursed.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul takes that exact law and puts it on Christ: he redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13). Another King was hanged on a tree outside a city and taken down before sunset, and a stone was rolled over him.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword. And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai. But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction. Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua. So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day. And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai. But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.'

Twelve thousand people, stated as a number and not dressed up. The book does not celebrate this and does not hide it; the same hard question that verse 21 of chapter 6 raised is raised again here, and it was answered there as honestly as it can be answered.

The detail about the arm is the one the writer chooses to dwell on. It stayed up the whole time. Whatever else was happening on that hillside, there was a man standing where everyone could see him, holding a spear out over a burning city until the thing was done — as Moses' hands had to be held up by two men until Amalek was beaten.

'Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua. So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day.'

The plunder is taken, and the writer is careful to say why: according to the word of the LORD. The same action that damned one man is righteous when God commands it. The clause is there so nobody misses the principle.

'And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.'

Now look at the timing, because it is the most important detail in the chapter.

The body comes down at sunset, and that is not squeamishness or convenience. It is obedience to a specific law: if a man is put to death and hanged on a tree, his body shall not remain on the tree overnight but shall be buried the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God, and the land must not be defiled (Deut. 21:22-23). Israel executes a Canaanite king and then keeps a commandment about how to handle the cursed, to the hour.

Paul knew that law and did something with it that no one else would have dared. Writing to the Galatians about how the curse of the law was dealt with, he says: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13).

Another King was hanged on a tree outside a city gate. He was taken down before sunset, because the law required it and the sabbath was coming. A stone was rolled over him. And the curse that fell on a Canaanite king because he was an enemy of God fell on this one although he was not, so that his enemies could stop being cursed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The campaign stops. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal of uncut stones that no iron tool has touched, exactly as Moses commanded, and burnt offerings and peace offerings are made on it (vv. 30-31). He writes a copy of the law on stones in front of everybody (v. 32). The whole nation is then drawn up in the valley, half facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal, with the ark and the priests between them, sojourners standing with the native born (v. 33), and Joshua reads the whole law aloud, blessing and curse (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Ebal and Gerizim are twenty miles north of Ai, in country nobody had taken. Israel broke off a war, marched the entire nation — women, children and foreigners — deep into unconquered territory, and held a service. This is not a pause between campaigns. It is a claim staked in the middle of the land.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 35 is exact about who was there: the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them. Not a word was left out and nobody was left outside. The foreigners standing in that assembly are what happened to Rahab's household, and to everyone since who has come in from outside.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings. And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool."'

Before anything else, take in where this is happening. Ebal is at Shechem, about twenty miles north of Ai, in the middle of the country. Nobody has conquered it. There are walled cities on every side and no line of supply, and Israel has just fought one battle and buried its own dead not long before.

Into that, the entire nation marches away from the war to hold a service.

The first structure Israel builds in the promised land is not a fort, a wall, a storehouse or a palace. It is an altar, and it is built to a specification: uncut stones, no iron tool ever laid on them (Ex. 20:25; Deut. 27:5-6). The one place where human skill is forbidden is the place where atonement is made. Whatever else a man may improve by his craftsmanship, he may not improve the way back to God.

Two kinds of offering are made on it. Burnt offerings, which went up entirely — nothing kept back, the whole animal consumed. And peace offerings, which were eaten: the only sacrifice that ended in a shared meal, the sign that the quarrel was over and the parties were at table. Atonement first, then dinner.

'And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.'

Then he writes out the law on stones, in public, so that the words stand in the open air in the middle of the land. A nation that had spent forty years being carried and fed now takes its first act of settled ownership, and the act is to put God's words up where the country can read them.

verseByVerse.quote: And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel. And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal.'

The valley between Ebal and Gerizim is a natural amphitheatre; the two ridges face each other across it, and a voice carries. Israel is drawn up on both sides with the ark in the middle.
