The two mountains had been assigned their parts by Moses long before anyone stood there. Gerizim was the mountain of blessing and Ebal the mountain of curse (Deut. 27:12-13), and the nation is deliberately arranged so that half of them are looking at each.

Note where the altar was built. Not on Gerizim, where the blessing is pronounced, but on Ebal — the mountain of the curse. That is where the blood was shed and the peace offering was eaten. If there is going to be any dealing with God at all, it happens at the place where the curse is, because that is the thing standing in the way.

'And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.'

Two things in that last verse are easy to read past and should not be.

The first is not a word. The whole law, including the parts that indict the people listening, read out loud in one sitting. Nothing was selected, and nothing was softened for the occasion.

The second is the list of who was standing there: the women, the little ones, and the foreigners living among them. Children too young to follow much of it were brought and made to stand through the reading. Non-Israelites who had attached themselves to this people — and there was at least one household in the crowd who had walked out of Jericho — heard the covenant read as though it belonged to them.

So the first great assembly in the promised land stands in a valley, in unconquered country, between a mountain of blessing and a mountain of curse, with an altar smoking on the wrong one. Every word of the law is read over them, and every word of it will eventually be broken by them. The law was written on stones that day. Centuries later God promised, through a prophet watching the whole arrangement fail, to write it somewhere it could not be broken: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33).

8.theology:
Restoration on the original terms. The words God gives Joshua after the disaster are the words he gave him before it. Nothing is withheld and no conditions are added, because the promise never rested on Joshua's record in the first place. It is the pattern of Peter on the beach, who was not asked how he could have done it but whether he loved him (John 21:15-17).

Miracle and means are both his. The shout at Jericho and the ambush at Ai were both commanded by God, and it is a mistake to make either one the spiritual method. Christians divide into those who think faith waits and those who think faith works, and each side has a favourite chapter here. The question in Joshua is never which approach is holier; it is what God has actually said.

The same act, damned and commanded. Achan died for taking spoil; Israel is ordered to take spoil, and the writer notes that they did it according to the word of the LORD (v. 27). The moral weight sat entirely on the command and not on the object, which is the thing to remember wherever Christians build permanent rules out of God's particular instructions.

Hanged on a tree, taken down by sunset. The king of Ai is executed and his body removed before nightfall in exact obedience to Deuteronomy 21:22-23, which gives the reason: a hanged man is cursed by God, and the land must not be defiled. Paul takes that law and applies it to the cross — Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13). And the altar in this chapter is built on Ebal, the mountain of cursing, not on Gerizim. Atonement is always made where the curse is.
8.examples:
Then: A defeated army went back to the town that had beaten it, won by pretending to run away again, and then walked twenty miles into enemy country with its wives and children to stand in a valley and listen to the whole law read out, every word, including the parts about what would happen if they broke it.

Now: The word to take from this chapter is the first one. God opened the conversation after the failure, and used the sentence he had used before it. If you are carrying something you assume has permanently changed the terms — a collapse, a disqualifying failure, a year you would not repeat — notice what God did not say to Joshua. He did not review the incident. He said do not be afraid, take the whole army, and go back to the place where it went wrong.

9.title: The Gibeonite Deception
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this,<sup>2</sup>they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.<sup>3</sup>But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,<sup>4</sup>they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended,<sup>5</sup>with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly.<sup>6</sup>And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."<sup>7</sup>But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?"<sup>8</sup>They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?"<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt,<sup>10</sup>and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth.<sup>11</sup>So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."'<sup>12</sup>Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly.<sup>13</sup>These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."<sup>14</sup>So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.<sup>16</sup>At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.<sup>18</sup>But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.<sup>19</sup>But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them.<sup>20</sup>This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them."<sup>21</sup>And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.<sup>22</sup>Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us?<sup>23</sup>Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."<sup>24</sup>They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.<sup>25</sup>And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."<sup>26</sup>So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them.<sup>27</sup>But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 changes the kind of danger. Jericho and Ai were assaults; this is a confidence trick. The Gibeonites hear what Israel's God has been doing, work out that they cannot win, and decide to survive by fraud — patched sandals, split wineskins, bread deliberately left to go hard, and a story about a four-hundred-mile journey.

The disguise is aimed at a specific sentence of Israel's own law. Deuteronomy allows terms of peace with a city that is very far off and forbids it absolutely with the cities of Canaan (Deut. 20:10-18). Gibeon needs to be a distant city, and every prop on that donkey exists to make one word of Israel's statute book apply to them. They know Israel's law better than the kings to the north know their own danger.

Israel nearly catches it — perhaps you live among us (v. 7) — and is then talked round by a speech built entirely out of true statements with a hole in the middle. Egypt is mentioned, and Sihon and Og; Jericho and Ai, which happened five miles away last month, are not. Then Israel inspects the evidence competently, finds it genuine, and the chapter turns on seven words: but did not ask counsel from the LORD (v. 14).

The rest is what God does with a blunder. The oath was sworn in his name and therefore holds, even against a furious congregation, and the Gibeonites live — sentenced to cut wood and carry water for the altar. Which is a strange curse for a Canaanite city, and stranger still in the light of where the tabernacle eventually stood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Three Ways of Hearing the Same News
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of the whole country — hill country, lowland and coast, six nations named — hear what has happened at Jericho and Ai (v. 1), and they do the one thing that has not been tried yet: they combine. Six armies gather as one to fight Joshua and Israel (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Three groups in this book hear the same reports and do three different things. Rahab heard and asked for mercy. These kings hear and form a coalition. The Gibeonites, in the next verse, hear and start sewing patches onto sandals. The news was identical every time.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this, they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this, they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.'

Six nations and every region of the country, and for the first time they act together. Until now Canaan has been a patchwork of city-states that were at least as interested in each other as in Israel. Two burned towns have done what nothing else could and made them one.

What is striking is that this is a response to evidence. These kings are not ignoring what happened at Jericho; they have heard the reports and drawn a conclusion, and the conclusion is to organise.

Set the three reactions in this book side by side, because the writer clearly means us to. Rahab heard, and asked for mercy. These kings hear, and form an alliance. The Gibeonites, in the very next verse, hear the identical news and start patching sandals.

Nobody in Canaan is short of information. The reports have been travelling for forty years and everyone has them. What separates these people is not what they know but what they do with it — which is the oldest pattern in Scripture, where the same word softens one man and sets another one hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–13 — Worn Sandals and Mouldy Bread
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon hears the same reports and takes a third route (v. 3). They load donkeys with split and mended wineskins, put on patched sandals and worn clothes, take bread that has gone dry and crumbly, and walk into the camp at Gilgal claiming to be from a distant country (vv. 4-6). Israel is suspicious and says so — perhaps you live among us (v. 7) — so the Gibeonites talk. They cite the name of the LORD, Egypt, Sihon and Og (vv. 9-10), quote their own elders (v. 11), and then produce the exhibits: bread that was warm when they left home, wineskins that were new, garments and sandals worn out by the length of the road (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every fact in their speech is chosen. They mention Egypt and the two Amorite kings — old news that would have reached a distant country — and say nothing whatever about Jericho and Ai, which happened last month and only a neighbour would know. The gaps in the story are as carefully made as the story.
verseByVerse.examples: They are also standing inside a clause of Israel's own law. Deuteronomy permits terms of peace with a city that is very far and forbids it absolutely with the cities of Canaan (Deut. 20:10-18). The Gibeonites are not improvising a lie; they have worked out precisely which sentence of Israel's law they need to be standing in, and then dressed for it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended, with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly. And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended, with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly.'

Read the inventory. Sacks worn out. Wineskins split and stitched back together. Sandals patched. Clothes worn. Bread deliberately left until it crumbles.

This took time and thought. Somebody in Gibeon sat down and worked out what a man would look like after four hundred miles on the road, and then produced it — not one prop but a whole wardrobe, down to the state of the food.

The fake is aimed at a very specific target. Israel's law had two different rules for two kinds of city: terms of peace could be offered to a town that was very far off, and were forbidden absolutely to the cities of Canaan (Deut. 20:10-18). Gibeon needed to be a distant city, and everything on that donkey exists to establish one word of Israel's own statute book.

These men know Israel's law. They have studied the God they are afraid of well enough to find the clause with room in it, which is more attention than the kings up the road have paid.

'And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."'

Then they walk into Gilgal — the camp where the stones from the Jordan are standing, where the nation was circumcised, where the Passover was kept — and open with the lie.

verseByVerse.quote: But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?" They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?" They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt, and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth. So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."' Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly. These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?"'

Israel very nearly catches it. The first response is suspicion, and it is exactly the right suspicion: perhaps you live among us. Somebody in that meeting had read Deuteronomy and knew what question to ask.

That makes what follows worse rather than better. This is not a nation blundering in ignorance. They saw the danger, named it out loud, and were then talked out of it.

'They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt, and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan."'

Now watch what is in the speech and, more importantly, what is not.

They mention Egypt, which was forty years ago and half a continent away. They mention Sihon and Og, which happened east of the Jordan before Israel crossed. Both are exactly the sort of famous, well-travelled news that would have reached a country four hundred miles off.

They say nothing at all about Jericho. Nothing about Ai. Those happened in the last few weeks, five miles from where everyone is standing, and only a neighbour would have heard yet. Verse 3 has already told us that this is precisely what they heard and why they came.

The lie is built out of true statements with a hole cut in the middle of them, which is how the most effective lying is generally done.

'"Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly."'

Then the exhibits are handed over for inspection. And notice the one clause in the whole performance that is entirely true: they came because of the name of the LORD your God. They had heard the report and were terrified, and that part needed no invention at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — They Did Not Ask Counsel from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does the due diligence. They take some of the provisions and examine them — the bread really is dry, the skins really are split — and the evidence checks out (v. 14). And then the seven words that the whole chapter turns on: but did not ask counsel from the LORD. Joshua makes peace, cuts a covenant, and the leaders of the congregation swear to it (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not laziness and it is not wickedness. They investigated competently and reached a reasonable conclusion from real evidence. What they did not do was ask the one party who knew where these men lived.
verseByVerse.examples: The means were standing in the camp. The high priest carried the Urim and Thummim for exactly this — so that Israel could put a question to God and get an answer (Num. 27:21). It was not that God was silent. Nobody asked him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.'

Everything in this chapter turns on seven words in the middle of verse 14.

First, notice what Israel did do. They took some of their provisions — they handled the bread, broke it, looked at it. This is an inspection. The leaders examined physical evidence and tested the story against it, and the evidence was genuine: the bread really had gone hard, the skins really were split.

The failure here is not laziness, and it is not wickedness. It is competence without enquiry. They did the sensible thing thoroughly and reached a reasonable conclusion from real data, and every single piece of that data had been manufactured for them the week before.

Then: but did not ask counsel from the LORD.

The means were in the camp. Eleazar the priest carried the Urim and Thummim for exactly this purpose — so that a leader could bring a question to God and receive an answer (Num. 27:21). It was not that God was unavailable, or silent, or that the question was too small. Nobody asked.

Be honest about why they did not. The case looked closed. When the evidence is ambiguous we pray; when it is obvious we act. The Gibeonites' entire strategy was to make the case look obvious, and it worked, and it will work again on anybody who only prays about the decisions that are difficult.

Then the covenant is cut and the leaders swear. That oath is about to become the most important thing in the chapter, and at the moment it is sworn nobody thinks it matters much at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later the truth is out: these men are neighbours, and their towns are Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim, a day's march away (vv. 16-17). Israel does not attack them, because the leaders had sworn by the LORD, and the whole congregation grumbles about it (v. 18). The leaders' answer is short and it settles the matter: we have sworn by the LORD, we may not touch them, and if we break it wrath will come on us (vv. 19-20). So the Gibeonites live, as woodcutters and water-carriers for the congregation (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The treaty was obtained by fraud, and everybody knows it. Israel could have voided it on those grounds in ten seconds, and the congregation clearly wanted to. The leaders hold to it because of whose name was invoked, not because of who deserved it.
verseByVerse.examples: That the oath was genuinely binding was proved centuries later, and expensively. Saul broke it and killed Gibeonites, and a three-year famine came on Israel in David's reign with the reason given plainly: there is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death (2 Sam. 21:1).

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them. And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them. And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day.'

Three days. The lie about a four-hundred-mile journey survives seventy-two hours, and then Israel walks to their cities in the same three days it took to discover them.

There is something almost comic about the arithmetic, and it makes the point sharply: the truth was a short walk away the entire time. A question asked at Gilgal, of God or of anyone who knew the district, would have settled it before the ink was dry.

'But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.'

Now the army is standing outside four Canaanite towns it is under orders to destroy, and it does not attack — and the reason given is not military and not moral. It is a name. The leaders had sworn by the LORD, the God of Israel.

Every argument for voiding the treaty is available and obvious. It was obtained by fraud. The other party lied about a material fact. No court anywhere would enforce it.

The congregation makes those arguments loudly, and the word for what they do is the word used all through the wilderness years: they murmured. This is the old sin surfacing in a new situation, and this time they are grumbling in favour of obedience to a command about Canaanites, which shows how easily a bad instinct can find a good text to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them." And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them."'

The leaders' reasoning has two steps and both should be kept.

The first: we have sworn by the LORD. When a man swears in God's name he is calling God as guarantor of what he says. Breaking it does not merely make the man a liar; it makes God look like the sponsor of a lie. That is why the third commandment is about taking the name in vain, and it is far wider than swearing in the street.

The second: lest wrath be upon us. They are not being sentimental about promises. They believe that breaking this oath would bring God's anger down on the nation, and they are right, and it can be checked.

Four hundred years later King Saul, in a burst of zeal for Israel, attacked and killed Gibeonites. In David's reign a famine came for three successive years, and when David asked why, the answer was: there is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death (2 Sam. 21:1). Four centuries had not weakened it. The oath sworn by deceived men to lying men was still binding on their great-grandchildren.

'And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation.'

The settlement costs Israel something and it costs the Gibeonites their independence, and neither party gets what it wanted. But a nation that had been deceived kept its word to the people who deceived it, at its own expense, because of whose name was on it.

That is the man the psalmist describes as fit to dwell on God's holy hill: the one who swears to his own hurt and does not change (Ps. 15:4). It is a rare thing in any century. The world keeps its promises while they remain convenient, and here a whole nation, furious and within its rights, kept one that was not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua summons them and asks the obvious question — why did you deceive us (v. 22)? — and pronounces the sentence: you are cursed, and some of you will always be servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God (v. 23). Their answer is honest at last: we were told your God had given you this land and commanded the destruction of everyone in it, so we feared greatly for our lives (v. 24), and now we are in your hand, do what seems right (v. 25). Joshua delivers them from the people and they are not killed (v. 26), and the last verse fixes their work: woodcutters and water-carriers for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence Joshua passes is a curse, and the reader should feel how strange a curse it is. It condemns a Canaanite people to spend the rest of their history carrying firewood and water to the altar of the God of Israel. Every other Canaanite city in this book is destroyed; these men are sentenced to lifelong proximity to the sacrifices.
verseByVerse.examples: And it goes further than Joshua could have known. Centuries later the tent of meeting stood at Gibeon, and Solomon went up to the high place there to sacrifice, and it was at Gibeon that God appeared to him in the night and told him to ask for whatever he wanted (1 Kings 3:4-5; 1 Chron. 16:39; 2 Chron. 1:3). The town that lied its way out of destruction ended up with the tabernacle standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us? Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God." They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing. And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us? Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."'

Joshua does not pretend nothing happened. The deception is named, and a sentence is passed, and it is called a curse.

But look at what the curse actually is. They are condemned to cut wood and carry water for the house of my God — which means that of all the Canaanites in this book, the ones who lied are the ones sentenced to spend their lives near the altar. Every other city in these chapters is burned. Gibeon is put on the sanctuary's staff.

'They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you — so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing."'

Their explanation is the first honest thing they have said, and it is not an excuse. It is a statement of fact: we were told what your God had ordered, we believed it, and we were terrified.

They had better theology than the kings did. Six armies to the north had heard the same thing and concluded that they could fight it. Gibeon heard it and concluded that they could not, and everything they did afterwards — the lying included — followed from taking God at his word.

'"And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."'

That is total surrender, offered by people who have no cards left. They do not argue that the treaty binds Israel, though it does. They put themselves in his hand and stop negotiating.

verseByVerse.quote: So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them. But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them. But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.'

Two phrases in these verses carry more than they look.

The first: Joshua delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel. The danger to the Gibeonites at this point is not the Canaanite kings; it is the congregation of Israel, which is still grumbling and would happily have finished them. Joshua stands between an angry nation and the men who fooled it.

The second: for the altar of the LORD, in the place that he should choose. The phrase about the place God would choose is Deuteronomy's language for the future sanctuary, the one central site not yet identified. Joshua is attaching these men not to a temporary arrangement at Gilgal but to whatever God is going to do next, permanently.

Consider the work itself. Wood for the fire and water for the washing: unglamorous, endless, and absolutely necessary. No sacrifice was offered in Israel without somebody having carried the fuel, and no priest washed without somebody having drawn the water. The Gibeonites do not preach, prophesy or lead. They keep the altar supplied, and Scripture troubles to record it.

Then the ending nobody in this chapter could have foreseen. Centuries pass. The tabernacle — the tent of meeting Moses made in the wilderness — comes to rest at Gibeon, and stays there for generations. Zadok the priest is stationed before it there (1 Chron. 16:39). When Solomon becomes king, he goes up to the great high place to sacrifice, and the reason given is that the tent of meeting of God was at Gibeon (2 Chron. 1:3). And it is at Gibeon, in the night, that God appears to him and says: ask what I shall give you (1 Kings 3:4-5).

The town that lied to save its life ended up with the tent of meeting standing in it, and one of the great encounters between God and a king of Israel took place on its high ground. God took a prayerless blunder, a wardrobe of stage props and a nation's fury, and out of the three of them made a place where he met people. He has never yet been prevented from doing that by the poor quality of the material.

9.theology:
Prayerlessness is not laziness. The men of Israel investigated. They handled the bread and tested the story against the evidence, and the evidence was real. What they did not do was ask the only party who knew where these men lived, and the means were in the camp — the priest carried the Urim and Thummim precisely so that questions could be put to God (Num. 27:21). The trap was built to make the case look obvious, and that is the whole danger: anyone who only prays about the difficult decisions will be taken by the easy one.

An oath in God's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud. Every argument for voiding the treaty was available and the congregation made them loudly. The leaders refused, on two grounds: the name of the LORD had been invoked, and wrath would follow if they broke it. They were right, and it can be checked — four centuries later Saul killed Gibeonites, and a three-year famine came in David's reign with the reason stated plainly (2 Sam. 21:1). This is the man of Psalm 15, who swears to his own hurt and does not change.

Same news, three responses. Rahab heard the reports and asked for mercy. The kings of Canaan heard them and formed a coalition. Gibeon heard them and sewed patches onto sandals. Nobody in this country lacked information; the reports had been circulating for forty years. What divided them was not knowledge — and the Gibeonites, for all their lying, had the better theology, because they believed what God had said about the land and the kings did not.

What God did with the blunder. Joshua's sentence condemns them to cut wood and draw water for the altar of the LORD, in the place that he should choose — Deuteronomy's phrase for the future sanctuary. Centuries later the tent of meeting itself stood at Gibeon; Solomon went up to that high place to sacrifice because the tabernacle was there, and it was at Gibeon that God appeared to him and told him to ask for whatever he wanted (1 Kings 3:4-5; 1 Chron. 16:39; 2 Chron. 1:3). A prayerless decision and an elaborate lie ended with the tent of meeting pitched in the deceivers' town.
9.examples:
Then: Four Canaanite towns survived the conquest because they dressed up in old clothes, carried stale bread across a five-mile journey, and told a story with the recent news left out of it. Israel checked the evidence, found it convincing, and signed. Three days later they were standing outside the towns of the people they had sworn to protect.

Now: The verse to take away is the seven words in the middle of verse 14, and the reason they are frightening is that nothing else in the chapter went wrong. There was no rebellion, no laziness, no obvious sin — only a sensible decision made on good evidence without asking God, because the case looked clear. Think of the last significant decision you did not pray about. Almost certainly it was the one where the answer seemed obvious.

10.title: The Sun Stands Still
10.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,<sup>2</sup>he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors.<sup>3</sup>So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel."<sup>5</sup>Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.<sup>6</sup>And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.<sup>11</sup>And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.<sup>12</sup>At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon."<sup>13</sup>And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day.<sup>14</sup>There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.<sup>15</sup>So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.<sup>16</sup>These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.<sup>17</sup>And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah."<sup>18</sup>And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them,<sup>19</sup>but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand."<sup>20</sup>When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,<sup>21</sup>then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave."<sup>23</sup>And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.<sup>24</sup>And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."<sup>26</sup>And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening.<sup>27</sup>But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.<sup>28</sup>As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>29</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>31</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>32</sup>And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah.<sup>33</sup>Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining.<sup>34</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>35</sup>And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish.<sup>36</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it<sup>37</sup>and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it.<sup>38</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it<sup>39</sup>and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.<sup>40</sup>So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded.<sup>41</sup>And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon.<sup>42</sup>And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.<sup>43</sup>Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
10.overview:
The treaty Israel should never have made becomes the reason for the greatest day in the campaign. Five Amorite kings mobilise — and their target is not Israel but Gibeon, the city that changed sides (v. 4). Punishing the traitor comes first, which is the usual order: people who throw in their lot with God's people inherit their enemies, and generally meet them sooner.

Gibeon calls in the oath, and Joshua marches all night out of the Jordan valley and up about a mile of ascent to fight for the men who had lied to his face a fortnight earlier. Nobody reopens the question of whether the covenant was binding. Then God takes the field: a panic, a pursuit down the pass at Beth-horon, and hailstones that kill more of the enemy than Israel's swords do (v. 11).

And in the middle of it Joshua speaks to the sun and the moon in front of the whole army. Two things are usually missed there. The narrator is quoting poetry, and says so — is this not written in the Book of Jashar (v. 13), a lost collection also quoted when David laments Saul (2 Sam. 1:18). And the sun and moon were the chief gods of Canaan; Joshua gives the enemy's deities their orders in the name of the LORD, and they obey.

Verse 14 then says where the wonder actually lies, and it is not in the astronomy: there has been no day like it, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man. The chapter ends with five kings under the feet of five officers, a catalogue of captured cities written in one repeated sentence, and eight words of explanation for all of it — because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Coalition Against the Traitors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem hears about Ai and about Gibeon's peace with Israel, and is badly frightened — Gibeon is a great city, bigger than Ai, and its men are fighters (vv. 1-2). He sends to four other kings, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, with a proposal (v. 3), and note who the target is: come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon (v. 4). Five armies march, and they besiege not Israel but the city that changed sides (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's blunder in chapter 9 has just drawn the entire southern coalition out of five fortified cities and concentrated it in one place in open country. Nothing Joshua could have planned would have done that.
verseByVerse.examples: The name of the king of Jerusalem is Adoni-zedek, lord of righteousness. Centuries earlier another king of that city met Abram and blessed him, and his name was Melchizedek, king of righteousness (Gen. 14:18) — the man Hebrews takes as the pattern of Christ's priesthood. Same city, same title, and this one is marching to destroy Abraham's descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors. So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying, "Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel." Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai... and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors.'

What terrifies Jerusalem is not the fall of Ai. It is the defection of Gibeon.

The reasoning is given in the verse and it is entirely military. Gibeon is a large city with a good army, in a commanding position. While it was Canaanite it was part of the wall; now it is a gap, and a gap with fighting men in it.

'So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying, "Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel."'

Read the target of the campaign carefully. Five kings mobilise, and they do not march on Israel. They march on Gibeon.

Punishing the traitor comes before fighting the invader — and it is a settled pattern. People who throw in their lot with God's people inherit their enemies, and generally meet them sooner than the people they joined. Gibeon lied its way into this covenant, and within days it is under siege by everyone it used to drink with.

Now the name of the man organising it. Adoni-zedek means lord of righteousness. And there was another king of that same city, centuries earlier, who came out to meet Abram with bread and wine and blessed him, and his name was Melchizedek, king of righteousness (Gen. 14:18) — the figure the letter to the Hebrews takes as the pattern of the priesthood of Christ.

Same city. Almost the same name. One came out to bless the father of the nation; this one is raising an army to destroy his descendants. Jerusalem has been capable of both since the beginning.

'Then the five kings of the Amorites... gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.'

Look at what has just happened strategically. Israel's prayerless blunder in chapter 9 has pulled five armies out of five fortified cities and put them all in one place in open country. Joshua could not have arranged it, and did not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon sends word to Gilgal, and the message is a claim on the treaty: do not relax your hand from your servants... come up to us quickly and save us (v. 6). Joshua takes the whole army (v. 7), God says do not fear them, I have given them into your hands (v. 8), and the attack lands at first light after a march that took all night (v. 9). Then God does the fighting: he throws the coalition into a panic, and Israel chases them down the pass at Beth-horon (v. 10) while the LORD throws large stones out of the sky — and more of them die from the hail than from Israel's swords (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel marches all night to rescue the people who conned them a chapter earlier. The oath they got by fraud is now costing them a forced march up a mountain, and nobody reopens the question of whether it was binding.
verseByVerse.examples: Gilgal is in the Jordan valley, several hundred feet below sea level; Gibeon sits about half a mile higher, some twenty miles away. This is a night climb of roughly a mile of ascent by an army that then fought a battle at the top of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us." So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us."'

The message is a claim on the treaty, and it is put in the language of the treaty: your servants. They are not asking a favour. They are calling in an oath.

There is real nerve in it. These are the men who lied to Joshua's face a fortnight ago and were caught; the last time they spoke to him he called them cursed. Now they send word that the covenant obliges him to march.

'So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.'

He goes. There is no recorded hesitation, no council, no revisiting of whether an oath obtained by fraud is really binding — and Israel had every reason to think about it, because this treaty had cost them nothing but embarrassment until now, and is about to cost them a night march and a battle.

That is what covenant faithfulness looks like when it becomes expensive. God's people keep their word to people who do not deserve it, at their own cost, because of who they learned it from.

'And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."'

Then God speaks — the same two things he always says in this book. Do not fear. I have given. The perfect tense again, before the march has even started.

See where the promise lands. Israel is going into battle to honour a treaty God was never consulted about, made by men he had told to consult him. He does not say you made this bed. He says he has already handed them the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal. And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah. And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal.'

One sentence, and it hides an extraordinary piece of soldiering.

Gilgal lies in the Jordan valley, several hundred feet below sea level. Gibeon stands in the hills, roughly half a mile higher and about twenty miles away. Joshua took an entire army up that climb in the dark, arrived before dawn, and attacked immediately.

Israel had walked round a city for a week and shouted; here they climb a mountain all night. There is no formula in this book for what obedience will require on a given day.

'And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon.'

The credit goes immediately elsewhere. Israel achieved surprise, and the writer says the rout came because the LORD threw them into a panic. Whatever the tactical brilliance of the night march, what actually broke the coalition was terror arriving from outside.

'And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.'

Then the sky opens on a retreating army in a narrow pass. The descent at Beth-horon is a steep, rocky defile; men running downhill through it in armour could not scatter and could not shelter.

The writer adds the arithmetic, which is the point: the hail killed more of them than Israel did. On the greatest day of the southern campaign, the army that marched all night was outperformed by the weather.

It is also aimed weather. Israelites were in that pass too, chasing them. The stones fell on one side of a running battle and not the other, which is the sort of detail the narrator gives without comment and lets the reader do the arithmetic on.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the battle Joshua speaks, in the sight of Israel, to the sun and the moon: stand still at Gibeon, and in the Valley of Aijalon (v. 12). The narrator reports what happened and then quotes his source — is this not written in the Book of Jashar? — adding that the sun did not hurry to set for about a whole day (v. 13). Then the verse that says where the wonder actually lies: there has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel (v. 14). And then, flatly, everyone goes back to camp (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 does not say that the astonishing thing was the astronomy. It says the astonishing thing was that God listened to a man. The heavens moving is the smaller half of that sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Sun and moon were not neutral objects to anybody watching. They were the two great gods of Canaan, worshipped in every town Israel was marching towards. Joshua gave them orders in the name of the LORD, in public, and they did as they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon." And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel. So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon."'

Take the sentence in stages, because there is more in it than the famous half.

First: Joshua spoke to the LORD, and then said this in the sight of Israel. The command to the sun is a prayer said out loud in front of the army. Whatever happened next, he had committed himself publicly and there was no quiet way back.

Second: consider what he is addressing. The sun and the moon were not neutral objects to anybody standing on that battlefield. They were the two great gods of Canaan, worshipped in every town Israel was marching towards, and one of the cities in this chapter, Beth-shemesh country, carries the sun's name. Joshua gives the enemy's chief deities their orders in the name of the LORD, in public, and they do as they are told.

'And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day.'

Now the narrator does something easy to read past: he cites a source. The Book of Jashar was a collection of Hebrew verse, now lost, quoted once more in the Old Testament when David laments Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1:18). So the words about the sun and moon are poetry, quoted from a song Israel already knew.

That matters for how the sentences work, and it does not settle the question of what happened. Poetry can describe a real event with complete accuracy and still describe it as poetry does — and the narrator's own comment in the second half of verse 13, that the sun did not hurry to set for about a whole day, is written as plain report.

Readers have taken this in more than one way. Some hold that the earth's rotation was genuinely halted or slowed. Some hold that it was a prolongation of light rather than a stopping of motion, or a darkening — the verb in verse 12 can mean be still or be silent — with the hailstorm cloud giving Israel cool cover through what should have been the worst heat of the afternoon. What no honest reading can do is remove God from the middle of it, because that is what both the poem and the narrator are for.

'There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.'

Here is the verse that tells us where the wonder actually is, and it is not in the astronomy.

The unique thing about that day, in the writer's own judgment, is not that the sky did something. It is that the LORD heeded the voice of a man. A God who requires nothing from anybody, who set the sun in its place, listened to a soldier standing in a field and did what he asked.

Keep hold of that when the mechanics of the miracle start to absorb all the attention. The question the chapter raises is not primarily what happened to the light. It is what kind of God takes instructions from a man who is out of daylight and still has work to do — the same God of whom James says, when he wants ordinary Christians to pray, that Elijah was a man with a nature like ours (James 5:17).

'So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.'

Then the flattest sentence imaginable. The sun stands still over Canaan, and the army walks home to camp.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–27 — Feet on the Necks of Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The five kings run and hide in a cave at Makkedah (v. 16). Joshua has large stones rolled over the mouth and a guard posted, and tells the army not to stop — keep after the enemy, do not let them reach their cities (vv. 17-19). When the pursuit is over and everyone is back, not a man dares to open his mouth against Israel (vv. 20-21). Then the cave is opened, the kings are brought out, and Joshua has his commanders put their feet on their necks (vv. 22-24), with a sermon attached: do not be afraid, be strong and courageous, this is what the LORD will do to all your enemies (v. 25). The kings are executed and hanged on five trees, taken down at sunset, and thrown into the cave they hid in, with large stones set over the mouth (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The foot on the neck is the oldest picture of total defeat there is, and Scripture keeps it. God tells the Messiah to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1), and Paul says Christ must reign until every enemy is under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25) — and then promises an ordinary congregation that God will soon crush Satan under theirs (Rom. 16:20).
verseByVerse.examples: Note what Joshua says over the kings in verse 25. It is his own commissioning, word for word from 1:9, handed on to the men under him. What God said to him on the day Moses died, he now says to his officers with the evidence lying at their feet.

verseByVerse.quote: These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah. And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah." And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them, but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand." When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities, then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah. And it was told to Joshua... And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them, but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand."'

Five kings in a hole in the ground. The men who summoned four allies and marched on a city are now lying in the dark hoping nobody looks in.

Joshua's response is the mark of a commander who knows what the day is for. He does not go to the cave. He seals it with stones, leaves a few men on the door, and orders everyone else to keep chasing — because the kings are not going anywhere and the armies still are.

The reason he gives for the urgency: do not let them enter their cities. Every man who reaches a walled town becomes a siege. The pursuit in the open is the cheap part of the war, and Joshua will not trade it for the satisfaction of dealing with five captives now.

'When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out... then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.'

The army comes back safe — the writer bothers to say it, after a night march and a day of battle.

Then an odd Hebrew phrase, and it should be had whole: not a man moved his tongue against the people of Israel. It is the language of total silence, of a country with nothing left to say. The kings who had been sending each other messages at the start of the chapter are in a cave, and everyone else has stopped talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave." And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon. And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks. And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight." And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening. But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave."... And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks.'

The gesture is not gratuitous cruelty and it is not a spontaneous humiliation. It is a formal act, performed by named officers in front of the whole army, and it means one thing in the ancient world: total and final conquest. The foot on the neck is the picture of an enemy turned into furniture.

Scripture keeps the image and never softens it. God tells the Messiah to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1) — the most quoted verse in the New Testament. Paul says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet, the last of them being death itself (1 Cor. 15:25-26).

Then Paul does something with it that ought to stop a reader. Writing to a small, squabbling congregation in Rome, he tells them: the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Rom. 16:20). Not under his feet. Under theirs. What the chiefs of Israel did at Makkedah is promised to ordinary Christians.

'And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."'

Listen to what Joshua says over the necks of those kings. It is his own commissioning, word for word: do not be afraid, do not be dismayed, be strong and courageous (1:9).

What God said to him at the beginning, on the day Moses died, he now says to the men under him — and he can point at the floor while he says it. Courage in this book keeps travelling outward: from God to Joshua in chapter 1, from the people back to Joshua at the end of that same chapter, and now from Joshua to his officers with the evidence under their boots.

'And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening. But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave.'

Once again the bodies come down at sunset, in exact obedience to the law about a hanged man being cursed and not left overnight (Deut. 21:22-23) — the second time in three chapters that Israel executes Canaanite kings and then keeps a commandment about the cursed, to the hour.

The burial has a terrible neatness. They are thrown into the cave they chose as a hiding place, and large stones are rolled against the mouth of it — the same stones that had kept them in that morning now keep them in for good. The place a man picks to hide from God has a way of becoming the place he stays.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a list, and it is deliberately repetitive: Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Gezer's king coming to help and falling with him, Eglon, Hebron, Debir (vv. 28-39). Each entry uses the same words — captured, struck with the edge of the sword, none remaining, as he had done to the city before. Verse 40 sums up the whole southern country, hill country and Negeb and lowland and slopes, and verse 41 gives the map from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza. Verse 42 gives the reason for all of it in eight words, and verse 43 sends the army home to Gilgal.
verseByVerse.theology: The flat, formulaic repetition is the writer's method rather than his laziness. City after city falls in identical language, and the effect is of something advancing that nothing in the country can vary or slow. The morality of it is the question dealt with at 6:17-19, and this chapter does not re-argue it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 42 is the sentence the whole book exists to say: because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Every campaign in the chapter is credited to somebody who never appears in the casualty lists.

verseByVerse.quote: As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah. And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it. And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah. Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it. And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish. Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it. Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho.'

From here the chapter becomes a list, and the list is written in one repeated sentence. Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir. Each one captured. Each one struck with the edge of the sword. Each time, he left none remaining, and as he had done to the city before it.

The flatness is deliberate. A writer who wanted to celebrate would vary the telling, name the heroes, describe the fighting. This one uses the same words six times over, and the effect on a reader is not excitement but inevitability — something moving through a country at a steady pace that nothing in it can alter.

Two details break the pattern, and both should be caught. Lachish takes two days (v. 32), the only city in the list that does not fall on the first — a small honest note in a chapter that could easily have rounded everything off. And when Horam king of Gezer marches out to help Lachish, he is dealt with in a single verse and his city is never taken (v. 33). He came to the aid of a doomed ally and lost his army for it.

The moral weight of these verses is the same weight carried at Jericho, and it was faced there rather than here: what the ban was, what Scripture puts around it, and the part of the question that stays open (6:17-19). Nothing in this catalogue softens it and nothing in it adds to it. The writer simply records what happened, city by city, without a word of triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon. And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon.'

The summary works outwards from the battle to a map. Four kinds of terrain, then two boundary points about fifty miles apart, and the whole southern half of the country inside them.

The phrase just as the LORD God of Israel commanded is doing the same job it did at Ai, where taking plunder was righteous because God said so and had been fatal at Jericho because he had said the opposite. Nothing in these chapters is Israel's initiative.

'And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.'

Then the reason, in eight words, and it is the sentence the whole book was written to say. Not because Joshua marched at night, though he did. Not because the coalition made a strategic error in besieging Gibeon, though they did. Because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.

'Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.'

The chapter ends where it ended before, with the army walking home to the same camp — back to the twelve stones out of the Jordan, and the place where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away.

The God who threw hail down a mountain pass, who took orders from a man about the length of an afternoon, and who put five kings under the feet of five ordinary officers, brought the whole army back to the field where its story in the land began. Nothing in the south of that country had been able to stand in front of him, and he had done all of it for a people who had been slaves inside living memory and had walked into the land on dry ground behind a box.

10.theology:
Covenant faithfulness when it costs. Israel marches through the night to rescue the men who deceived them, and the narrative records no debate about it. The oath was obtained by fraud and it is kept anyway, uphill, at night, at risk — and God meets the army on the way with do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands (v. 8). He does not tell them they made this bed. Keeping your word to people who do not deserve it is not naivety in this book; it is an imitation of God.

The long day, and where the miracle is. Verses 12-13 are quoted poetry from the Book of Jashar, and the narrator names his source. Readers have taken the event in more than one way — a halting of the earth's rotation, a prolonging of usable light, a darkening under the hail cloud through the heat of the afternoon, since the verb can mean be still or be silent. What no honest reading removes is God from the middle of it. And verse 14 does not locate the marvel in the sky at all: what had never happened before or since was that the LORD heeded the voice of a man.

The gods of Canaan take orders. Sun and moon were worshipped throughout the country Israel was invading. Joshua addresses them out loud, in front of the army, in the name of the LORD, and they do as they are told. The theological claim underneath the miracle is the same one the whole book makes: the LORD is not a regional deity competing for territory. He is the Lord of all the earth, and the opposition's gods are on his staff.

Feet on the necks of kings. The image is the ancient world's picture of final conquest, and Scripture keeps it: the Messiah sits until his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1), and Christ reigns until every enemy is under his feet, death last of all (1 Cor. 15:25-26). Then Paul takes the image and hands it to an ordinary congregation — the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Rom. 16:20). And what Joshua says over those kings is his own commissioning, passed on: do not be afraid, be strong and courageous (v. 25; cf. 1:9).
10.examples:
Then: An army climbed a mile of hill road in the dark to save the people who had swindled it, arrived at dawn, watched the sky kill more of the enemy than they did, and stayed on the field so long that the day itself became a national memory. Then five kings were pulled out of a cave and buried in it, behind the stones they had chosen for shelter.

Now: Two things transfer directly.
