The first is the march: a promise made carelessly is still a promise, and God met Israel on the road they took to keep it rather than lecturing them about how they got there. The second is verse 14. Before you decide what you think happened to the sun, notice what the writer thought was remarkable — that God listened to a man. Whatever you were about to conclude about the size of your own requests, he heard a soldier ask for more daylight.

11.title: The Northern Campaign Completed
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,<sup>2</sup>and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west,<sup>3</sup>to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.<sup>4</sup>And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.<sup>5</sup>And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.<sup>10</sup>And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire.<sup>12</sup>And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded.<sup>13</sup>But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned.<sup>14</sup>And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed.<sup>15</sup>Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>16</sup>So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland<sup>17</sup>from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death.<sup>18</sup>Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.<sup>19</sup>There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.<sup>20</sup>For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>21</sup>And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.<sup>22</sup>There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.<sup>23</sup>So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
11.overview:
The north assembles what the south could not: every king from the hill country to the coast, a horde like the sand on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots (v. 4). The comparison is deliberate. Like the sand on the seashore is the promise God swore to Abraham about his own descendants (Gen. 22:17), and here it describes the army that has come to finish them.

God's answer comes with a clock on it — do not be afraid, tomorrow at this time (v. 6) — and with an order that has nothing to do with winning the battle: hamstring the horses, burn the chariots. Israel could have equipped itself as the strongest power in the region by nightfall. The point is not that technology is wicked but that a nation which owns chariots will eventually trust them, and Moses had already written the rule for a king who had not yet been born (Deut. 17:16). Israel did not keep it: Solomon bought fourteen hundred chariots and imported horses from Egypt (1 Kings 10:26-29).

Hazor, the head of the northern kingdoms, is burned; the other cities are left standing, because Israel is going to live in them. And verse 15 gives the verdict the writer wants on Joshua's whole career, in a chain with four links and no slippage: as the LORD commanded Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did — he left nothing undone.

Then the giants that had frightened a generation into the desert are cut off in a single verse (v. 21), a remnant is noted in three Philistine towns including Gath, and the conquest narrative ends in six words: and the land had rest from war.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Chariots at the Waters of Merom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jabin of Hazor does what Adoni-zedek did, on a larger scale: a summons to every king in the north, hill country, Arabah, lowland and coast, six nations named (vv. 1-3). What assembles is the largest force in the book — a horde like the sand on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots (v. 4) — camped at the waters of Merom (v. 5). God's word to Joshua comes with a timetable attached: do not be afraid, tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them (v. 6). And with an odd instruction: hamstring the horses, burn the chariots. Israel attacks suddenly, the coalition breaks, and Joshua does exactly what he was told with the captured equipment (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel has no chariots. The enemy's advantage is not numbers alone but technology, and God's answer is not to give Israel better technology but to destroy the enemy's and forbid his people to keep any of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase in verse 4 — like the sand that is on the seashore — is the promise God made to Abraham about his own descendants (Gen. 22:17). Here it describes the army coming to kill them. The writer knew what he was doing with it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph, and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west, to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah. And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots. And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph, and to the kings who were in the northern hill country... And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.'

The south has fallen and the north has been watching. Jabin of Hazor sends out the same invitation Adoni-zedek sent, and gets a far bigger response — every region of the northern country, six nations, coast to hill country.

Two things about this army are not true of anything Israel has faced before.

The first is the size, and the writer chooses his comparison with care: like the sand that is on the seashore. That is not a stock phrase for a crowd. It is the promise God swore to Abraham about his own descendants — I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen. 22:17). The words that describe God's promise are here describing the army that has come to end it.

The second is the equipment: very many horses and chariots. A chariot in that world was the decisive weapon, expensive, fast and terrifying, and infantry generally broke in front of it. Israel has none. They are a nation of foot soldiers who were slaves within living memory, and they are looking at massed armour.

'And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.'

They camp together, which is their mistake and God's arrangement. Every king in the north is now in one valley, and the entire northern war will be settled in a single morning.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire." So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them. And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining. And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel."'

The same sentence as always — do not be afraid, I will give — and this time with a clock on it. Tomorrow at this time. God does not merely promise the outcome; he names the hour, in front of an army that has just seen what is camped at Merom.

'"You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire."'

Then an instruction that has nothing to do with winning the battle and everything to do with what happens afterwards. When the field is taken, the captured horses are to be crippled and the captured chariots burned.

Militarily this is close to insane. Chariots and trained horses were the most valuable plunder on any ancient battlefield, and Israel could have equipped itself in a day and become the strongest power in the region by nightfall.

God will not have it, and the reason is not that technology is wicked. It is that a nation which owns chariots will, sooner or later, trust them. Moses had written the rule into the law of the king before Israel had a king at all: he must not acquire many horses for himself (Deut. 17:16). The psalmist puts it in a sentence: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7).

Follow that thread to the end, because Israel did not keep it. Solomon, the wisest king they ever had, accumulated fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, and imported horses from Egypt in droves (1 Kings 10:26-29). The nation eventually bought back, at great expense, precisely what Joshua was ordered to burn.

'And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.'

Joshua does it. Standing on a won field with the best military hardware in Canaan lying around him, he sets fire to it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua turns back and takes Hazor, which had been the head of all those kingdoms, kills its king and burns the city (vv. 10-11). The other royal cities are captured, but verse 13 notes something practical: none of the cities standing on their mounds were burned, only Hazor. The spoil and livestock are taken as plunder while every person is destroyed (v. 14). And then verse 15, which is the summit of Joshua's whole career: as the LORD commanded Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did — he left nothing undone.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is not squeamishness; it is housekeeping. Israel is about to live in these towns. They burn the capital that organised the war and leave standing the houses they will move into — the houses Moses had promised them, which they did not build (Deut. 6:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: The chain in verse 15 has four links and no slippage in any of them: the LORD commanded Moses; Moses commanded Joshua; Joshua did it; nothing was left out. It is the sentence the writer wants on Joshua's record, and it is the exact opposite of what will be said about the generation in the book of Judges.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms. And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire. And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded. But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned. And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed. Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms... And he burned Hazor with fire.'

Hazor was the largest and most important city in the north, and the writer says so plainly: it had been the head of all those kingdoms. Killing the coalition in the field was the battle; burning its capital is the end of the war.

'But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned. And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder.'

Verse 13 is a piece of quiet housekeeping and it explains a great deal about this campaign. The other cities are not burned, because Israel is going to live in them.

That was the arrangement Moses had described: houses full of good things that you did not fill, cisterns you did not dig, vineyards and olive trees you did not plant (Deut. 6:10-11). Israel takes the capital that organised the war and leaves standing the towns it will move into — and the same principle covers the plunder, which is taken here by permission exactly as at Ai.

'Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.'

This is the sentence the writer wants on Joshua's record, and it has four links with no slippage in any of them. The LORD commanded Moses. Moses commanded Joshua. Joshua did it. And then the clause that goes further than the others: he left nothing undone.

It is easy to hear that as a compliment about diligence. It is more than that. Almost every failure in the rest of Israel's history is a failure of exactly this kind — not open defiance but things left undone, tribes that did not drive out the inhabitants, commands obeyed in the parts that suited. The book of Judges opens with a list of them.

Partial obedience is the ordinary form disobedience takes among religious people, because it looks so much like the real thing from a distance. The verdict on Joshua is that there was nothing outstanding.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The summary covers the whole country, from Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad under Hermon in the north, and states plainly that this took a long time (vv. 16-18). Verse 19 records that not one city made peace except Gibeon — and verse 20 gives the reason behind the reason: it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts. Then the Anakim, the giants who had frightened a whole generation into the wilderness, are cut off from the hill country, with a remnant surviving in three Philistine cities (vv. 21-22). And the chapter ends in six words that the book has been walking towards: and the land had rest from war (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 is hard and verse 19 is its control. Peace was available — the text says so by noting the one city that took it. The hardening is judicial: God gives a people over to what they have already chosen, exactly as with Pharaoh (Ex. 9:16; Rom. 9:17-18), and in the same book he takes a prostitute and four Gibeonite towns out of the same judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: The Anakim were the reason Israel spent forty years in a desert. Ten spies had come back saying we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:33), and the nation believed them. One verse disposes of the giants here, and the difference between the two generations was never the size of the men in the hills.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death. Joshua made war a long time with all those kings. There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle. For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Joshua took all that land... from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death. Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.'

Two boundary points, roughly the whole length of the country, and then a sentence that has been missing from most of this book: Joshua made war a long time.

The narrative has been moving fast — a city a verse, a campaign a chapter — and here the writer stops to say that it took years. Whatever the pace of the telling, the living of it was slow.

'There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.'

Read this verse before the next one, because it is the control on it. Peace was available. The writer says so by noting the one city that took it.

Gibeon got its treaty by fraud, and it need not have been fraud; the terms existed and any city could have sought them. Rahab needed no treaty at all, only belief. What the country did, almost without exception, was fight.

'For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.'

Then one of the hardest sentences in this book. Their resistance was not merely their own choice; behind it stood God, hardening.

Scripture does not soften this anywhere. It says the same of Pharaoh, who hardened his own heart repeatedly and of whom God also said, for this purpose I have raised you up (Ex. 9:16), a verse Paul quotes when he says God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Rom. 9:17-18).

Two things keep this from being arbitrary cruelty, and both are in this chapter. The first is verse 19: peace was on the table, and one city took it. The second is the rest of the book: the same God who hardened these kings had, weeks earlier, taken a Canaanite prostitute out of a burning city and put her in the family of the Messiah. Hardening in Scripture is judicial. It is God confirming people in the direction they have already set, and it is never the whole story of what he was doing in that country.

What it does mean is that the outcome was never in the balance. The kings gathering at Merom believed they were making a decision. They were being gathered.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities. There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain. So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.'

One verse, almost in passing, and it settles a question that had cost the nation forty years.

The Anakim were the giants. When twelve spies went into this country the first time, ten came back and named them specifically: we saw the Nephilim there... and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them (Num. 13:33). That report turned a nation round at the border and sent it back into the desert until everyone who believed it was dead.

Joshua was one of the two who did not believe it. He is now an old man cutting those same giants out of those same hills, and the writer gives it a single verse.

The difference between the two generations was never the size of the men in the hill country. The giants were exactly as advertised. What changed was who the people were measuring them against.

'There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.'

Then a small note that the writer had no way of knowing would matter so much. A remnant survived, in three Philistine cities on the coast — and one of them is Gath.

Four hundred years later a champion came out of the Philistine camp to challenge Israel, nearly ten feet tall, and the text is careful to say where he came from: Goliath of Gath (1 Sam. 17:4). An army of Israelites was paralysed by him, exactly as their ancestors had been, and a shepherd boy who had not been at Merom killed him with a stone.

'So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.'

Six words end the conquest. And the land had rest from war.

Consider what stands behind them. Four hundred years in Egypt, a night with blood on the doorframes, a sea, forty years of walking in circles, a river, thirteen laps of a walled city, thirty-six funerals, a night march up a mountain, and years of fighting after that. And now: the land had rest.

It did not last, and the book knows it. The next chapters will list what was not taken, and Judges will open with the tribes failing to finish. The writer of Hebrews puts it exactly: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on — and therefore there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-9).

The rest under Joshua was real, and it was a copy. The one who gives the real thing carries the same name and made the offer in the plainest words anyone has ever used about it: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). The land had rest from war because God fought it. So does the soul.

11.theology:
Burning the chariots. God does not answer superior technology by supplying better technology. He destroys the enemy's and forbids his people to keep any of it (v. 6), because possession leads to reliance — some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7). The command anticipates the law of the king (Deut. 17:16) and the failure of the wisest king Israel ever had (1 Kings 10:26-29). Every generation has its own version of the captured chariot: the thing that would make the church formidable, and would quietly make God unnecessary.

Nothing left undone. Verse 15 is the high-water mark of the book, and its force is in the last clause rather than the first. Israel's later collapse is almost never open defiance; it is things left undone, tribes that did not finish, commands obeyed in the parts that suited — and the book of Judges opens with the list. Partial obedience is the ordinary form disobedience takes among religious people, because from a distance it looks like the real thing.

The hardening, and its control. Verse 20 says God hardened their hearts so that they would come out to battle and be destroyed, and Scripture nowhere softens this — it says the same of Pharaoh (Ex. 9:16; Rom. 9:17-18). Verse 19 is the control on it: peace was available, and the writer proves it by naming the one city that took it. Hardening here is judicial rather than arbitrary, God confirming a people in the direction they had already set — while in the same book taking a prostitute out of a burning city and four Gibeonite towns out of the same judgment.

Rest, and the rest that remains. Six words close the conquest: and the land had rest from war. It did not last, and the Bible says so — the next chapters list what was not taken, and Judges opens with the failure. Hebrews draws the conclusion exactly: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on, and so a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-9). The rest under Joshua was real and it was a copy; the one who gives the original carries the same name (Matt. 11:28).
11.examples:
Then: A nation of foot soldiers walked towards massed chariots at Merom, won, and then spent the evening crippling horses and burning the best military equipment in the country because God had told them to. Years of fighting later, an old man cut the giants out of the hills that had terrified his own generation when he was young, and the land was quiet.

Now: Two questions come straight out of this chapter. The first is what your chariots are — the resource, position or security that would make you formidable and would quietly make God optional. Joshua stood on a won field and set fire to his. The second is verse 15: not whether you have disobeyed anything, but whether anything has been left undone. That is where Israel actually lost the land, and it never felt like rebellion at the time.

12.title: The Roll Call of Defeated Kings
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward:<sup>2</sup>Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead,<sup>3</sup>and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah;<sup>4</sup>and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei<sup>5</sup>and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon.<sup>6</sup>Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments,<sup>8</sup>in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):<sup>9</sup>the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;<sup>10</sup>the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;<sup>11</sup>the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;<sup>12</sup>the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;<sup>13</sup>the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;<sup>14</sup>the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;<sup>15</sup>the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;<sup>16</sup>the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;<sup>17</sup>the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;<sup>18</sup>the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;<sup>19</sup>the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;<sup>20</sup>the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;<sup>21</sup>the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;<sup>22</sup>the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;<sup>23</sup>the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one;<sup>24</sup>the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
12.overview:
The chapter is a list, and it repays being read as one. Thirty-one kings, two east of the Jordan and twenty-nine west of it, each entered with a single word after his name: one. It is not a battle poem. It is an inventory, written the way a quartermaster writes, and the flatness is the effect the writer wants. Each name was a throne with an army, a wall and a god behind it, and each is entered in a ledger with a digit beside it.

Notice where the tally starts. Not at Jericho, but east of the river, with Sihon and Og — victories won under Moses before Joshua commanded anything, and Moses is called the servant of the LORD twice in one verse (v. 6). The writer refuses to let the book become a monument to Joshua. What one leader began and another finished is counted in a single column, because it had a single author.

Two things in the list are easy to miss. Fourteen of these kings appear nowhere else in the book — no battle, no story, only a name — so the list is longer than the narrative, and most of what God did in those years was never written up. And the king of Jerusalem is counted (v. 10) although Jerusalem was not taken; the Jebusites were still there in Judges 1:21, and David captures the city four centuries later.

That last point is the hinge into the second half of the book. A defeated king is not an occupied city, and the very next verse says so: there remains yet very much land to possess (13:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Two Kings East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll opens on the wrong side of the river and before Joshua's time. Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon, with his territory mapped from the Arnon to the Jabbok (vv. 1-3), and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, ruling Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan (vv. 4-5). Verse 6 names who beat them and what became of the land: Moses the servant of the LORD, and the eastern tribes who were given it as a possession.
verseByVerse.theology: The tally of the conquest begins with two victories Joshua had nothing to do with. The writer is refusing to let the book be about Joshua — what was begun under one leader and finished under another is counted as a single work with a single author.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses is called the servant of the LORD twice in verse 6, which is the title the book opened with in its first sentence (1:1). Joshua does not get it here. He is still, in this book's vocabulary, the assistant who succeeded, and the honour of the old title is left where it was.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward: Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead, and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah; and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon. Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward.'

The chapter is a list, and the first thing to notice is where the list starts. Not at Jericho. It starts east of the Jordan, before the crossing, in a campaign Joshua did not command.

'Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer... and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei.'

Two kings, and both were formidable. Sihon had refused Israel passage and come out to fight them; Og was one of the last of the Rephaim, the giant peoples, and Deuteronomy records the size of his iron bed as a matter of public curiosity — nine cubits long, something over thirteen feet (Deut. 3:11).

These two had been beaten before Israel ever saw the Jordan, and their story is told in Numbers. Rahab had heard about them on her roof and named them in her list of what God had done (2:10); the Gibeonites cited them in their sales pitch (9:10). They are the reason the whole country was frightened before the invasion started.

'Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.'

The title is given twice in one verse: Moses the servant of the LORD. It is the phrase this book opened with in its very first sentence, and the writer keeps it for Moses.

He could easily have started the tally at chapter 6 and made this a monument to Joshua. He starts it with a dead man's victories instead, which says something about how he understands the whole enterprise. What Moses began and could not finish, Joshua completed — and neither of them is the subject of the sentence. The land was taken by one God across two generations and two leaders, and the accounting is kept in one column.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–24 — Thirty-One, Counted One at a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list turns west, sets the boundaries from Baal-gad to Mount Halak, and runs through every kind of terrain and all six nations (vv. 7-8). Then the roll itself: Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer, Debir and twenty-two more, each one followed by the same single word — one. The northern names come at the end, Hazor among them, and Megiddo, and the chapter closes with the total: in all, thirty-one kings (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Fourteen of these kings are never mentioned anywhere else in the book. Geder, Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor, Goiim, Tirzah — no battle, no story, not a verse. The list is longer than the narrative, which means most of what God did in those years was never written down.
verseByVerse.examples: The king of Jerusalem is counted in verse 10, and Jerusalem was not taken. Judges 1:21 records the Jebusites still living there, and David captures the city some four hundred years later (2 Sam. 5:6-9). A defeated king is not an occupied city, and the very next verse of this book says so: there remains yet very much land to possess (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments, in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments).'

Now the western list, and the two boundary markers set the scale: Baal-gad under Hermon in the far north, Mount Halak on the edge of the Edomite desert in the far south. The whole length of the country.

The clause in brackets is doing quiet work. Joshua gave their land to the tribes — the conquest is already being spoken of as an inheritance being distributed, which is what the next nine chapters are about. The war is finished; the paperwork is not.

'in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.'

Six kinds of country and six nations, and every one had its own way of being difficult. Hill country favours the defender. The lowland is chariot country. The Arabah is furnace-hot below sea level. The Negeb is desert.

Israel is a nation of former slaves who had spent forty years in one kind of terrain, and they have now fought in all six. The geography is listed here for the same reason the kings are: so that the reader can see the size of what was given.

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
verseByVerse.commentary:
'the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one...'

Then the roll itself, and it has a sound. After every name comes the same word: one. Jericho, one. Ai, one. Jerusalem, one.

The effect is deliberately unexciting. This is not a battle poem; it is an inventory, written the way a quartermaster writes, and the flatness is the point. These were thrones. Each name is a walled city with a court, an army and a god, and each one is entered in a ledger with a single digit beside it.

What terrified a generation is now stock-taking.

The early names walk the reader back through the book. Jericho, where the wall fell flat. Ai, where thirty-six men died for a coat buried under a tent. Then Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon in a row — the five kings of the southern coalition, in the order they came out of the cave at Makkedah.

But now look at the third name on the list, because it will not stay quiet. The king of Jerusalem, one.

Adoni-zedek is dead, and Jerusalem is not taken. The book of Judges records that the Jebusites went on living there alongside Benjamin (Judg. 1:21), and the city is not captured until David takes it about four centuries later (2 Sam. 5:6-9). A defeated king is not an occupied city.

That gap between the victory and the possession is the honest note this list is quietly sounding, and the very next verse of the book will say it out loud: you are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one; the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one... the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one; the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.'

The list runs north and finishes, and something becomes obvious as it goes: most of these names have never appeared in this book.

Fourteen of them turn up here and nowhere else — Geder, Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor, Goiim, Tirzah. No battle is described. No story is told. There is nothing but a name and the word one.

The list is longer than the narrative. Whole campaigns happened that the writer never wrote up, and if the account of the conquest were all we had, we would assume Israel fought about eight battles. They fought at least thirty-one, and chapter 11 already told us it took a long time.

Most of what God does never gets written down. There is no chapter for the king of Lasharon, and he is on the list.

Two names on this roll should be stopped over. Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, whose chariots were burned and whose city was ash — entered with the same single digit as everybody else. And Megiddo, the town on the pass that controlled the road across the plain of Jezreel, which is Har-Megiddo, the mountain of Megiddo, the name John hears in his vision for the place where the kings of the whole world are gathered at the end (Rev. 16:16). The king of Megiddo is number twenty-six on Joshua's inventory.

'in all, thirty-one kings.'

The chapter ends by adding them up, and the total is the last word. Not a description, not a prayer, not a doxology — a number.

The New Testament has a passage that does the same thing in the same spirit. Paul, describing what happened at the cross, uses the language of a Roman victory parade: God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, leading them in triumph — and the place he did it was a cross (Col. 2:15). The same accounting is still being kept, and the last enemy on the list has a name too, and it is death (1 Cor. 15:26).

Thirty-one thrones stood in that country, and every one of them had an army, a wall and a god behind it, and not one of them is standing. The LORD God of Israel counted them out, one at a time, and gave the ground they had been sitting on to a nation of former slaves who could not have taken a single city on their own.

12.theology:
One work, two leaders. The roll begins with Moses' victories east of the Jordan, which Joshua had no part in, and the title the servant of the LORD is given to Moses twice in the verse that closes them (v. 6). The conquest is presented as a single act of God spanning two generations and two mediators — what was begun under the man who could not enter, and finished under the man who carried the name Yeshua (see 1:1 and Heb. 4:8).

The list is longer than the story. Fourteen of these kings are named only here. Campaigns were fought, cities fell, men died, and the writer never wrote them up — chapter 11 has already said the war took a long time. If the narrative were all we had, we would assume eight or nine battles. There is no chapter for the king of Lasharon, and he is on the list, which is a fair description of most faithful work in most centuries.

Victory is not yet possession. Jerusalem's king is counted and Jerusalem stands; the Jebusites are still in it generations later (Judg. 1:21). The book is honest about the gap between a decisive victory and a completed occupation, and it puts the honest sentence immediately after the triumphant list. The whole Christian life sits in that gap: the decisive battle fought and won, the ground still being walked.

The accounting continues. A tally of defeated kings is exactly the picture Paul reaches for about the cross — God disarmed the rulers and authorities, put them to open shame, and led them in a triumphal procession (Col. 2:15). The same ledger is still open, and the final entry is already named: the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26).
12.examples:
Then: Somebody sat down and wrote out the names of thirty-one kings with the word one after each, and added them up at the bottom. It is the least dramatic page in the book and it is the receipt for everything in the eleven chapters before it.

Now: Two things to take from a list. Fourteen of these kings have no story, and they are still counted — which anybody doing work nobody writes up should keep. And the king of Jerusalem is on the list while the city is still occupied, which is the shape of the Christian life exactly: the decisive victory is a matter of record, and there is a great deal of ground you have not yet walked on. The next verse of the book says so, and says it to a man who was old and tired.

13.title: Land Still to Be Possessed
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess.<sup>2</sup>This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites<sup>3</sup>(from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim,<sup>4</sup>in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites,<sup>5</sup>and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath,<sup>6</sup>all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."<sup>8</sup>With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them:<sup>9</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon;<sup>10</sup>and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites;<sup>11</sup>and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah;<sup>12</sup>all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out.<sup>13</sup>Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.<sup>14</sup>To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.<sup>15</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans.<sup>16</sup>So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;<sup>17</sup>with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon,<sup>18</sup>and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath,<sup>19</sup>and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,<sup>20</sup>and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,<sup>21</sup>that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.<sup>22</sup>Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain.<sup>23</sup>And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.<sup>24</sup>Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,<sup>26</sup>and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir,<sup>27</sup>and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan.<sup>28</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages.<sup>29</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans.<sup>30</sup>Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities,<sup>31</sup>and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans.<sup>32</sup>These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.<sup>33</sup>But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
13.overview:
The war is over and the book changes shape. What follows is a land registry, and it opens on an old man being told that he is old and that there remains yet very much land to possess (v. 1). Both halves of that are true at once: God gave the whole country in chapter 1, the land had rest from war in chapter 11, and most of it is still occupied here.

The first item on the unfinished list is the Philistine coast, all five cities named. Those cities will trouble Israel for four hundred years — Samson, the capture of the ark, Saul's death on Gilboa — and one of them is Gath, where the giants were left standing two chapters earlier. Four centuries of grief are entered here as unfinished business.

Verse 13 sounds the note that will run through the rest of the book and then open Judges: Geshur and Maacath were not driven out, and they dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. Nobody rebelled; the war simply stopped short of the orders. Centuries later David married a princess of Geshur, and their son Absalom fled there and came back to raise the revolt that nearly ended the kingdom.

And the whole survey is framed by one tribe that receives none of it. Verse 14 and verse 33 stand at either end like bookends, and both say the same thing: Levi has no fields, because the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.
13.theology:
Given and not yet taken. Chapter 1 says God has given the land; chapter 13 says very much of it remains to be possessed; and verse 6 puts both sides in a single sentence — I myself will drive them out, and only allot the land. Israel is told to draw boundaries around fields still held by other people. That is the position of every Christian: in possession of every spiritual blessing and still required to put on the armour and stand.

What is left undrivenout does not stay still. The failure at verse 13 is not defiance and it costs nothing that year. Four hundred years later it is a marriage alliance, a grandson in exile, and a rebellion (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). Scripture keeps records of this kind, and what a generation tolerates because it is tired is inherited by people who did not choose it.

The one name in a list of fields. Balaam is the only person named in the register (v. 22), and what he did should be remembered. He could not curse Israel — blessings came out every time he tried — so he taught Balak to seduce them instead, and twenty-four thousand died at Peor (Num. 31:16). The risen Christ names that tactic when he rebukes a compromising church (Rev. 2:14). The danger to God's people was never chiefly military.

Levi's portion. Eleven tribes walked away from the allotment holding a map. Levi was handed nothing at all, and the explanation is one sentence: the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance. The rest of Scripture treats that as the richest outcome of the day, in surveyor's language — the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot; the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places (Ps. 16:5-6), and God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:26). Everything else in this chapter has since changed hands.
13.examples:
Then: An old soldier was told there was more to do than he had time for, and Israel was ordered to divide up a country it did not yet hold. The tribes were read their allotments one by one, and when the reading finished the men of Levi were still standing there with nothing in their hands.

Now: Two things to take. The first is verse 13, and the question it asks is not whether you have rebelled against God but what you have simply stopped short of finishing, and let go on living in the middle of your life because the war got long. Geshur was a small compromise for about four hundred years. The second is the test at the end: if everything on your side of the register were repossessed tomorrow, what would you still have? The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens on an old man being told he is old. Joshua is advanced in years, and God says it back to him in the same breath as the news that there remains yet very much land to possess (v. 1). What follows is an inventory of what is not yet taken — the whole Philistine coast with its five cities, the Geshurites, the Sidonians, Lebanon as far as Lebo-hamath (vv. 2-5). Then two sentences that sit side by side without apology: I myself will drive them out, and only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance (v. 6). Divide it among the nine and a half tribes (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The land was given in chapter 1 and most of it is still occupied in chapter 13. That is not a contradiction the book is embarrassed by; it states both facts in one verse. The inheritance is theirs by deed and not yet theirs in fact, and the same is true of everything a Christian has in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: The first item on the unconquered list is the Philistines, with all five of their cities named. They are about to be Israel's chief enemy for the next four hundred years — through Samson, through the loss of the ark, through Saul's death on Gilboa, until David finally breaks them. The trouble of four centuries is listed here as unfinished business.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess. This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites (from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim, in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites, and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath, all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you. Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess."'

God tells an old man that he is old. The narrator says it, and then God says it back to him in almost the same words, and there is nothing cruel in it — it is the plainest kind of honesty, spoken to a man who has been fighting for years and is not going to finish.

What he is told alongside it is harder: there remains yet very much land to possess. Not a little. Very much.

Set that against chapter 1, where God said every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, and against 11:23, where Joshua took the whole land and it had rest from war. Both of those are true, and so is this. The land is given, most of it is unoccupied, and the man who was supposed to take it is out of time.

'"This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines... there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron."'

The first entry on the unfinished list is the Philistine coast, and all five of their cities are named. Anyone who knows what comes next will feel the weight of it. Those five cities will harass Israel for the next four hundred years — through Samson, through the capture of the ark, through Saul's death on Mount Gilboa, until David finally breaks them. And one of them is Gath, where the giants were left standing two chapters ago.

Four centuries of trouble are listed here as an item of unfinished business.

'"I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you."'

Then two sentences that ought to pull against each other and do not. God says he will drive them out. God says Israel is to divide the land up and take it.

Israel is told to allot territory that is still full of Philistines — to draw the boundaries of fields nobody has walked on, and hand out title deeds to towns still held by somebody else. That is a strange instruction and it is exactly the instruction the church lives under. Paul writes to people who have every spiritual blessing already and tells them in the next breath to put on the armour and stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — What Was Not Driven Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The record turns to the two and a half tribes east of the Jordan, whose land Moses had given them: the tableland, the cities of Sihon, Gilead, Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og (vv. 8-12). Then verse 13, dropped into the middle of a property register without comment: the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, and they dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. And then verse 14, which is not about land at all: to Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance, because the offerings made by fire to the LORD are their inheritance.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the first of a series that will run through the next nine chapters and then open the book of Judges: the towns that were not taken. Nobody rebelled. The war simply stopped somewhere short of the orders, and the writer keeps a list.
verseByVerse.examples: Geshur did not stay quiet. Centuries later David married Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur; their son Absalom murdered his half-brother and fled to his grandfather's kingdom for three years, and came home to raise the revolt that nearly ended David's reign (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). What was left in the midst of Israel here came back as a son-in-law.

verseByVerse.quote: With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them: from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon; and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites; and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah; all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out. Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward... all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim).'

The eastern register runs through familiar ground: the tableland, Sihon's cities, Gilead, Bashan, Og's kingdom. The land these tribes asked for before the Jordan was ever crossed, now formally entered in the record.

'Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.'

Then one sentence, dropped into a property list with no comment attached.

Nobody rebelled. There is no story here of defiance or of a command refused. The war simply stopped somewhere short of the orders, and two peoples went on living where they had always lived. The phrase to this day means they were still there when the book was written.

This is the first of a series. The same note will sound through the next nine chapters — Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, Manasseh could not, Ephraim did not — and the book of Judges opens by collecting them all into a list and then explaining what it cost.

Geshur did not stay quiet. Four hundred years later, David took a wife named Maacah, the daughter of the king of Geshur, and her son was Absalom. When Absalom murdered his half-brother he ran to his grandfather's kingdom and stayed three years, and when he came home he raised the rebellion that drove his father barefoot out of Jerusalem (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8).

What was tolerated here as a small piece of unfinished business came back, centuries later, as a son-in-law and very nearly ended the house of David.

'To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.'

Then, without transition, one tribe is taken out of the register entirely.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–33 — Fields for Eleven Tribes, and God for One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a survey: Reuben's towns on the tableland (vv. 15-23), Gad's territory in Gilead and the valley (vv. 24-28), and the half-tribe of Manasseh with all Bashan and the sixty towns of Jair (vv. 29-31). One person is named in the middle of all this property — Balaam son of Beor, killed with the sword (v. 22). Verse 32 closes the eastern register, and then the chapter ends where verse 14 began, and says it more plainly: to Levi, Moses gave no inheritance, for the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The lists are dull on purpose and they are a receipt. Every boundary and village in them was a sentence spoken to a childless man in Genesis, and here it is surveyed, divided and handed over. God's promises do not arrive as sentiments; they arrive as addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter is framed by the tribe that got none of it. Verse 14 and verse 33 sit at either end of the survey like bookends, and both say the same thing in different words: Levi has no fields, and Levi has the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans. So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba; with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon, and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath, and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley, and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth, that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land. Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain. And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans... with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon, and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath, and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah...'

Now the survey proper begins, and it reads like what it is: a land registry. Town after town, boundary after boundary, for three tribes.

It is easy to skim and there is one thing to see before doing so. Every one of these names started life as a promise made to a man with no children, standing in a country he did not own, being told to count the stars. Here it is, four hundred years later, written up as a schedule of properties with the villages listed.

God's promises do not arrive as feelings. They arrive as addresses.

'Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain.'

Then, in the middle of a chapter about fields, a man.

Balaam is the only person named in this entire register, and he is worth the interruption. He was the prophet-for-hire whom Balak paid to curse Israel and who found he could not do it — every time he opened his mouth a blessing came out instead. He is the great comic failure of the book of Numbers.

What he did afterwards is not comic at all. Unable to curse them, he advised Balak on how to ruin them from the inside: send the women, and let Israel destroy itself at Peor (Num. 31:16). Twenty-four thousand died in that plague, and it worked when cursing had not.

The New Testament remembers him for exactly this. The risen Christ, writing to a church that was tolerating compromise, names the problem as the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel (Rev. 2:14).

So the one human name in a list of real estate is a reminder that the danger to God's people was never chiefly military. Nobody could curse them. They had to be talked into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans. Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah, and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir, and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan. This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages. And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans. Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities, and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans. These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho. But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad... And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh... Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities... These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.'

Gad gets the middle of the eastern territory, half-Manasseh gets Bashan and sixty towns, and the register closes with a note about where the distribution was made: the plains of Moab, on the wrong side of the river, by a man who never crossed it.

'But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.'

The chapter ends by coming back to the one tribe left out, and saying it more plainly than verse 14 did.

Picture the day. The tribes are drawn up and the allotments are read out. Reuben is given the tableland with Heshbon and Dibon and the towns around them. Gad is given Gilead and the valley. Manasseh is given Bashan and sixty cities with walls. Men are hearing the names of places they will farm, and boundary lines their grandchildren will argue about, and each family walks away holding something they can stand on.

Levi is handed nothing. No fields. No boundary stones. No town with a wall round it. When the reading is finished, the men of Levi are still standing there with empty hands, and the reason is given in one sentence: the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.

That could be read as a consolation prize, and the rest of the Bible will not let it be read that way. A man who has heard this verse and understood it writes: the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance (Ps. 16:5-6). That is surveyor's language — portion, lot, lines, inheritance — used by a man describing God.

Another gets to the bottom of it: whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:25-26).

Here is the test the chapter puts to a reader, and it is a hard one. Everything Reuben was given that morning could be taken away, and eventually was — Assyria carried those eastern tribes off first, and the tableland belongs to other people now. Every acre in this chapter has changed hands many times.

Ask what you would still have if everything on your side of the register were repossessed. The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

14.title: Caleb's Inheritance
14.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit.<sup>2</sup>Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes.<sup>3</sup>For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.<sup>4</sup>For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance.<sup>5</sup>The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.<sup>6</sup>Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.<sup>7</sup>I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart.<sup>8</sup>But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God.<sup>9</sup>And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'<sup>10</sup>And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old.<sup>11</sup>I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming.<sup>12</sup>So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."<sup>13</sup>Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.<sup>14</sup>Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
14.overview:
The allotment of the western land begins by lot — a method that removes every human lever, so that no tribe can lobby and no family can be quietly cheated (Prov. 16:33). And then the register stops for one man.

Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal, and the two of them are the only adults left alive from Kadesh-barnea. He rehearses the day: ten men came back and made the nation's heart melt, and he did not — I wholly followed the LORD my God, a phrase used of him four times in this chapter. Being right cost him thirty-eight years in the desert with the men who were wrong.

He is eighty-five, he has counted the years exactly, and his request is not for a quiet valley: give me this hill country, the ground where the Anakim are, with great fortified cities. The giants that produced the report that cost a nation forty years are still sitting on the land he is asking for — and the last clause of the request keeps it from being bravado: it may be that the LORD will be with me.

He gets Hebron, which is the one place in Canaan already thick with promise: Abraham's oaks, and the cave of Machpelah where the patriarchs are buried. Its old name was Kiriath-arba, the city of Arba, and Arba was the greatest of the giants. An old man asked for the town named after the biggest man in the country, and the chapter ends, and the land had rest from war.
14.theology:
The lot, and who is really deciding. Land drawn by lot looks like chance and functions as its opposite: it removes lobbying, favour and force from the distribution entirely. Every family that ends up on hard ground knows exactly whose decision it was — the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).

Wholly followed. The phrase is repeated four times over one man (vv. 8, 9, 14, and Moses' oath in v. 9), and the Hebrew is stronger than English carries — something like filled up after the LORD. It is the exact opposite of the verdict the rest of these chapters keep recording about the tribes: they did not drive out, they could not drive out, they left them living in the midst.

Faithfulness is not exempted from other people's consequences. Caleb was right at forty and it bought him thirty-eight years in a wilderness he had argued against, burying men who had been wrong. God kept him alive through all of it and gave him the ground at eighty-five. Being on the right side of a decision does not remove a believer from the country that made the wrong one.

Asking for the giants. The request in verse 12 is for the hardest terrain on the map, named with its difficulties attached — and it ends it may be that the LORD will be with me. Certainty about the promise and humility about himself, in one sentence. Hebrews tells sluggish Christians to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises (Heb. 6:12), and this is what that looks like at eighty-five.
14.examples:
Then: An old man walked up to the man dividing the country and asked for the one district everybody else was avoiding, because God had mentioned it to him forty-five years earlier and he had not forgotten the address.

Now: Two questions come out of this chapter, and the second is the harder. What promise are you still counting the years on — and would you recognise it if it arrived? Caleb knew the number of years exactly. And then: what would you ask God for if you were sure he had already granted it? Most requests get smaller with age. Caleb's got steeper, and he still would not say more than it may be that the LORD will be with me.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The western allotment begins, and the writer records who did it: Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes (v. 1).
