The method is stated plainly — their inheritance was by lot (v. 2) — and the arithmetic is explained: two and a half tribes are already settled east of the Jordan, Joseph counts as two tribes because of Manasseh and Ephraim, and Levi gets no territory at all, only towns to live in with pasture (vv. 3-4). Verse 5 closes it: they did as the LORD commanded, and allotted the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Drawing lots looks like leaving things to chance and is the opposite. It removes every human lever — no tribe can lobby, no elder can trade a favour, and the strongest tribe cannot argue its way to the best ground. The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).
verseByVerse.examples: Levi is dealt with in half a verse: no portion, only cities to live in and grazing for the animals. The tribe that carried the ark across the Jordan ends the day with somewhere to sleep and nowhere to farm.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit. Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes. For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them. For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance. The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit. Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses.'

The land is divided by lot, and the priest is named before the general. Whatever this is, it is not a military distribution of spoils.

Casting lots sounds to a modern ear like leaving matters to chance, and it is the opposite of that. What a lot removes is human leverage. No tribe can lobby for the coastal plain; no elder can call in a favour; the largest tribe cannot argue its way onto the best soil, and the smallest cannot be quietly cheated. Every family that ends up somewhere difficult knows exactly who put them there, and the proverb says it plainly: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).

'And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance.'

Levi is disposed of in half a verse: no portion, some towns to live in, and grass for the animals. That is the second time in two chapters, and it will come round a third time in chapter 21.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — I Wholly Followed the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then one man steps out of the crowd. Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal and opens with a reminder that they two are the only men alive who were there: you know what the LORD said to Moses... concerning you and me (v. 6). He rehearses it — forty years old when he was sent to spy out the land, and he brought back the report as it was in his heart (v. 7); his brothers made the people's heart melt, and he did not (v. 8); and Moses swore that the ground his foot had walked on would be his, because he wholly followed the LORD (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase runs through the chapter four times and it is Caleb's whole testimony: he wholly followed the LORD. The Hebrew is stronger than English can easily carry — it is the language of being filled up with following, of going after God with nothing held back.
verseByVerse.examples: Twice he is called the Kenizzite (vv. 6, 14), and Kenaz is an Edomite clan name (Gen. 36:11, 15). The most single-minded Israelite in the book was very probably not born an Israelite at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God. And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me."'

One man steps out of a delegation and opens with the two of them. Concerning you and me — because Joshua and Caleb are the only two men standing in that camp who were adults at Kadesh-barnea. Everybody else present was a child then, or unborn. The rest of that generation is buried in the desert behind them.

He is also called the Kenizzite, and the term is repeated at the end of the chapter. Kenaz is a clan name that turns up in the family of Esau (Gen. 36:11, 15), which makes it likely that Caleb's people came into Judah from outside. The man who is about to be commended four times for following God with his whole heart was, in all probability, not born into the covenant at all.

'"I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God."'

His account of the worst day in Israel's history is brief and it does not spare anyone. Ten men came back and made a nation's heart melt — that verb again, the one used of Jericho and of the kings of Canaan. What frightened Israel out of the land was not the Anakim. It was a report.

Caleb says what he did instead: I wholly followed the LORD my God. The phrase will be used of him four times in this chapter. The Hebrew behind wholly followed is literally something like filled up after — going after God with the whole of oneself and nothing kept in reserve.

Notice what it cost him to be right. Being one of two men who told the truth did not get Caleb the land at forty; it got him forty more years in a desert with the people who had been wrong. Faithfulness bought him a share in everybody else's consequences.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Give Me This Hill Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caleb does the arithmetic out loud. Forty-five years since Moses swore it, all of them spent watching a generation die in a desert, and the LORD has kept him alive through every one (v. 10). He is eighty-five, and claims to be as strong for war and for going and coming as he was at forty (v. 11). And then the request, which is not for a quiet field: give me this hill country — the ground where the Anakim are, with great fortified cities — and a sentence of pure humility at the end of it: it may be that the LORD will be with me (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks for the hardest ground on the map. The giants that had frightened ten men into a forty-year detour are still living in those hills, and the eighty-five-year-old who brought back the minority report is asking for that particular address.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause keeps the whole speech from being bravado. Not the LORD will be with me, but it may be. Forty-five years of waiting had not made him presumptuous about God; he asks for giants and does not tell God what to do about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old."'

He has been counting. Forty-five years, and he knows the number, because a man who is waiting on a specific promise keeps the date.

Consider what those years contained. Thirty-eight of them were spent walking in circles for a decision he had argued against, watching the men who made it die one funeral at a time. Then seven years of war. He was forty when God swore it and he is eighty-five now, and the promise has been in his pocket the whole time.

'"I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming."'

That is either a remarkable piece of preservation or an old man's optimism, and the chapter treats it as the first. What is not in doubt is the direction of it. Most men at eighty-five are taking an inventory of what they can no longer do. Caleb is applying for work.

'"So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."'

Now the request, and it is the sentence the chapter exists for.

He does not ask for a quiet valley near water. He asks for the hill country — and then, in case anybody is under any illusion, he says exactly what is up there. The Anakim. Great fortified cities. The very things that produced the report that cost a nation forty years are still sitting on the ground he is requesting.

Then the last clause, which keeps the whole speech from being bluster: it may be that the LORD will be with me. Not a prediction. Not a claim on God. Forty-five years of waiting had made him certain about the promise and left him entirely humble about himself.

That is what a finished faith sounds like. It asks for the giants and does not presume on God, in the same breath.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron (v. 13), and the writer notes that Hebron belongs to Caleb's family to this day, and gives the reason once more: because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel (v. 14). Verse 15 adds the town's old name, Kiriath-arba, with a note that Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim — and then the sentence that closed the conquest returns: and the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.theology: Of all the ground in Canaan, Hebron is the one place already thick with promise. Abraham lived there under the oaks, and bought the cave of Machpelah there as the only piece of the land he ever owned — the grave where he, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried (Gen. 23; 49:31). Caleb asks for the family plot.
verseByVerse.examples: The town was named after a giant. Kiriath-arba means the city of Arba, and Arba was the greatest of the Anakim. An old man asked for a town named after the biggest man in the country, and got it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance. Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance. Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel.'

Joshua blesses him first and then hands over the deed. Two old men, the last of a generation, settling a promise made in a desert nearly half a century before.

Of all the ground on the map, look at what Caleb has asked for. Hebron is where Abraham pitched his tent by the oaks of Mamre. It is where he bought the cave of Machpelah for four hundred shekels — the only square foot of Canaan that any patriarch ever legally owned — and it is the grave of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah (Gen. 23; 49:31).

Caleb, who may well have come into Israel from Edomite stock, asked for the family plot. The outsider wanted the place where the promise was buried.

'Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.'

The writer adds the old name almost as a footnote, and it is not a footnote. Kiriath-arba means the city of Arba, and Arba was the greatest of the giants. The town Caleb spent forty-five years waiting for was named after the biggest man in Canaan.

An eighty-five-year-old asked for the city named after a giant, and the chapter ends: and the land had rest from war.

The letter to the Hebrews, urging Christians not to become sluggish, tells them to be imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises (Heb. 6:12). It does not name Caleb. It could have. He believed God at forty, said so when it was unpopular, paid for it with thirty-eight years he had not earned, and then walked up to the hardest hill in the country at eighty-five and asked for it by name.

15.title: The Allotment of Judah
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south.<sup>2</sup>And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward.<sup>3</sup>It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka,<sup>4</sup>passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary.<sup>5</sup>And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.<sup>7</sup>And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel.<sup>8</sup>Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).<sup>10</sup>And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah.<sup>11</sup>The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea.<sup>12</sup>And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>13</sup>According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak).<sup>14</sup>And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.<sup>15</sup>And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher.<sup>16</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>17</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.<sup>18</sup>When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?"<sup>19</sup>She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>20</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>21</sup>The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,<sup>22</sup>Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,<sup>23</sup>Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,<sup>24</sup>Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,<sup>25</sup>Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),<sup>26</sup>Amam, Shema, Moladah,<sup>27</sup>Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet,<sup>28</sup>Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah,<sup>29</sup>Baalah, Iim, Ezem,<sup>30</sup>Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,<sup>31</sup>Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,<sup>32</sup>Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages.<sup>33</sup>And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,<sup>34</sup>Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam,<sup>35</sup>Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,<sup>36</sup>Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages.<sup>37</sup>Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,<sup>38</sup>Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel,<sup>39</sup>Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,<sup>40</sup>Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish,<sup>41</sup>Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>42</sup>Libnah, Ether, Ashan,<sup>43</sup>Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,<sup>44</sup>Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages.<sup>45</sup>Ekron, with its towns and its villages;<sup>46</sup>from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.<sup>47</sup>Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.<sup>48</sup>And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,<sup>49</sup>Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),<sup>50</sup>Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,<sup>51</sup>Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages.<sup>52</sup>Arab, Dumah, Eshan,<sup>53</sup>Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,<sup>54</sup>Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages.<sup>55</sup>Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,<sup>56</sup>Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,<sup>57</sup>Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages.<sup>58</sup>Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,<sup>59</sup>Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages.<sup>60</sup>Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages.<sup>61</sup>In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,<sup>62</sup>Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages.<sup>63</sup>But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
15.overview:
Judah is dealt with first and at greatest length — sixty-three verses, a perimeter walked landmark by landmark, and about a hundred and twenty towns counted in batches. It is the longest inventory in the book and it is a deed of property.

Two names on the boundary are not neutral. The northern line runs through the Valley of Achor (v. 7), where a man of Judah was buried under stones for stealing from God; and it runs up the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (v. 8), ge-hinnom, which comes into the New Testament as Gehenna. Judah's title deeds are drawn through the valley of its own worst day and past the valley that became a word for hell.

In the middle of the register the writer stops for a family. Caleb clears the three named giants out of Hebron; Othniel — who will be Israel's first judge (Judg. 3:9-11) — takes a town to win a wife; and Achsah gets off her donkey and asks her father for water, because a field in the Negeb without springs is not a farm. He gives her the upper springs and the lower springs, which is more than she asked.

And the last verse is not a total. The Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Judah could not drive out. The greatest tribe, with the largest allotment, ends its chapter unable to take the one city on its border that mattered — and it stays in foreign hands for four hundred years.
15.theology:
Promises arrive as addresses. Forty verses of town names are the cashing of a sentence spoken to a childless man who was told to count the stars. God does not fulfil his word in the abstract; he fulfils it in Kabzeel and Jagur and Adadah, until somebody has to count them in batches. Biblical language about inheritance can float free and become a mood, and this chapter nails it to a map.

Two valleys on one boundary. Achor is where Achan of Judah was stoned and buried (7:24-26); Hinnom becomes Gehenna. Judah's surveyors walked past both every time they checked the northern line. And Hosea took the first of those names and turned it into a door of hope (Hos. 2:15) — God has a habit of reissuing the address of the worst thing that ever happened.

Asking well. Achsah has land and no water, so she gets down off her donkey and says give me a blessing and then names the thing she actually needs (vv. 18-19). Her father, who waited forty-five years for one promise and then asked for a mountain full of giants, gives her both the upper and the lower springs. The man who knew how to ask raised a daughter who knew how to ask, and neither of them was refused.

Could not. The verb changes at the end. In 13:13 Israel did not drive out; in 15:63 Judah could not. A hundred and twenty towns delivered exactly as promised, and one that was not — and the one was the city where the temple would stand and, outside its wall, the hill where the Lion of Judah would be crucified.
15.examples:
Then: Surveyors walked a boundary past a heap of stones over a thief and along a ravine that would one day give hell its name, counted a hundred and twenty towns into batches, and finished by writing down the name of the one city they could not take.

Now: Take the two verses in the middle. Achsah had been given something real that was useless without one more thing, and she asked for it directly and got more than she named. Most Christians ask God for the field and never mention the springs. And take the last verse as the honest companion to it: a great deal delivered, and one thing standing that will not move yet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first and largest allotment is Judah's, and the chapter opens by walking its perimeter. South to the wilderness of Zin on the edge of Edom (v. 1), east along the Salt Sea (v. 5), then the northern line traced landmark by landmark — Beth-hoglah, the stone of Bohan, the Valley of Achor, En-shemesh, En-rogel (vv. 6-7) — up the Valley of the Son of Hinnom past the shoulder of the Jebusite, that is, Jerusalem (v. 8), out west past Beth-shemesh and Timnah and Ekron, and ending at the Great Sea (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Two names on this boundary are not neutral. The line runs through the Valley of Achor, where a man of Judah was buried under stones for stealing from God (7:24-26); and it runs along the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, ge-hinnom, which the New Testament knows as Gehenna. Judah's title deeds are drawn through the valley of its own worst day and past the valley that became a word for hell.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 puts Jerusalem on the boundary and calls it the Jebusite. The city that will one day be the centre of everything is at this point a foreign town on the edge of somebody's farmland, and verse 63 says what happened when Judah tried to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south. And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward. It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel. Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim. Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim). And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah. The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea. And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south.'

Judah is dealt with first and at greatest length, which is the writer's way of saying what this tribe is going to be. The lot has fallen, and what follows is a surveyor walking the perimeter.

Most of the names on this circuit mean nothing to a modern reader and meant a great deal to an ancient one: a spring, a ridge, a stone somebody had set up. Two of them should be stopped at.

'And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal.'

The northern boundary of Judah runs through the Valley of Achor.

That is the valley where a heap of stones was raised over Achan, who was buried there with everything he owned for taking a Babylonian coat out of Jericho — and Achan was a man of Judah (7:1, 18). This tribe's title deeds run straight through the site of its own worst day. Every generation of surveyors after this walked past the stones.

'Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem).'

Then the second name. The Valley of the Son of Hinnom is ge-hinnom in Hebrew, which comes into Greek as Gehenna — the word Jesus uses more than anyone else in the New Testament for final judgment. In Joshua's day it is simply a ravine outside a Canaanite town. Later it will be where children are burned to Molech, and later still a name for hell itself.

Judah's boundary is drawn between the valley where God judged a man of Judah and the valley that becomes the Bible's word for judgment. The property description is grimmer than any of the surveyors knew.

The town on that shoulder is called the Jebusite. Jerusalem is at this point a foreign city on the edge of somebody's farm, mentioned in passing as a landmark. Everything the Bible will eventually say about that city is still ahead of it, and Judah cannot take it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register stops for a family. Caleb receives Hebron by the LORD's own command (v. 13) and drives out the three sons of Anak by name (v. 14), then moves on Debir and offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes it (vv. 15-16). Othniel his kinsman takes it and marries her (v. 17). Then a scene: she urges him to ask her father for a field, gets down off her donkey, and asks Caleb herself — give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water — and he gives her the upper springs and the lower springs (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The three giants of verse 14 are named: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. These are the men the ten spies described forty-five years earlier when they said Israel looked like grasshoppers. An eighty-five-year-old took their town, and the writer troubles to give their names because they had been a legend and now they are a line in a property record.
verseByVerse.examples: Othniel goes on to become the first of the judges, the man God raises up to deliver Israel when the nation collapses in the next book (Judg. 3:9-11). Israel's first deliverer is introduced here as a young man who captured a town to win a wife.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak). And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak. And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron. And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.'

The land register stops for a family, and it begins with an old man doing what he said he would do.

See that the giants are given names. Sheshai, Ahiman, Talmai. These are the men the spies had reported on forty-five years earlier — the ones who made a nation feel like grasshoppers. They had been a legend for two generations, and they are cleared out of Hebron in half a verse by a man of eighty-five, and the writer records their names the way an estate agent records a previous owner.

'And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir... And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.'

Caleb is still fighting and still recruiting. The offer is of its time and it is also shrewd: he is looking for a son-in-law with nerve, and the test is a walled town.

Othniel takes it. Remember the name, because the next book of the Bible opens with Israel collapsing into idolatry, and the first man God raises up to rescue them is this one — Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came (Judg. 3:9-11). Israel's first judge is introduced here as a young man who captured a town to win a wife.

'When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.'

The best scene in the chapter, and it takes two verses.

She has been given land in the Negeb, which is dry country. A field down there without water is a technicality, not a farm. So she urges her husband to ask, and then gets off the donkey and asks her father herself, and what she says is give me a blessing.

Then the specific request: springs. Not more land — she has land. She asks for the one thing that makes the land she already has worth having.

Caleb, who spent forty-five years waiting on one promise and then asked for a mountain full of giants, does not haggle with his daughter. He gives her the upper springs and the lower springs, which is more than she asked for. The man who knew how to ask has raised a daughter who knows how to ask.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–63 — A Hundred and Twenty Towns, and One That Would Not Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a list, grouped by region and counted as it goes: twenty-nine towns in the far south towards Edom (vv. 21-32), then the lowland in four groups of fourteen, sixteen, nine and the Philistine coast (vv. 33-47), then the hill country in six groups (vv. 48-60), then six more in the wilderness by the Salt Sea (vv. 61-62). And then the last verse, which is not a total: the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites live with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day (v. 63).
verseByVerse.theology: The litany repays reading aloud once rather than studying. It is a deed of property running to a hundred and twenty addresses, and every one of them was a sentence spoken to a man who owned nothing in this country but a burial cave.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on a failure, and the wording has shifted. Earlier the writer said Israel did not drive out Geshur and Maacath (13:13). Here he says Judah could not drive out the Jebusites. Jerusalem stays in foreign hands for another four hundred years, until a shepherd from Bethlehem takes it (2 Sam. 5:6-9).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans. The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, Ziph, Telem, Bealoth, Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor), Amam, Shema, Moladah, Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet, Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah, Baalah, Iim, Ezem, Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah, Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah, Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages. And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah, Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam, Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah, Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages. Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel, Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon, Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish, Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages. Libnah, Ether, Ashan, Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib, Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages. Ekron, with its towns and its villages; from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages. Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans. The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, Ziph, Telem, Bealoth...'

Then the register proper, and it runs for forty verses. Towns in the far south towards Edom, twenty-nine of them with their villages. Towns in the lowland, counted in groups of fourteen, sixteen and nine. Then the Philistine coast — Ekron, Ashdod, Gaza — which is listed as Judah's and is not Judah's, since chapter 13 has already said the Philistines were never driven out.

This is the point at which most readers' eyes slide down the page, and the sliding repays resisting for a moment, because the flatness of the list is doing something.

Every name here is a real place with real people in it: a well, a threshing floor, a few dozen families, somebody's grandmother. Ziklag is in this list, and David will live there as an outlaw. Beersheba is in it, where Abraham planted a tamarisk tree. Adullam is in it, where David hid in a cave.

The whole catalogue is the cashing of a promise made to one childless man who was told to look at the stars. God does not fulfil his word in the abstract. He fulfils it in Kabzeel and Jagur and Adadah, town by town, until a surveyor has to count them in batches to keep track.

Sentences of Scripture about inheritance can float free and become moods. This chapter nails them to a map.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages. Arab, Dumah, Eshan, Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah, Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages. Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah, Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah, Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages. Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages. Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages. In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages. But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages... In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages.'

The list finishes in the hill country and then out in the wilderness by the Salt Sea, with six towns that are barely towns. The last of them is Engedi, an oasis on a cliff above the Dead Sea where David will one day hide from Saul and cut the corner off his robe rather than kill him.

The counting is meticulous to the end — eleven cities, nine cities, ten, six, two, six — and then the chapter stops counting and says something else.

'But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.'

The last verse of the longest inventory in the book is a failure, and the wording has changed. In chapter 13 the writer said Israel did not drive out Geshur and Maacath. Here he says Judah could not drive out the Jebusites.

So the greatest tribe, with the largest allotment and a hundred and twenty towns to its name, ends its chapter unable to take the one city on its boundary that mattered. Jerusalem stays in foreign hands for another four centuries. The Jebusites are still there in the book of Judges, still there under Saul, and it takes a shepherd from Bethlehem to walk up that hill and take it (2 Sam. 5:6-9).

It is the honest shape of this whole section of the book. A hundred and twenty towns delivered exactly as promised, and one that was not — and the one is the site of the temple, and the hill outside its wall.

Judah did not know what was on that ridge. The tribe whose boundary ran through the Valley of Trouble and along the ravine that would give hell its name could not take the city where the lamb of God would be crucified. It was left standing, in foreign hands, on the border of the tribe out of which the Lion of Judah would come.

16.title: The Allotment of Ephraim
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel.<sup>2</sup>Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites.<sup>3</sup>Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea.<sup>4</sup>The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.<sup>5</sup>The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon,<sup>6</sup>and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah,<sup>7</sup>then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan.<sup>8</sup>From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans,<sup>9</sup>together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.<sup>10</sup>However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
16.overview:
The house of Joseph receives a broad band across the middle of the country, and there are two tribes here rather than one because of a deathbed in Egypt: Jacob adopted Joseph's two sons as his own and crossed his hands to put the younger in front (Gen. 48:5, 14). The brother who was sold to traders ends up with a double share of the land his brothers were haggling over him in.

Ephraim's boundaries are traced in the usual manner, and towns are set apart for Ephraim inside Manasseh's territory so that the two are deliberately interleaved. Then the chapter ends on a single verse that is the reason it is in the Bible.

They did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer... but have been made to do forced labor (v. 10). Ephraim did not lose a battle for Gezer. Ephraim found an arrangement. Removing an entrenched population from a fortified town was expensive; a permanent labour supply was profitable. The command was quietly replaced by a policy, and everybody did well out of it.

The postscript is four hundred years long. Israel never took Gezer. Pharaoh king of Egypt eventually captured it, burned it, killed the Canaanites living there, and gave the town to his daughter as a dowry when she married Solomon (1 Kings 9:16).
16.theology:
Compromise is usually profitable. Nobody in Ephraim decided to disobey God. They made a practical decision about something God had told them to end, and the practical decision paid better than obedience would have. That is what makes verse 10 worth more attention than the nine boundary verses before it: it is the ordinary shape of disobedience among people who would be shocked to be called disobedient.

What is kept because it is useful does not stay in its place. The book of Judges opens by collecting all these verses into one list and then delivering the verdict: the peoples left in the land became thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3). Israel finished up worshipping the gods of the labour force.

Unfinished business gets finished by somebody else. Gezer was never taken by Israel. An Egyptian king took it four centuries later and handed it over as a wedding present (1 Kings 9:16). What God's people leave undone does not quietly disappear; it is settled eventually, by other hands and on other terms.
16.examples:
Then: A tribe looked at a fortified town full of people it had been told to remove, weighed the cost, and put them on the payroll instead. It was the sensible decision and it was still there when the book was written.

Now: The test in this chapter is not whether there is open sin in your life. It is whether there is something God told you to end that you have instead made useful — the arrangement that is easier to keep than to break, and that happens to pay. Ephraim's Canaanites were not rebels in the camp. They were staff.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lot of the house of Joseph runs from the Jordan at Jericho up into the hill country to Bethel (v. 1), on past Ataroth and the territory of the Archites (v. 2), down west through Lower Beth-horon to Gezer, and out to the sea (v. 3). Verse 4 records the two tribes taking it: Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph counts as two tribes because Jacob adopted his two sons as his own on his deathbed, crossing his hands to put the younger in front (Gen. 48:5, 14). The boy who was sold into Egypt gets a double share of the country his brothers sold him out of.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel. Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites. Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea. The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel... The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.'

The territory runs right across the middle of the country, from the Jordan to the Mediterranean, and it is given to Joseph — who has been dead for a very long time.

The reason there are two tribes here rather than one goes back to a bedroom in Egypt. Jacob, dying, took Joseph's two sons and adopted them as his own: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are (Gen. 48:5). Then he crossed his hands over their heads and put the younger boy in front of the older, and would not be corrected about it.

So the brother who was thrown into a pit and sold to traders gets a double portion of the land his brothers were bargaining over him in. Nobody in this chapter says anything about that. The map says it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim's perimeter is traced in the usual way: east at Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon (v. 5), north at Michmethath, then round by Taanath-shiloh and Janoah (v. 6), down to Ataroth and Naarah, touching Jericho and ending at the Jordan (v. 7), and west from Tappuah along the brook Kanah to the sea (v. 8). Verse 9 adds the towns set apart for Ephraim inside Manasseh's territory.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is a small administrative kindness with a long history behind it. Ephraim gets towns inside his brother's allotment, which means the two tribes of Joseph are deliberately kept interleaved rather than cleanly separated.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon, and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah, then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan. From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans, together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon... From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea.'

The perimeter walk again: ridges, brooks, towns and a coastline. Ephraim gets the central hill country, which is good ground and defensible, and it will hold the tabernacle at Shiloh for most of the next four hundred years.

'together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.'

Verse 9 records a small piece of administration with a family history under it. Ephraim is given towns inside Manasseh's territory — the two brothers are deliberately interleaved rather than cleanly divided.

Whatever the practical reason, the effect is that the sons of Joseph cannot forget each other. Their fields touch. And the next chapter will show what these two tribes do when they have a grievance, which is come as a pair.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse, and it is the point of the chapter: however, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not that Ephraim lost a battle. It is that they found an arrangement. Removing the Canaanites was hard and expensive; putting them to work was profitable. The command was replaced by a labour policy, and everybody did rather well out of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Gezer never became Israelite by conquest. Four centuries later Pharaoh king of Egypt captured it, burned it and killed the Canaanites living in it, and handed it over as a dowry when his daughter married Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). Ephraim's unfinished business was eventually settled by a foreign king, as a wedding present.

verseByVerse.quote: However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.'

One verse, and it is the reason this chapter is in the Bible.

Everything before it is a boundary description. This is a policy decision, and read it carefully, because the failure is not what a reader expects. Ephraim did not lose a battle for Gezer. Ephraim found an arrangement.

The Canaanites stayed, and they were put to work. That is the whole sentence: not driven out, made to do forced labour. It is not defeat; it is profit. Somebody looked at the cost of removing an entrenched population from a fortified town and looked at the value of a permanent labour supply, and made the sensible decision.

This is the second time the book has recorded something like it, and it will not be the last. The pattern should be named, because it is the ordinary form spiritual compromise takes. Nobody in Ephraim decided to disobey God. They decided to be practical about something God had told them to end, and the practical arrangement was genuinely more profitable than obedience.

What a person keeps because it is useful will not stay in the servants' quarters. Judges, which is the sequel to all these verses, gives the verdict in advance: the peoples left in the land became thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3). Israel ended up worshipping the gods of the people they had put to work.

Gezer has a postscript that says everything. Israel never took it. Four hundred years later Pharaoh king of Egypt marched up, captured Gezer, burned it, killed the Canaanites who were living in it, and gave the town to his daughter as a wedding present when she married Solomon (1 Kings 9:16).

The job Ephraim declined to finish was eventually done by an Egyptian, as a dowry. What God's people leave undone does not stay undone; it simply gets done by somebody else, on somebody else's terms, a long time later.

17.title: The Allotment of Manasseh and the Complaint of Joseph
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war.<sup>2</sup>And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans.<sup>3</sup>Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>4</sup>They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.<sup>5</sup>Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan,<sup>6</sup>because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah.<sup>8</sup>The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea,<sup>10</sup>the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar.<sup>11</sup>Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath.<sup>12</sup>Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>13</sup>Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?"<sup>15</sup>And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you."<sup>16</sup>The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel."<sup>17</sup>Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only,<sup>18</sup>but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
17.overview:
Manasseh's register is interrupted almost as soon as it begins. Zelophehad had no sons, and his five daughters are named in full — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah — for the fourth time in Scripture. They come to the priest and the general and cite a ruling: the LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers. Years earlier they had brought that case to Moses himself, who took it to God, and God said they were right and made it law (Num. 27:1-11). Now they hold a new administration to it, and Manasseh ends up with ten portions instead of five.

Then two verbs in two verses that between them tell the story of this whole half of the book. Manasseh could not take the six best towns in the north (v. 12) — and then, when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labour and still did not drive them out (v. 13). The excuse expired and the arrangement stayed.

The chapter ends with the house of Joseph asking for more land on the grounds that God has blessed them. Joshua — himself an Ephraimite, being lobbied by his own tribe — offers them no extra allotment at all. He offers them a forest and an axe.

Their real objection then comes out: the good land has iron chariots on it. Joshua does not deny it. He names the chariots himself, adds that the enemy is strong, and repeats the instruction with a promise attached: the hill country shall be yours, and you shall drive them out.
17.theology:
Five women in a land register. The daughters of Zelophehad are the most frequently named women in the Pentateuch, and the reason is a case they argued and won. They did not plead; they cited a judgment and asked that it be honoured by a new administration, and it was. In a section of Scripture built out of place names, five sisters are named and named again.

When the excuse expires. Could not in verse 12 is stated as fact, not sin; some things really are beyond a person's strength for a season. Verse 13 is the sting: when the people of Israel grew strong, the reason for the failure passed — and the arrangement made in weakness was kept because by then it paid. That is the sequence to watch in oneself, and it is not the same sin as the first failure.

Blessing as a claim. The house of Joseph argues that because God has blessed them they are owed more room (v. 14). Joshua takes the argument seriously and turns it round: if you are numerous, behave like it — and gives them a forest to clear. Growth is not a title to easier ground.

He refuses his own tribe. Joshua is an Ephraimite (Num. 13:8, 16), and these are his own people asking their own kinsman for special treatment. He gives them nothing but work and a promise, and he does not pretend the iron chariots are not there — he names them, adds that the enemy is strong, and repeats the instruction anyway. Honest leadership tells people the size of the difficulty and sends them at it.
17.examples:
Then: Five sisters held a new government to a promise the previous one had made, and got their fields. A tribe with the largest allotment in the country came to complain that it was not enough, and went away with permission to cut down a forest.

Now: Verse 13 is the searching one. Most people can name something they could not deal with at the time — and the honest question is not whether the excuse was true then, but whether it is still true. Israel grew strong and kept the arrangement. And when the house of Joseph finally said what was really wrong, it was not the size of the land but the iron chariots on the part of it worth having. Joshua's answer named the chariots and did not change the instruction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Five Women in a Land Register
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh's allotment begins with Machir, a man of war, who has Gilead and Bashan (v. 1), and the clans of the rest (v. 2). Then the register stops: Zelophehad had no sons, only daughters, and they are named — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah (v. 3). They come to Eleazar and Joshua and the leaders and say plainly, the LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers, and they are given one (v. 4). So Manasseh receives ten portions rather than five, because the daughters inherited alongside the sons (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: These five had already been to court once. In Numbers they brought the same case to Moses, who took it to God, and God ruled in their favour and made it law for Israel (Num. 27:1-11). They are now standing in front of a new administration, asking that the ruling be honoured, and it is.
verseByVerse.examples: Their names are given in full here for the fourth time in Scripture (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11, and this). In a section of the Bible made of place names, five women are named and named again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war. And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father. Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan, because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war.'

The register opens as expected, with a firstborn and a soldier. Then it stops.

'Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.'

Five women are named, in the middle of a chapter about property, in a culture where land ran through sons. Their father is traced back four generations to establish that they are Manasseh's own, and then all five names are written out.

This is the fourth time Scripture has listed them (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11, and here). They are the most frequently named women in the Pentateuch, and the reason is a case they brought years earlier.

Their father had died in the wilderness with no sons, which under the custom of the time meant his name and his portion simply disappeared. The five of them went to Moses and the whole assembly at the tent of meeting and made an argument: why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Moses did not rule on it. He took the case to God, and God said, the daughters of Zelophehad are right, and made it a statute for Israel (Num. 27:1-11).

'They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.'

Now, a generation later, with Moses dead and a new administration doing the distribution, the five of them come and stand in front of the priest and the general and ask for the ruling to be honoured.

They do not plead and they do not argue their merits. They cite the judgment: the LORD commanded Moses. And it is granted at once — so Manasseh ends up with ten portions instead of five, because five sisters held a government to a promise its predecessor had made.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — Could Not, and Would Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh's boundary is traced from Asher to Michmethath, down past En-tappuah and the brook Kanah to the sea, with Ephraim to the south (vv. 7-10). Verse 11 lists six good towns Manasseh held inside Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Taanach and Megiddo. And then verses 12-13: they could not take possession of those cities, the Canaanites persisted in living there, and when Israel grew strong they put them to forced labour but did not utterly drive them out.
verseByVerse.theology: The two verbs in two verses are the whole story of this half of the book. First could not, when Israel was weak. Then, when Israel grew strong and the thing became possible, they chose a labour arrangement instead. The excuse expired and the arrangement stayed.
verseByVerse.examples: The six towns are the best real estate in the north: Beth-shean commanding the Jordan valley road, Megiddo commanding the pass into the plain of Jezreel. Manasseh had the title and never got the keys, and those towns will be trouble to Israel for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim. Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea, the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar. Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath. Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages.'

The boundary walk is standard, and then six towns are listed that Manasseh held on paper. They are the best sites in the north: Beth-shean, sitting where the Jordan valley meets the plain; Taanach and Megiddo, guarding the pass that every army in the ancient world used to get across the country.

'Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.'

Two verses, two verbs, and between them they tell the whole story of this half of the book.

The first is could not. In the early days Manasseh was not strong enough, and that is stated as a fact rather than a sin. Some things are genuinely beyond a person's strength for a season, and Scripture says so without scolding.

Then the second sentence, and it changes everything: when the people of Israel grew strong. The weakness passed. The reason for the failure expired. And at the exact moment the thing became possible, Manasseh did not do it. They put the Canaanites to forced labour instead, which was profitable, and left it there.

Watch that sequence in yourself. The excuse is often true when it is first offered. What matters is what happens when it stops being true — whether the arrangement made in weakness is dismantled once the strength arrives, or quietly kept because by then it suits everybody.

Megiddo is on that list of towns Manasseh never took. Three centuries later Israel will still be fighting for that pass, and its name will end up in the last book of the Bible as the place where the kings of the earth gather.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Ask for More, Get a Forest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house of Joseph comes to Joshua with a grievance: why one lot and one portion, when we are a numerous people whom the LORD has blessed all along (v. 14)? Joshua's answer is not more land but an axe — if you are numerous, go up to the forest and clear ground for yourselves (v. 15). They come back with the real objection: the hill country is not enough, and the Canaanites in the plain have chariots of iron (v. 16). And Joshua repeats himself with the promise attached: you are numerous and have great power, the hill country shall be yours, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders, and you shall drive out the Canaanites though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua is himself an Ephraimite (Num. 13:8, 16). These are his own people asking their own kinsman for a better deal, and he gives them nothing but work and a promise. Nepotism would have been easy and nobody would have objected.
verseByVerse.examples: Their two complaints do not agree with each other. In verse 14 they are too numerous for the land; in verse 16 the land is not enough for them and the enemy is too strong. A people large enough to need more room is large enough to take it, and Joshua says so in almost those words.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?" And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you." The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel." Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only, but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?"'

A deputation arrives with a grievance, and the shape of it repays hearing. They have not been treated unjustly; they have had the largest single block of land in the country. What they want is more, and the argument they use is that God has blessed them.

That is a real and modern piece of reasoning: we have grown, therefore we are owed more room. God's evident favour becomes the ground of a claim.

Note who they are talking to. Joshua is from Ephraim — Hoshea the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, as the list of spies has it (Num. 13:8, 16). These men are his own tribe, coming to their own kinsman at the top, and nobody in Israel would have blinked if he had found them something.

'And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you."'

He gives them work instead. Not another allotment — an axe, and a forest, and the suggestion that a large people can make its own room.

There is something bracing in the answer, and it is not unkind. He takes their own argument seriously: you say you are numerous, so behave like it. The land is there. It is covered in trees and it will take years.

'The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel."'

Now the real objection surfaces, and the two halves of it contradict each other. In verse 14 they were too big for the land. Here the land is not enough — and then, in the same breath, they explain that the good land has iron chariots on it.

That is the honest sentence in the whole exchange. They did not want more territory in general. They wanted the plain, which is flat, fertile and farmable, and they did not want to fight the people who were sitting on it.

'Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only, but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."'

Joshua does not soften and he does not sneer. He gives them back their own words with the promise attached: you are numerous, you have great power, the hill country shall be yours, and you shall drive them out.

He also refuses to pretend. He repeats the iron chariots and adds though they are strong. The difficulty is real, he says it twice, and it does not change the instruction. The last word this old general gives his own tribe is not sympathy and not extra land. It is that the ground is theirs and the trees will have to come down.

18.title: Shiloh and the Remaining Allotments
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.<sup>2</sup>There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned.<sup>3</sup>So Joshua said to the people of Israel, "How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?<sup>4</sup>Provide three men from each tribe, and I will send them out that they may set out and go up and down the land. They shall write a description of it with a view to their inheritances, and then come to me.<sup>5</sup>They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall continue in his territory on the south, and the house of Joseph shall continue in their territory on the north.<sup>6</sup>And you shall describe the land in seven divisions and bring the description here to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God.<sup>7</sup>The Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. And Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave them."<sup>8</sup>So the men arose and went, and Joshua charged those who went to write the description of the land, saying, "Go up and down in the land and write a description and return to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD in Shiloh."<sup>9</sup>So the men went and passed up and down in the land and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions. Then they came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh,<sup>10</sup>and Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD. And there Joshua apportioned the land to the people of Israel, to each his portion.<sup>11</sup>The lot of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to its clans came up, and the territory allotted to it fell between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph.<sup>12</sup>On the north side their boundary began at the Jordan. Then the boundary goes up to the shoulder north of Jericho, then up through the hill country westward, and it ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven.<sup>13</sup>From there the boundary passes along southward in the direction of Luz, to the shoulder of Luz (that is, Bethel), then the boundary goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the mountain that lies south of Lower Beth-horon.<sup>14</sup>Then the boundary goes in another direction, turning on the western side southward from the mountain that lies to the south, opposite Beth-horon, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city belonging to the people of Judah. This forms the western side.<sup>15</sup>And the southern side begins at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. And the boundary goes from there to Ephron, to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.<sup>16</sup>Then the boundary goes down to the border of the mountain that overlooks the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. And it then goes down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the shoulder of the Jebusites, and downward to En-rogel.<sup>17</sup>Then it bends in a northerly direction going on to En-shemesh, and from there goes to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it goes down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,<sup>18</sup>and passing on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah it goes down to the Arabah.<sup>19</sup>Then the boundary passes on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-hoglah. And the boundary ends at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan: this is the southern border.<sup>20</sup>The Jordan forms its boundary on the eastern side. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin, according to their clans, boundary by boundary all around.<sup>21</sup>Now the cities of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to their clans were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz,<sup>22</sup>Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,<sup>23</sup>Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,<sup>24</sup>Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, Geba—twelve cities with their villages:<sup>25</sup>Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,<sup>26</sup>Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,<sup>27</sup>Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,<sup>28</sup>Zela, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim —fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin according to its clans.
18.overview:
The whole congregation of Israel gathers at Shiloh, and there they set up the tent of meeting — the tabernacle. This is a significant moment: Shiloh, in the territory of Ephraim, becomes the central place of worship for the nation, the resting place of the ark and the tabernacle for the next several centuries, until the days of Eli and Samuel.
