The land has been subdued; now the worship of God is centralized in the place he has chosen. The order is instructive: God establishes his dwelling in the midst of his people as the center around which their national life is to revolve.

But seven tribes have still not received their inheritance, and here Joshua delivers one of the most penetrating rebukes in the book: 'How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?' (v. 3). The land is given — God has handed it over — yet seven tribes have grown passive, dragging their feet, failing to go in and possess what is already theirs. Joshua's question cuts to the heart of spiritual lethargy: why do you delay? Why do you leave unpossessed what God has freely given?

This is the rebuke of spiritual passivity, and it speaks powerfully to the church in every age. The inheritance is given; the victory is won; the promises are sure — and yet how often the people of God live as spiritual sluggards, content to camp on the edge of blessings they never enter, putting off the labor of possessing what grace has freely granted. 'How long will you put off?' is a question that searches every complacent heart. The danger here is not active rebellion but passive delay, the slow paralysis of a faith that admires the promise but never acts on it.

Joshua's remedy is practical and decisive: he sends out men to survey the remaining land, divide it into seven portions, and bring back a written description, so that he can cast lots and assign the inheritance (vv. 4–10). He will not let the passivity stand; he organizes the people to take possession. The chapter then records the allotment of Benjamin, the small but strategically vital tribe whose territory would include Jerusalem and Bethel, and from whom would come Saul, Israel's first king, and Paul, the apostle to the nations. The God who centralizes worship at Shiloh is the God who rouses his people from passivity to possess their inheritance.

sections.title: The Tabernacle Set Up at Shiloh
sections.commentary:
'Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.' This single verse marks a turning point. With the major conquest complete and the land subdued, the nation gathers to establish the center of its worship. The tabernacle — the dwelling place of God among his people, the place of sacrifice and atonement and the presence of the LORD — is set up at Shiloh, in the heart of the land.

The significance is profound. The order of priorities is revealed: once the land is subdued, the very next concern is the worship of God. Israel does not first build palaces or fortresses or markets; they erect the tabernacle. The presence of God among his people, and the worship due to him, is established as the center around which the whole national life will revolve. Shiloh would remain the central sanctuary for centuries, the place where Hannah would pray and Samuel would minister, until its tragic fall (cf. Jer. 7:12).

There is a deep principle here for the people of God. The conquest, the inheritance, the rest in the land — all of it finds its true purpose and center in the worship of God. We are not saved merely to possess blessings but to dwell with God and worship him. The tabernacle at the center of the land prefigures the great truth that God's ultimate purpose is to dwell among his people: 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man' (Rev. 21:3). And it points to Christ, the true tabernacle, who 'dwelt among us' (John 1:14, literally 'tabernacled'), the meeting place between God and man. The land subdued, the tabernacle raised — the center of Israel's life was the presence of God in their midst.

sections.title: Joshua's Rebuke of Passivity
sections.commentary:
Seven tribes have still not received their inheritance, and Joshua confronts them with a question that pierces the heart of spiritual lethargy: 'How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?' (v. 3). Notice the tension at the center of the rebuke: the land 'has given you' — it is already theirs by God's gift — and yet they 'put off going in.' The inheritance is granted; the people are passive. The problem is not God's withholding but Israel's delay.

This is one of the great diagnoses of the spiritual life in all of Scripture. The danger Joshua confronts is not active rebellion but passive procrastination — the slow paralysis of a people who possess the promise but will not act on it. They are not fighting against God; they are simply dragging their feet, content to remain where they are, leaving the inheritance unpossessed. 'How long will you put off?' The question exposes the spiritual sloth that admires the promise but never enters into it.

How searching this is for the church. The believer in Christ possesses every spiritual blessing (Eph. 1:3); the victory is won, the promises are sure, the inheritance is granted. And yet how often we live as spiritual sluggards, camped on the borders of blessings we never enter, putting off the obedience, the prayer, the growth, the service that would take possession of what grace has freely given. We delay walking in the holiness Christ has secured, we postpone the joy and assurance that are ours, we leave the land unpossessed. Sproul observed that the great enemy of many Christians is not heresy or open sin but spiritual lethargy — the failure to lay hold of what God has already given. Joshua's question rings down the centuries to every complacent heart: 'How long will you put off?' The remedy is not more grace (the land is already given) but the rousing of faith to go up and possess it.

sections.title: The Survey and Division of the Land
sections.commentary:
Joshua does not merely rebuke the passive tribes; he provides a practical remedy. He sends out a team of men — three from each of the seven tribes — to survey the remaining land, walk through it, describe it in writing, and divide it into seven portions. They return with the written survey to Joshua at Shiloh, and there he casts lots before the LORD to assign the inheritance (v. 10). The passivity is broken by organized, deliberate action under godly leadership.

There is wisdom here in how Joshua addresses spiritual lethargy. He does not simply scold the people and leave them to their inertia; he gives them a concrete task, a clear process, a path forward. He organizes the survey, divides the labor, and provides the structure by which the inheritance can be possessed. Godly leadership rouses the passive not only by exhortation but by practical provision — showing the people the way and putting them to work.

And note that the final assignment is made 'by lot before the LORD at Shiloh.' Even as the people are roused to active possession, the inheritance is still received as God's sovereign gift, assigned by his appointment through the lot (Prov. 16:33). Human diligence and divine sovereignty work together: the people survey and labor, but God assigns. Calvin observed that the casting of lots before the LORD preserved the truth that the land was God's gift, even as the people were stirred to take possession of it. So in the Christian life, we labor to possess our inheritance, working out our salvation, even as we confess that it is God who works in us and assigns to each his portion by grace. The survey is done, the land divided; now the remaining tribes will receive what God has appointed.

sections.title: The Allotment of Benjamin
sections.commentary:
The first of the seven remaining allotments is given to Benjamin, the smallest of the tribes, whose territory lay between Judah to the south and Ephraim to the north. Though small, Benjamin's portion was strategically and spiritually vital. It included Bethel, where Jacob had seen the ladder to heaven; Gibeon, the city of the deceived covenant; Jericho, the firstfruits of the conquest; and — most significantly — Jerusalem lay on its border with Judah, the city that would become the holy city, the city of the great King.

The little tribe of Benjamin would play an outsized role in the history of redemption. From Benjamin would come Saul, Israel's first king, the people's choice who failed. And from Benjamin would also come Saul of Tarsus — the apostle Paul, who described himself as 'of the tribe of Benjamin' (Phil. 3:5; Rom. 11:1), the chief of sinners transformed into the apostle to the nations. The smallest tribe gave Israel both its first failed king and its greatest missionary. God's choice often falls on the small and unlikely, that his grace might be displayed.

The careful description of Benjamin's borders and cities completes the chapter. There is a quiet glory in this geography too: the territory of Benjamin would witness some of the most significant moments in redemptive history, from Jacob's ladder at Bethel to the events surrounding Jerusalem. The God who assigns to the smallest tribe so significant an inheritance is the God who delights to use the small and the unlikely for his great purposes. 'God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong' (1 Cor. 1:27). Benjamin, least among the tribes, received a portion at the very heart of the land — a reminder that in the kingdom of God, the last and the least are often given the greatest place.

18.theology:
Worship at the Center. Once the land is subdued, the first concern is to set up the tabernacle at Shiloh (v. 1). The presence of God among his people and the worship due to him become the center of national life. This prefigures God's ultimate purpose to dwell among his people (Rev. 21:3) and points to Christ, the true tabernacle who 'dwelt among us' (John 1:14).

The Sin of Spiritual Passivity. 'How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD has given you?' (v. 3). The danger is not rebellion but procrastination — possessing the promise yet failing to act on it. The believer possesses every spiritual blessing in Christ (Eph. 1:3) yet too often camps on the borders of unentered blessings. The remedy is faith roused to possess what grace has given.

God Chooses the Small and Unlikely. The smallest tribe, Benjamin, receives a strategically vital inheritance and would give Israel both Saul the king and Paul the apostle. 'God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong' (1 Cor. 1:27). In the kingdom of God, the last and least are often given the greatest place.
18.examples:
Then: Israel gathered at Shiloh and raised the tabernacle, centering their life on the worship of God. But seven tribes had grown passive, leaving their inheritance unpossessed, until Joshua confronted them: 'How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land the LORD has given you?'

Now: The believer's great enemy is often not open sin but spiritual lethargy — possessing every blessing in Christ yet living as a sluggard, camped on the borders of unentered grace, postponing the holiness, joy, and service that are already ours. Joshua's question searches every complacent heart: 'How long will you put off?' The remedy is not more grace but faith roused to go up and possess what God has freely given — with the worship of God at the center of it all.

19.overview:
Chapter 19 completes the allotment of the land, recording the inheritances of the remaining six tribes — Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan. The territories are described with the same careful attention to borders and cities, each portion the fulfillment of God's ancient promise. Among these allotments are places that would become deeply significant in the gospel story: the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, of which Isaiah prophesied 'the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' (Isa. 9:1–2), the region of Galilee where Jesus would conduct so much of his ministry. Nazareth, Capernaum, and the Sea of Galilee all lay within these tribal lands. The unassuming geography of Joshua 19 is the very soil where the light of the world would one day walk.

The tribe of Dan is given a portion, but the chapter notes that 'the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them' and they had to go up and fight for additional territory in the north (v. 47) — a foreshadowing of Dan's later troubles and apostasy. Once again, incomplete possession and compromise shadow the inheritance.

But the climax of the chapter, and indeed of the whole allotment narrative, comes in the final verses (vv. 49–50): after all the tribes have received their inheritance, Joshua receives his own — last of all. The leader who has overseen the distribution of the entire land, who has assigned every other tribe its portion, takes his inheritance only when everyone else has been provided for. And he asks for a modest town, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, which he then rebuilds and settles.

Here is the portrait of the servant leader. Joshua, who could have claimed the choicest territory first, waits until last, ensuring that all the people are settled before he takes his own portion. He gives before he receives. This is the very pattern of Christ, the greater Joshua, who 'though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich' (2 Cor. 8:9) — who did not grasp at his rights but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7), who gave his inheritance away that his people might be made joint-heirs with him. The servant leader gives before he receives; and the greatest Servant gave everything, that we might inherit all things.

sections.title: The Inheritance of Simeon
sections.commentary:
The second lot falls to Simeon, and the narrator notes a striking detail: Simeon's inheritance lay 'in the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah,' because Judah's portion was too large for them (v. 9). Simeon received no separate, contiguous territory of its own but cities scattered within Judah's borders. This is the partial fulfillment of Jacob's prophetic word over Simeon (and Levi): 'I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel' (Gen. 49:7), a word spoken in judgment for the violence of Simeon and Levi at Shechem.

There is sobering theology here. The sins of the patriarch echoed down the generations in the scattered, dependent inheritance of his descendants. Simeon never developed into a strong, distinct tribe; absorbed within Judah, it gradually faded from prominence and is not even mentioned in Moses' final blessing (Deut. 33). The consequences of sin can ripple through generations, shaping the inheritance of those who come after.

Yet even here, grace works. By being scattered within Judah — the royal tribe, the tribe of the Messiah — Simeon was bound up with the line of promise. What was spoken as judgment ('I will scatter them') God wove into a strange mercy, placing Simeon within the inheritance of the King. Calvin observed that God's providence often turns the consequences of sin toward unexpected good. The scattering that judged Simeon's violence also drew the tribe into proximity with Judah and the coming Redeemer. The God who divides the land remembers both justice and mercy, weaving even the long consequences of ancient sin into his redemptive purpose.

sections.title: The Northern Tribes: Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali
sections.commentary:
The allotments of the northern tribes — Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali — are recorded, their territories spreading across the fertile regions of the north, including the area around the Sea of Galilee. To the casual reader these are mere lists of borders and towns. But the eye of faith sees something extraordinary here, for this is the geography of the gospel.

The territories of Zebulun and Naphtali, in particular, would become the very stage of Jesus' Galilean ministry. Isaiah prophesied of these lands: 'In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious... Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' (Isa. 9:1–2). And Matthew, recording the beginning of Jesus' ministry, quotes this very prophecy and applies it to Christ settling in Capernaum, 'in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali' (Matt. 4:13–16). Nazareth, where Jesus grew up; Cana, where he turned water to wine; Capernaum, his ministry base; the Sea of Galilee, where he called his disciples and walked on the waves — all lay within these tribal allotments.

What a wonder this is. The unassuming borders staked out in Joshua 19, in tribes that would never rival Judah in prominence, mark the very soil where the light of the world would walk. The people who would dwell in these northern lands, often despised by the southern Judeans ('Can anything good come out of Nazareth?'), would be the first to see the great light. God's redemptive purpose runs through the most unlikely geography. The Galilee of the nations, the despised north, became the cradle of the gospel. Ferguson observed that the land allotments of Joshua are not merely historical records but the marking out of the stage on which the drama of redemption would unfold. The God who assigned Zebulun and Naphtali their portions was even then preparing the place where his Son would shine.

sections.title: The Tribe of Dan and Its Lost Territory
sections.commentary:
The last allotment falls to Dan, but the account carries a shadow: 'When the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them, the people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem... and settled in it' (v. 47). Dan was unable to hold its assigned coastal territory, pressed by the Philistines and Amorites, and so migrated north to seize Leshem (Laish), renaming it Dan. This relocation is recorded more fully in Judges 18 — and it is a dark chapter, for there Dan set up an idolatrous shrine with a stolen Levite and graven image, becoming a center of false worship that would later be exploited by Jeroboam.

Here again the theme of incomplete possession and compromise shadows the inheritance. Dan failed to possess what God had given, and in seeking territory on its own terms, the tribe drifted into idolatry. The failure to fully possess the assigned inheritance led not to neutral loss but to spiritual corruption. The tribe of Dan would become so associated with apostasy that it is conspicuously omitted from the list of the sealed tribes in Revelation 7.

The lesson echoes through the allotment narratives: what we fail to possess in faith, we often seek to grasp on our own terms, and that grasping leads us into compromise and ruin. Dan's lost territory and idolatrous relocation is a warning written into the geography of Israel. The inheritance God gives is to be possessed in faith and obedience; when his people abandon the path of faith and seek their portion by their own devices, they fall into the very snares God warned against. Calvin noted that Dan's failure and subsequent idolatry stand as a sober testimony to the danger of departing from the inheritance and the worship God appoints. The tribe that would not possess its God-given portion ended in the idolatry that would help destroy the nation.

sections.title: Joshua's Own Inheritance: The Servant Leader
sections.commentary:
And now, the climax of the whole allotment narrative. 'When they had finished distributing the several territories of the land as inheritances, the people of Israel gave an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun' (v. 49). Last of all — after every tribe, every clan, every family has been provided for — Joshua receives his own portion. The leader who oversaw the distribution of the entire land, who could have claimed the choicest territory first, waits until everyone else is settled before he takes his inheritance. And he asks for a modest town, Timnath-serah in the hill country of his own tribe of Ephraim, which he then rebuilds and settles.

Here is the portrait of the servant leader, and it shines with the light of the gospel. Joshua gives before he receives. He does not use his authority to enrich himself; he ensures the people are cared for before he takes his own small portion. This is the very inversion of worldly leadership, which grasps first and most. Jesus would teach his disciples this same lesson: 'whoever would be great among you must be your servant... even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many' (Matt. 20:26–28).

And in this, Joshua images his greater namesake. The true Joshua — Jesus — though he was rich, for our sake became poor, that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). He did not grasp at his rights as God but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). He gave his very life, his whole inheritance, that his people might be made joint-heirs with him (Rom. 8:17). The servant Joshua took his portion last; the servant Christ gave his portion away entirely, that we might inherit all things. Begg observed that Joshua's modest, last-of-all inheritance is the mark of the true servant of God, who seeks the good of the people before his own. The leader who fought every battle and divided the whole land asked, in the end, for one small town — and in his self-forgetful service, he points us to the Servant who gave everything, that we might receive an inheritance that can never fade.

19.theology:
The Geography of the Gospel. The northern allotments of Zebulun and Naphtali (vv. 10–39) became the stage of Jesus' Galilean ministry — 'the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' (Isa. 9:1–2; Matt. 4:13–16). The unassuming borders of Joshua are the very soil where the light of the world would walk; God's redemptive purpose runs through the most unlikely geography.

The Long Consequences of Sin, and the Danger of Incomplete Possession. Simeon's scattered inheritance fulfills Jacob's word of judgment (Gen. 49:7), and Dan's lost territory leads to idolatry (v. 47; Judg. 18). What we fail to possess in faith we grasp on our own terms, and that grasping leads to compromise and ruin. Sin's consequences ripple through generations.

The Servant Leader Who Gives Before He Receives. Joshua takes his inheritance last of all, asking only for a modest town (vv. 49–50). He gives before he receives — imaging the greater Joshua, who though rich became poor (2 Cor. 8:9), emptied himself as a servant (Phil. 2:6–7), and gave his whole inheritance that his people might become joint-heirs with him.
19.examples:
Then: The remaining tribes received their portions, including the northern lands where Christ would one day shine his light. And when all the people were settled, Joshua took his inheritance last of all — a single modest town — the servant leader who provided for everyone else before himself.

Now: Worldly leadership grasps first and most; the way of Christ is to serve and give before receiving. Joshua's last-of-all inheritance points us to the greater Joshua, who gave his very life that we might inherit all things. We who follow him are called to the same self-forgetful service — seeking the good of others before our own, knowing that the Servant who gave everything has secured for us an inheritance that can never fade.

20.title: The Cities of Refuge
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Say to the people of Israel, 'Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses,<sup>3</sup>that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.<sup>4</sup>He shall flee to one of these cities and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city and explain his case to the elders of that city. Then they shall take him into the city and give him a place, and he shall remain with them.<sup>5</sup>And if the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unknowingly, and did not hate him in the past.<sup>6</sup>And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.'"<sup>7</sup>So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.<sup>8</sup>And beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, they appointed Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland, from the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh.<sup>9</sup>These were the cities designated for all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them, that anyone who killed a person without intent could flee there, so that he might not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, till he stood before the congregation.
20.overview:
Among the most beautiful and gospel-laden institutions in all the law are the cities of refuge, established here in Joshua 20. Six cities — three on each side of the Jordan — were appointed as places of asylum, where a person who had killed another unintentionally could flee for safety from the 'avenger of blood,' the kinsman who, by ancient custom, would seek to avenge the death. The cities of refuge were God's gracious provision to distinguish between murder and manslaughter, to protect the innocent-yet-involved from blood vengeance, and to provide a sanctuary of mercy in a world of justice.

The institution is a masterpiece of justice tempered with mercy. God's law took the shedding of blood with utmost seriousness — life is sacred, made in the image of God. Yet God also distinguished between the murderer, who killed with intent and malice, and the manslayer, who killed accidentally, 'without intent or unknowingly' (v. 3). For the latter, God provided refuge — a place to flee, a sanctuary where they would be safe until a fair trial, and where, if found innocent of murder, they could dwell in safety.

The cities of refuge are one of the clearest types of Christ in the Old Testament. The writer of Hebrews seems to allude to them when he speaks of those who 'have fled for refuge' to 'lay hold of the hope set before us' (Heb. 6:18). Christ is the believer's city of refuge — the only place of safety from the avenging justice we have provoked. As the manslayer fled to the city and was safe within its walls, so the sinner flees to Christ and is safe from the wrath to come. Outside the city, death; inside, life. There is no safety except in the refuge.

And there is a stunning detail that crowns the type. The manslayer was required to remain in the city of refuge 'until the death of the high priest' (v. 6) — and at the high priest's death, he was free to return home, fully released. The death of the high priest set the refugee free. Here is the gospel in shadow: it is by the death of our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, that we are released from our guilt and set free. His death is our liberation. The refugee waited for the death of the high priest to be free; we look back to the death of our High Priest, by which we are free indeed.

sections.title: God's Command to Appoint Cities of Refuge
sections.commentary:
'Then the LORD said to Joshua, Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses' (vv. 1–2). The cities of refuge were not Joshua's innovation but God's own command, given long before through Moses (Num. 35; Deut. 19). Now, with the land divided, the time has come to establish them. Their purpose is stated plainly: 'that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood' (v. 3).

The institution reveals the heart of God's justice. In the ancient world, the death of a person demanded a response; the 'avenger of blood' (the goel, the kinsman-redeemer) bore the responsibility to avenge a slain relative. But God, in his wisdom and mercy, distinguished between the murderer and the manslayer. The one who killed with malice and intent deserved death; but the one who killed accidentally — the man whose axe-head flew off its handle, the one whose action caused unintended death — was not to be treated as a murderer. For him, God provided refuge.

Here we see that God's justice is never crude or indiscriminate. He weighs the heart, the intent, the circumstances. He does not lump the accidental killer with the cold-blooded murderer. And in providing a place of refuge, God reveals himself as a God of mercy even in the administration of justice. The cities of refuge stand as a monument to a God who is both just and merciful — who upholds the sanctity of life and yet provides a sanctuary for the one who needs protection. Calvin observed that the cities of refuge displayed both God's care for the sanctity of human life and his tender provision for the one who, though involved in death, was not guilty of murder. Justice and mercy meet in God's gracious provision.

sections.title: The Refuge and the Avenger of Blood
sections.commentary:
The procedure is described: the manslayer flees to the city of refuge, stands at the entrance of the gate, and explains his case to the elders, who take him in and give him a place among them. The avenger of blood may not be given the manslayer, for he killed his neighbor 'unknowingly, having had no enmity against him in the past' (v. 5). The refugee is safe within the city until he can stand trial before the congregation, and — crucially — 'until the death of him who is high priest at the time' (v. 6).

This is one of the richest gospel pictures in the Old Testament. Consider the manslayer's situation: he is pursued by the avenger of blood, under the shadow of death, and his only hope is to reach the city of refuge. Outside the city, he is exposed to vengeance and death; inside, he is safe. There is no middle ground, no safety in the open country — he must reach the refuge or perish. So it is with the sinner pursued by the just wrath of God against sin. Our only hope is to flee to Christ, our city of refuge. Outside of Christ, there is only the avenging justice we have provoked; in Christ, there is safety and life.

The writer of Hebrews seems to draw on this very image when he speaks of those who 'have fled for refuge' to 'lay hold of the hope set before us' (Heb. 6:18). Christ is the refuge to which the guilty flee. And note the urgency: the manslayer had to run, to reach the city before the avenger overtook him. The gospel call has the same urgency — 'flee from the wrath to come' (Matt. 3:7), flee to Christ while there is yet time. Begg observed that the cities of refuge preach the gospel of a Savior who is near, accessible, and sufficient — a refuge to which the guilty may run and find safety. The roads to the cities of refuge were, by Jewish tradition, kept clear and well-marked, with signs reading 'Refuge!' at the crossroads — that none who needed to flee might lose the way. So the gospel keeps the way to Christ open and clearly marked: 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt. 11:28).

sections.title: The Death of the High Priest and the Refugee's Freedom
sections.commentary:
The most stunning detail of the whole institution is this: the manslayer must remain in the city of refuge 'until the death of him who is high priest at the time' (v. 6). At the death of the high priest, the refugee was free — released from the city, free to return home, no longer pursued by the avenger of blood. The death of the high priest set the refugee free.

Why the death of the high priest? Why should the refugee's liberty be tied to the life and death of Israel's high priest? The law does not fully explain it, but the gospel illumines it gloriously. The high priest was the representative of the people before God, the one who made atonement, the mediator. And his death, in some mysterious way, marked the end of the refugee's confinement and the beginning of his freedom. Here is a shadow cast forward across the centuries, pointing unmistakably to the death of our great High Priest, Jesus Christ.

It is by the death of our High Priest that we are set free. As the manslayer waited in the city until the high priest died, and was then released, so we are released from the guilt and bondage of sin by the death of Jesus, our great High Priest 'after the order of Melchizedek' (Heb. 6:20). His death is our liberation. The refugee could not buy his freedom, could not earn his release, could not shorten his confinement by any work of his own; he had only to wait for the death of the high priest. And we contribute nothing to our redemption; we are set free entirely by the death of Christ. Ferguson and many before him have marveled at this type: the death that liberates the refugee is the death of the priest, prefiguring the death of Christ that liberates the sinner. 'Christ has redeemed us' — not by our works, but by his death. The refugee looked forward to a death that would free him; we look back to the death of our High Priest, by which we are free indeed. 'If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36).

sections.title: The Six Cities Appointed
sections.commentary:
The six cities are named: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in Ephraim, and Hebron (Kiriath-arba) in Judah on the west side of the Jordan; and Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan on the east side. Three cities on each side of the Jordan, spread throughout the land, so that no one — wherever they lived — would be far from a place of refuge. The cities were distributed for accessibility; a manslayer anywhere in Israel could reach one in time.

This careful distribution preaches a quiet gospel truth: the refuge is accessible to all. God did not place a single city of refuge in one remote corner, requiring an impossible journey; he scattered six cities across the land, so that refuge was always within reach. The salvation God provides is not for a privileged few who happen to live near it, but is made accessible to all who need it. So the gospel: Christ, our refuge, is 'near you, in your mouth and in your heart' (Rom. 10:8); 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Rom. 10:13). The refuge is accessible to all who flee to it.

And note that these cities were also Levitical cities (ch. 21) — cities of the priestly tribe, places where the worship of God and the instruction of his law were present. The refuge was found among the people of God, in the place of God's presence and ministry. The fugitive fled not into isolation but into the community of God's people, under the shadow of the priesthood. So the sinner who flees to Christ flees into the household of God, the community of the redeemed, under the ministry of the great High Priest. The chapter notes that the cities were 'for the sojourner... among them' as well (v. 9) — the refuge was open even to the foreigner, the outsider. Grace knows no borders. The cities of refuge, accessible to all and open even to the stranger, are a standing testimony that God has provided a refuge for every sinner who will flee to it, near at hand, open wide, and sufficient to save.

20.theology:
Christ Our City of Refuge. As the manslayer fled to the city and was safe within its walls, so the sinner flees to Christ and is safe from the avenging justice we have provoked. Outside the refuge, death; inside, life. The writer of Hebrews draws on this image: we 'have fled for refuge' to 'lay hold of the hope set before us' (Heb. 6:18). There is no safety except in the refuge, and the way is kept open and clearly marked.

Freedom Through the Death of the High Priest. The refugee was released at the death of the high priest (v. 6) — a stunning shadow of the gospel. It is by the death of our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, that we are set free from the guilt and bondage of sin. We contribute nothing; we are liberated entirely by his death. 'If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36).

Justice and Mercy Meet. The cities of refuge display God's justice (upholding the sanctity of life, distinguishing murder from manslaughter) and his mercy (providing sanctuary for the one in need). Scattered across the land and open even to the sojourner (v. 9), they testify that God has provided an accessible refuge for every sinner who will flee to it.
20.examples:
Then: God appointed six cities of refuge, scattered across the land and open even to foreigners, where the one who killed unintentionally could flee from the avenger of blood and find safety. He remained there until the death of the high priest — and at that death, he was set free to return home.

Now: Every sinner is pursued by the just wrath of God against sin, and our only hope is to flee to Christ, our city of refuge. Outside of him is only the avenging justice we have provoked; in him is safety and life. And just as the refugee was freed by the death of the high priest, so we are set free — not by our works but by the death of our great High Priest, Jesus Christ. Flee to the refuge; the way is open, and he is sufficient to save.

21.title: The Levitical Cities and the Faithfulness of God
