21.overview:
Chapter 21 records the allotment of forty-eight cities to the Levites — the priestly tribe that received no territorial inheritance of its own, for the LORD was their inheritance (13:33). Since the Levites were to have no single tribal territory, God provided for them cities scattered throughout all the tribes, with pasturelands around them. This distribution was a stroke of divine wisdom: the priests and Levites, the ministers of God's worship and the teachers of his law, were dispersed among all the tribes, so that no corner of Israel would be without the presence and ministry of those set apart for God.

The scattering of the Levites was, in fact, the fulfillment of a word of judgment turned to blessing. Jacob had prophesied that Levi would be 'divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel' (Gen. 49:7) because of the violence at Shechem. But God transformed that scattering into a ministry: the tribe judged with dispersion became the tribe through whom the worship and instruction of God reached every part of the land. What was spoken in judgment, God wove into grace. The Levites, scattered, became the means by which the knowledge of God was spread throughout Israel.

There is a beautiful gospel principle here. The people set apart for God's service are dispersed among the whole people of God, so that the ministry of the Word and worship is present everywhere. This anticipates the New Testament reality of the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet. 2:9), scattered throughout the world as salt and light, that the knowledge of God might fill the earth. The Levites among the tribes are a picture of the church among the nations — God's people dispersed to bring his Word to every place.

But the crown of the chapter, and indeed of the whole conquest and allotment narrative, comes in the closing verses (vv. 43–45). Here the narrator pauses to summarize, and the summary rises to a doxology: 'Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers... The LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn... Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass' (vv. 43–45). This is the theological summit of the book — the great declaration of the absolute, unfailing faithfulness of God to every promise. Not one word failed. All came to pass. It is the verdict of history upon the character of God, and the anchor of every believer's hope.

sections.title: The Levites Request Their Cities
sections.commentary:
The heads of the Levite families come to Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the tribal heads at Shiloh, with a request grounded in God's command: 'The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities to dwell in, along with their pasturelands for our livestock' (v. 2). The Levites, having no territorial inheritance, ask for what God had appointed — cities scattered among the tribes. And the people of Israel respond by giving them forty-eight cities with their surrounding pasturelands, out of their own inheritances.

There is a quiet beauty in this transaction. The Levites do not seize their cities or demand them by right of power; they request them on the basis of God's word, and the tribes give them willingly from their own portions. The whole nation contributes to the support of those who minister in holy things. This is the principle that the New Testament would later affirm: 'those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel' (1 Cor. 9:14); the people of God are to support those who labor in the Word and in worship.

The Levites' dependence on the other tribes for their cities also reflects their distinctive calling. Having no land of their own, they were freed for full-time service to God and his people — teaching the law, leading worship, administering the sacrifices. Their lack of territorial inheritance was not a deprivation but a liberation for ministry, and their support came from the whole community. Calvin observed that God's provision for the Levites through the gifts of the tribes taught Israel that those who serve at the altar are to be sustained by the people they serve. The ministers of God were provided for, scattered among the tribes, supported by the whole nation — a picture of how God provides for those he sets apart for his service.

sections.title: The Distribution of the Forty-Eight Cities
sections.commentary:
The chapter records in careful detail the distribution of the forty-eight Levitical cities — to the priestly family of Aaron (the Kohathites who were priests), and to the other Levitical families (Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites). The cities are spread throughout all the tribes, on both sides of the Jordan, including the six cities of refuge from the previous chapter. The Levites were thus dispersed across the whole land, present in every region, embedded among every tribe.

This dispersion was a stroke of divine wisdom and grace. Because the Levites were the teachers of God's law and the ministers of his worship, their scattering throughout the land meant that the knowledge of God and the ministry of his Word reached every corner of Israel. No tribe was left without the presence of those set apart for God. The priests and Levites in their forty-eight cities were like lamps placed throughout the land, that the light of God's truth might shine everywhere.

And recall that this scattering was the fulfillment of Jacob's prophetic word: 'I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel' (Gen. 49:7), spoken in judgment over Levi's violence at Shechem. Yet God transformed the judgment into a ministry. The tribe condemned to dispersion became the means by which the worship and instruction of God permeated the whole nation. What was meant as a curse, God turned into a blessing — the scattered tribe became the teaching tribe. Ferguson observed that the dispersion of the Levites prefigures the church scattered among the nations, the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet. 2:9) sent out as salt and light, that the knowledge of God might fill the earth. The forty-eight cities, embedded among all the tribes, are a picture of God's people placed strategically throughout the world to bring his Word to every place. God's redemptive purpose runs even through the consequences of ancient sin, weaving judgment into grace.

sections.title: God Gave Them Rest on Every Side
sections.commentary:
The narrator now pauses to summarize the whole conquest and allotment, and the summary rises toward doxology: 'Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers. And they took possession of it, and they settled there. And the LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for the LORD had given all their enemies into their hands' (vv. 43–44).

Three great affirmations sound here. First, God gave them all the land he had sworn — the promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is fulfilled. Second, God gave them rest on every side — the long warfare is over, and the people dwell in peace, the rest that is a type of the rest that remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Third, not one enemy had withstood them — the promise of 1:5 ('No man shall be able to stand before you') is fulfilled to the letter. The God who promised has performed; the God who swore has accomplished.

This summary is the verdict of history upon the faithfulness of God. Every promise — land, rest, victory — has come to pass. The rest 'on every side' is especially precious. After centuries of slavery in Egypt, forty years of wilderness wandering, and seven years of conquest, the people of God finally dwell in rest in the land of promise. And this rest, real as it was, points beyond itself to the greater rest secured by the greater Joshua — the rest Christ gives to all who come to him (Matt. 11:28), and the eternal Sabbath rest of the new creation. Sproul observed that the rest God gave Israel was a genuine fulfillment and yet a foreshadowing, pointing forward to the final rest in Christ. The God who gave Israel rest on every side is the God who gives his people rest for their souls, and will one day give them rest forever. The conquest is complete; the inheritance is possessed; the rest is granted — all by the faithful hand of God.

sections.title: Not One Word Had Failed
sections.commentary:
And now the theological summit of the entire book, one of the most magnificent declarations of God's faithfulness in all of Scripture: 'Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass' (v. 45). Let the weight of it settle. Not one word. Not a single promise. All of them — every word of every good promise God had made — came to pass. The verdict of history upon the character of God is unanimous and unqualified: he is utterly, absolutely, unfailingly faithful.

This verse is the anchor of every believer's hope. The God who did not let one word fail to Israel is the God who has made his promises to us in Christ. And 'all the promises of God find their Yes in him' (2 Cor. 1:20). If not one word failed to Israel, not one word will fail to us. The promises of forgiveness, of adoption, of the indwelling Spirit, of resurrection, of glory, of an inheritance that cannot fade — every one of them is as sure as the land was sure to Israel. The faithfulness of God is not an abstract doctrine but a demonstrated fact, written in the history of his people, sealed in the cross and resurrection of his Son.

How this should steady the trembling heart. We doubt; we fear; we wonder whether God will keep his word to us. And the answer of Joshua 21:45 thunders across the centuries: not one word has ever failed. Calvin observed that this declaration was meant to fix forever in Israel's heart — and ours — the certainty of God's faithfulness, that we might rest all our confidence upon his unbreakable word. MacArthur stressed that the absolute reliability of God's promises is the bedrock of the believer's assurance. The God who kept every promise to Israel is keeping, and will keep, every promise to you. He cannot lie (Titus 1:2); he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13); not one word of all his good promises will fail. All will come to pass. This is the rock on which faith stands, the anchor that holds in every storm: the perfect, unfailing faithfulness of God to his every word. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his word will not pass away (Matt. 24:35).

21.theology:
Judgment Woven into Grace. The scattering of the Levites among all the tribes fulfilled Jacob's word of judgment (Gen. 49:7), yet God transformed it into a ministry — the dispersed tribe became the teaching tribe, spreading the worship and Word of God throughout the land. This prefigures the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet. 2:9), scattered as salt and light that the knowledge of God might fill the earth.

The Rest That God Gives and Foreshadows. 'The LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn' (v. 44). The conquest is complete, the enemies subdued, the inheritance possessed. This real rest is a type of the greater rest secured by the greater Joshua — rest for the soul now (Matt. 11:28) and the eternal Sabbath rest of the new creation (Heb. 4:9).

The Unfailing Faithfulness of God. 'Not one word of all the good promises... had failed; all came to pass' (v. 45) — the theological summit of the book. The God who kept every promise to Israel keeps every promise to us, for 'all the promises of God find their Yes in him' (2 Cor. 1:20). This is the bedrock of the believer's assurance: he cannot lie, he cannot deny himself, and not one word of his good promises will fail.
21.examples:
Then: The Levites, with no land of their own, received forty-eight cities scattered among all the tribes, so that the worship and Word of God reached every corner of Israel. And the narrator summed up the whole conquest with a declaration for the ages: 'Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made had failed; all came to pass.'

Now: We doubt and fear and wonder whether God will keep his word to us. The answer of Joshua 21:45 thunders across the centuries: not one word has ever failed. The God who kept every promise to Israel — land, rest, victory — is the God who has made every promise to us in Christ, where they all find their Yes. Forgiveness, adoption, resurrection, an unfading inheritance, eternal rest — every word is as sure as the land was to Israel. Rest your trembling heart on the rock of God's unfailing faithfulness.

22.title: The Eastern Tribes Return and the Altar of Witness
22.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Joshua summoned the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh,<sup>2</sup>and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you and have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you.<sup>3</sup>You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God.<sup>4</sup>And now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn and go to your tents in the land where your possession lies, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan.<sup>5</sup>Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.<sup>7</sup>Now to the one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession beside their brothers in the land west of the Jordan. And when Joshua sent them away to their homes and blessed them,<sup>8</sup>he said to them, "Go back to your tents with much wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with much clothing. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers."<sup>9</sup>So the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned home, parting from the people of Israel at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, their own land of which they had possessed themselves by command of the LORD through Moses.<sup>10</sup>And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel heard it said, "Behold, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built the altar at the frontier of the land of Canaan, in the region about the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the people of Israel."<sup>12</sup>And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them.<sup>13</sup>Then the people of Israel sent to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest,<sup>14</sup>and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the tribal families of Israel, every one of them the head of a family among the clans of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And they came to the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them,<sup>16</sup>"Thus says the whole congregation of the LORD, 'What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel in turning away this day from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar this day in rebellion against the LORD?<sup>17</sup>Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves, and for which there came a plague upon the congregation of the LORD,<sup>18</sup>that you too must turn away this day from following the LORD? And if you too rebel against the LORD today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.<sup>19</sup>But now, if the land of your possession is unclean, pass over into the LORD's land where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take for yourselves a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD or make us as rebels by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.<sup>20</sup>Did not Achan the son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity.'"<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh said in answer to the heads of the families of Israel,<sup>22</sup>"The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today<sup>23</sup>for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. Or if we did so to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself take vengeance.<sup>24</sup>No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?<sup>25</sup>For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.' So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Therefore we said, 'Let us now build an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice,<sup>27</sup>but to be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings and sacrifices and peace offerings, so your children will not say to our children in time to come, "You have no portion in the LORD."'<sup>28</sup>And we thought, 'If this should be said to us or to our descendants in time to come, we should say, "Behold, the copy of the altar of the LORD, which our fathers made, not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you."'<sup>29</sup>Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD and turn away this day from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle!"<sup>30</sup>When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation, the heads of the families of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh spoke, it was good in their eyes.<sup>31</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh, "Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD."<sup>32</sup>Then Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the chiefs, returned from the people of Reuben and the people of Gad in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the people of Israel, and brought back word to them.<sup>33</sup>And the report was good in the eyes of the people of Israel. And the people of Israel blessed God and spoke no more of making war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and the people of Gad were settled.<sup>34</sup>The people of Reuben and the people of Gad called the altar Witness, "For," they said, "it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
22.overview:
With the conquest complete and the land at rest, Joshua summons the eastern tribes — Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh — and releases them to return to their inheritance beyond the Jordan. They had kept their pledge faithfully (ch. 1, 4), crossing over armed to fight alongside their brothers for years until all Israel had rest. Now Joshua blesses them, charges them to love and serve the LORD with all their heart, and sends them home with great riches to share with their families.

But on their way home, at the Jordan, the eastern tribes build 'an altar of imposing size' (v. 10). When the western tribes hear of it, they are filled with alarm and gather for war, fearing that their brothers have built a rival altar in defiance of the LORD, who had commanded that sacrifice be offered only at the central sanctuary. The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh, ready to go to battle against their own brothers — a near civil war over a misunderstanding.

Before the swords are drawn, however, the western tribes do something wise: they send a delegation, led by Phinehas the priest, to confront the eastern tribes and inquire. And the eastern tribes explain: the altar was never meant for sacrifice. It was built as a witness, a memorial, so that in generations to come the western tribes could not say to the eastern, 'You have no portion in the LORD' (v. 25). Separated by the Jordan, the eastern tribes feared being cut off from the worshiping community; the altar was their testimony that they too belonged to the LORD and his people. The misunderstanding is resolved, war is averted, and the altar is named 'Witness.'

The chapter is a profound study in the unity of God's people — both its fragility and its preservation. It teaches the danger of rash judgment, the wisdom of inquiry before accusation, the zeal for pure worship that must never be quenched, and the deep longing of every believer to belong to the people of God. Above all, it shows that the unity of God's people is precious, easily fractured by misunderstanding, and to be guarded with both zeal for truth and patience in love.

sections.title: Joshua Blesses and Releases the Eastern Tribes
sections.commentary:
Joshua summons the eastern tribes and commends their faithfulness: 'You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you... you have not deserted your brothers these many days, down to this day' (vv. 2–3). They had honored their pledge from chapter 1 — crossing the Jordan armed, leaving their families and lands in the east, and fighting alongside their brothers through years of conquest until all Israel had rest. Now, their duty discharged, Joshua releases them to return home with his blessing.

But Joshua's parting charge is profoundly spiritual: 'Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law... to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul' (v. 5). Here is the heart of all true religion, packed into a single verse — love, obedience, clinging, wholehearted service. Joshua knew that the greatest danger to the eastern tribes was not external enemies but the drift of the heart away from the LORD, especially as they returned to settle in lands somewhat removed from the central worship of Israel.

This charge echoes the great commandment that Jesus himself would identify as the summit of the law: 'You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind' (Matt. 22:37). The faithful warriors are sent home not merely with riches and blessing but with the one essential exhortation: keep loving and clinging to the LORD. Begg observed that the danger for the eastern tribes — settled, prosperous, and somewhat distant from the center of worship — is the danger for every believer in times of ease: that the heart will slowly drift from wholehearted devotion. Joshua's word is a guard against that drift: love him, walk in his ways, cling to him, serve him with all your heart. The warriors return home crowned with this charge, the one thing needful.

sections.title: The Altar by the Jordan and the Threat of War
sections.commentary:
On their way home, at the Jordan, the eastern tribes build 'an altar of imposing size' (v. 10). When word reaches the western tribes, the reaction is swift and severe: 'the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them' (v. 12). They feared that their brothers had erected a rival altar, breaking faith with the LORD, who had commanded that sacrifice be offered only at the central sanctuary (Deut. 12). To them, this looked like apostasy, a second center of worship that would fracture the nation's devotion and provoke God's wrath upon all Israel.

It is worth pausing to admire what the western tribes' reaction reveals, even amid its rashness. They were zealous for the purity of worship and the unity of Israel's devotion to the one true God. They remembered the disaster of Peor (v. 17) and the sin of Achan (v. 20) — how the sin of some had brought wrath upon all. Their fear was not mere suspicion but a genuine, if mistaken, zeal for the holiness of God and the integrity of the covenant community. They would rather go to war against their own brothers than tolerate what they believed to be rebellion against the LORD.

Yet their zeal, however genuine, was on the brink of catastrophe — for it rested on a misunderstanding. They had judged before they had inquired. They had assumed the worst, mobilized for war, and stood ready to shed their brothers' blood over an altar whose purpose they did not yet understand. Sproul observed that zeal without knowledge, however well-intentioned, can lead the people of God into grievous error and division. The chapter sets before us a sobering picture: a community so zealous for truth that it nearly destroys itself through rash judgment. The peril is real and perennial — that we, in our jealousy for what is right, will condemn our brothers without understanding them, and rend the body of Christ over a misapprehension. The swords are drawn; the armies are gathered; and only inquiry can avert the disaster.

sections.title: Inquiry Before Accusation: Phinehas and the Delegation
sections.commentary:
Before the war begins, wisdom prevails. The western tribes send a delegation — Phinehas the priest (the very man whose zeal had once stopped a plague at Peor) and ten chiefs — to confront the eastern tribes and learn the truth. This is the crucial turn of the chapter. They do not attack first and ask questions later; they inquire before they accuse. And the eastern tribes give their explanation, which transforms everything.

The altar, they explain, was never built for sacrifice — 'far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD' (v. 29). It was built as a witness, a memorial. The eastern tribes, separated from the rest of Israel by the Jordan, feared that in generations to come the western tribes might say to their descendants, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?... You have no portion in the LORD' (vv. 24–25). The altar was their testimony, a standing witness that they too belonged to the LORD and his worshiping people, that the Jordan did not cut them off from the covenant community. It was not an act of rebellion but an act of longing — the longing to belong.

How much heartache, how much bloodshed, was averted by the simple act of inquiry! Had the western tribes attacked on their assumption, they would have slaughtered their brothers over a profound misunderstanding. Ferguson observed that this episode is a permanent lesson for the church: 'inquire before you accuse.' Before we condemn a brother, before we assume the worst, before we go to war over what we think we see, we are to seek understanding, to ask, to listen. 'If your brother sins, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone' (Matt. 18:15). The wisdom of Phinehas and the delegation — confronting honestly but inquiring first — saved the unity of Israel. And it stands as a rebuke to all our rash judgments and a model of how the people of God are to handle apparent offenses: with zeal for truth, yes, but tempered by the patience to understand. The altar that nearly caused a war was, in truth, a monument to faith.

sections.title: The Altar Named 'Witness' and Unity Preserved
sections.commentary:
The explanation satisfies the delegation. Phinehas declares, 'Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD' (v. 31). The report is brought back to the whole assembly, and the people are relieved and rejoice; they bless God, and the talk of war ceases. And the eastern tribes name the altar 'Witness,' saying, 'it is a witness between us that the LORD is God' (v. 34). What had nearly sparked a civil war becomes a monument to the unity of God's people and the shared confession that the LORD is God.

The resolution is a beautiful picture of the preservation of the unity of God's people. The fracture was real and dangerous, but it was healed — not by papering over the truth, but by honest inquiry, humble explanation, and shared zeal for the LORD. Both sides, it turns out, were jealous for the same thing: the worship of the one true God and their common belonging to him. The western tribes feared rebellion; the eastern tribes feared exclusion. Both were driven by love for the LORD and longing for unity. And when they understood one another, the threatened division became an occasion for renewed fellowship.

The altar named 'Witness' stands as a testimony to a profound gospel truth: the deep longing of every believer to belong to the people of God, and the preciousness of the unity that binds them. The eastern tribes' great fear was being cut off — 'you have no portion in the LORD.' And the gospel's great assurance is that none who belong to Christ can ever be cut off; the Jordan of distance, the barrier of difference, cannot separate those who are one in him. 'There is one body and one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism' (Eph. 4:4–5). The unity of God's people is precious, fragile, easily fractured by misunderstanding — and to be guarded with both zeal for truth and patience in love. The altar of Witness reminds every generation that we belong together, that the LORD is God of us all, and that our unity in him is worth every effort to preserve. 'Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!' (Ps. 133:1).

22.theology:
The Preciousness and Fragility of Unity. The near civil war over the altar shows how easily the unity of God's people is fractured by misunderstanding, and how it must be guarded with zeal for truth tempered by patience in love. The gospel makes the people of God one — 'one body, one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism' (Eph. 4:4–5) — and that unity is worth every effort to preserve (Ps. 133:1).

Inquire Before You Accuse. The western tribes nearly destroyed their brothers over a misunderstanding, but disaster was averted by inquiry before accusation. The lesson is permanent for the church: before we condemn, we are to seek understanding (Matt. 18:15). Zeal for truth must be joined to the patience to listen, lest we rend the body of Christ over a misapprehension.

The Longing to Belong. The eastern tribes' great fear was being told, 'You have no portion in the LORD' (v. 25); their altar was a witness that they too belonged. This longing finds its answer in the gospel: none who belong to Christ can ever be cut off; no barrier of distance or difference can separate those who are one in him.
22.examples:
Then: The faithful eastern tribes, returning home, built an altar by the Jordan — and their brothers, fearing rebellion, gathered for war. But before swords were drawn, they inquired, and learned the altar was a 'Witness' that the eastern tribes too belonged to the LORD. Civil war was averted; unity was preserved; God was glorified.

Now: We are forever tempted to rash judgment — to assume the worst of a brother, to condemn before we understand, to fracture the body of Christ over a misapprehension. The altar of Witness teaches us to inquire before we accuse, to temper zeal for truth with patience in love. And it assures us of the deep gospel comfort that none who belong to Christ can ever be told 'you have no portion in the LORD' — for in him we are one, and no barrier can separate us. Guard the unity of God's people; it is precious in his sight.

23.title: Joshua's Farewell Charge
23.text: <sup>1</sup>A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their surrounding enemies, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years,<sup>2</sup>Joshua summoned all Israel, its elders and heads, its judges and officers, and said to them, "I am now old and well advanced in years.<sup>3</sup>And you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes those nations that remain, along with all the nations that I have already cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west.<sup>5</sup>The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight. And you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left,<sup>7</sup>that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them,<sup>8</sup>but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day.<sup>9</sup>For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day.<sup>10</sup>One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you.<sup>11</sup>Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.<sup>12</sup>For if you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations remaining among you and make marriages with them, so that you associate with them and they with you,<sup>13</sup>know for certain that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you, but they shall be a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground that the LORD your God has given you.<sup>14</sup>"And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed.<sup>15</sup>But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you,<sup>16</sup>if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you."
23.overview:
Joshua is now 'old and well advanced in years' (v. 1), and like Moses before him, he gathers the leaders of Israel for a farewell charge. This is the testament of a man who has seen the faithfulness of God across a lifetime — through the wilderness, the Jordan, the conquest, and the rest. His final words are not reminiscences but exhortations, the urgent pleadings of a dying leader who longs for his people to remain faithful to the God who has been so faithful to them.

The charge centers on the Word of God and the danger of compromise. 'Be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left' (v. 6). The same exhortation God gave Joshua at his commissioning (1:7) Joshua now passes on to the nation. The secret of faithfulness, as at the beginning, is unwavering devotion to the Word — keeping it, doing it, never turning aside.

Joshua grounds his charge in the demonstrated faithfulness of God. 'The LORD your God who fights for you' (v. 3, 10) — this is the great refrain of the whole book, now invoked one last time. 'One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you' (v. 10). And again, the magnificent declaration of God's perfect faithfulness: 'not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you' (v. 14). The God who fought for them, who kept every promise, is worthy of unwavering allegiance.

But Joshua also issues a solemn warning. The same faithfulness of God that brought all good things to pass will, if Israel turns away, bring all the threatened evils to pass as well. 'If you transgress the covenant... then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land' (v. 16). The God who is faithful to his promises is faithful to his warnings. The danger Joshua most fears is the slow compromise of mingling with the remaining nations and turning to their gods. His farewell is a passionate plea to cling to the LORD and shun the idols — a plea that the next generation would tragically fail to heed.

sections.title: The LORD Has Fought for You
sections.commentary:
Joshua, aged and near death, summons all Israel — its elders, heads, judges, and officers — for his farewell. He begins not with himself but with God: 'You have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you' (v. 3). The great refrain of the book sounds one final time from the lips of its hero: the LORD has fought for you. Joshua wants the abiding memory of the conquest to be not Israel's valor but God's power, not human achievement but divine faithfulness.

And he points them forward as well as backward: 'The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight, and you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you' (v. 5). The God who has fought will continue to fight; the conquest is not yet complete, but the same faithful God will finish what he has begun. Joshua's confidence for the future rests entirely on the demonstrated faithfulness of God in the past.

This is the proper posture of faith. We look back at what God has done — the cross, the empty tomb, the unbroken chain of his mercies in our own lives — and from that demonstrated faithfulness we draw confidence for what lies ahead. 'He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?' (Rom. 8:32). Calvin observed that Joshua roots Israel's future hope in the memory of God's past faithfulness, the surest foundation for confidence. The God who fought for them yesterday will fight for them tomorrow. Joshua's farewell begins where all true faith begins: with the faithful God who fights for his people.

sections.title: Be Very Strong to Keep the Word
sections.commentary:
The heart of Joshua's charge is devotion to the Word of God: 'Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left' (v. 6). These are almost the exact words God spoke to Joshua at his own commissioning (1:7). The charge that launched Joshua's leadership now becomes the charge he passes to the nation as his final legacy. The secret of faithfulness, from beginning to end, is unwavering devotion to the Word — to keep it, to do it, to turn aside from it neither to the right nor the left.

Joshua then warns specifically against compromise with the remaining nations: 'that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them, but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day' (vv. 7–8). Here is the great danger Joshua foresees — not military defeat but spiritual seduction, the slow drift of mingling with the pagan nations and being drawn to their gods. The unconquered remnants that Israel failed to drive out (the theme that has shadowed the whole allotment) now threaten to become the snare Joshua most fears.

The contrast is stark and instructive: do not 'make mention' of their gods, but 'cling to the LORD.' That word 'cling' (the same Hebrew word used of a man cleaving to his wife in Gen. 2:24) speaks of intimate, covenant devotion — holding fast to the LORD with the whole heart. MacArthur observed that the call to 'cling to the LORD' is the positive counterpart to the warning against the idols; the heart that clings to God has no room for false gods. The defense against compromise is not merely avoidance of evil but active, clinging devotion to the LORD. Joshua's word stands for every generation: be very strong to keep the Word, turn aside neither right nor left, and cling to the LORD with all your heart.

sections.title: One Man Puts a Thousand to Flight
sections.commentary:
Joshua reminds Israel of the supernatural victories God has given: 'For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day. One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you' (vv. 9–10). The mathematics of faith defies the mathematics of the world. One Israelite routs a thousand enemies — not because of superior strength, but because 'the LORD your God fights for you.' The disproportion is the point: the victory is so lopsided that it can only be explained by the presence and power of God.

This is the heart of the book's theology, distilled into a single stirring line. 'One man of you puts to flight a thousand' echoes the covenant promise of Leviticus 26:8 and Deuteronomy 32:30. When God fights for his people, the odds are irrelevant; the enemy's numbers melt away; one with God is a majority. The same truth that emboldened Gideon's three hundred and David's sling and Jonathan's bold ascent ('nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few,' 1 Sam. 14:6) is here proclaimed by Joshua as the abiding confidence of God's people.

And from this Joshua draws his practical exhortation: 'Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God' (v. 11). Notice the logic. Because God fights for you so powerfully, therefore love him carefully, watchfully, with diligent devotion. The proper response to the God who routs a thousand for one is wholehearted love. Begg observed that Joshua's exhortation moves from the greatness of God's power to the duty of the heart's devotion — the God who fights for us so mightily deserves and demands our careful love. The believer who truly grasps that 'if God is for us, who can be against us?' (Rom. 8:31) will be moved not to presumption but to grateful, watchful love. One man puts a thousand to flight; therefore love the LORD your God with all your heart.

sections.title: Not One Word Has Failed — and the Solemn Warning
sections.commentary:
Joshua now sets before Israel the two edges of God's faithfulness. First, the comfort: 'And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed' (v. 14). The dying leader's testimony, drawn from a lifetime of experience, echoes the narrator's verdict in 21:45: not one word has failed. Joshua appeals to their own knowledge — 'you know in your hearts and souls' — for they have witnessed the faithfulness of God with their own eyes. The God who keeps every good promise is utterly worthy of trust.

But then comes the solemn warning, the other edge of the same faithfulness: 'But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have come to pass, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land... if you transgress the covenant... and go and serve other gods' (vv. 15–16). Here is a sobering truth: the same faithfulness of God that brought all the good promises to pass will, if Israel turns away, bring all the threatened judgments to pass as well. God is faithful to his warnings as surely as to his promises. The reliability of God cuts both ways — it is comfort to the obedient and terror to the rebellious.

This is a word the church must not soften. The God who cannot lie cannot fail to keep his warnings any more than his promises. 'Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap' (Gal. 6:7). The faithfulness of God is the believer's greatest comfort and, to the one who would presume upon grace while serving idols, a fearful warning. Sproul stressed that the same divine faithfulness that guarantees the promises guarantees the threats; we cannot claim the one while ignoring the other. Joshua's farewell holds both together: rejoice that not one good word has failed — and tremble, for not one warning will fail either. The remedy for both is the same: cling to the LORD, keep his Word, serve no other gods. The God who has been so faithful deserves nothing less than wholehearted, undivided allegiance — and the next generation's tragic failure to heed this charge would prove how desperately Israel, and we, need a faithfulness greater than our own: the faithfulness of the greater Joshua, who keeps the covenant we break.

23.theology:
The Word as the Secret of Faithfulness. 'Be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law... turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left' (v. 6). The charge that launched Joshua's leadership (1:7) becomes his final legacy. The defense against compromise is unwavering devotion to the Word joined to clinging love for the LORD (vv. 7–8).

The LORD Fights for His People. 'One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you' (v. 10). The mathematics of faith defies the world's: when God fights, the odds are irrelevant. 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (Rom. 8:31). The proper response is careful, wholehearted love for God (v. 11).

God's Faithfulness Cuts Both Ways. 'Not one word has failed of all the good things' (v. 14) — and just as surely, the threatened judgments will come if Israel turns to idols (vv. 15–16). The same faithfulness that guarantees the promises guarantees the warnings. This points beyond our broken covenant-keeping to the greater Joshua, who keeps the covenant we fail to keep.
23.examples:
Then: Aged Joshua gathered Israel for his farewell, reminding them that the LORD had fought for them — one man routing a thousand — and that not one word of God's good promises had failed. He charged them to cling to the LORD and keep his Word, warning that the same faithful God would bring judgment if they turned to idols.

Now: We draw confidence for the future from the demonstrated faithfulness of God in the past — supremely the cross and empty tomb. The God who fought for Israel fights for us; one with God is a majority. Yet Joshua's warning stands: God's faithfulness cuts both ways, guaranteeing his warnings as surely as his promises. The remedy is to cling to the LORD and keep his Word. And where we fail — as Israel would — we look to the greater Joshua, who kept the covenant we break and secured our standing forever.

24.title: The Covenant at Shechem
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem and summoned the elders, the heads, the judges, and the officers of Israel. And they presented themselves before God.<sup>2</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods.<sup>3</sup>Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many. I gave him Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. And I gave Esau the hill country of Seir to possess, but Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.<sup>5</sup>And I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt with what I did in the midst of it, and afterward I brought you out.<sup>6</sup>"'Then I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. And the Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.<sup>7</sup>And when they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians and made the sea come upon them and cover them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. And you lived in the wilderness a long time.<sup>8</sup>Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand, and you took possession of their land, and I destroyed them before you.<sup>9</sup>Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. And he sent and invited Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,<sup>10</sup>but I would not listen to Balaam. Indeed, he blessed you. So I delivered you out of his hand.<sup>11</sup>And you went over the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the leaders of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And I gave them into your hand.<sup>12</sup>And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites; it was not by your sword or by your bow.<sup>13</sup>I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant.'<sup>14</sup>"Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."<sup>16</sup>Then the people answered, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods,<sup>17</sup>for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight and preserved us in all the way that we went, and among all the peoples through whom we passed.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God."<sup>19</sup>But Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins.<sup>20</sup>If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good."<sup>21</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "No, but we will serve the LORD."<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD, to serve him." And they said, "We are witnesses."<sup>23</sup>He said, "Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel."<sup>24</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "The LORD our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey."<sup>25</sup>So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and put in place statutes and rules for them at Shechem.<sup>26</sup>And Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.<sup>27</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. Therefore it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God."<sup>28</sup>So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.<sup>29</sup>After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old.<sup>30</sup>And they buried him in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.<sup>31</sup>Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel.<sup>32</sup>As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph.<sup>33</sup>And Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, the town of Phinehas his son, which had been given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
24.overview:
The book of Joshua closes where covenants in Israel were often made — at Shechem, in the valley between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, the place where Abraham first built an altar in the land (Gen. 12:6–7) and where Joshua had earlier renewed the covenant (ch. 8). Here, in his final act, Joshua gathers all Israel for the most solemn covenant renewal of all. And he begins not with demands but with grace — a sweeping rehearsal of redemptive history, all in the first person of God: 'I took your father Abraham... I gave him Isaac... I sent Moses and Aaron... I brought you out... I gave you a land on which you had not labored' (vv. 3–13).

This is the gospel pattern: grace before demand, indicative before imperative. Before God calls Israel to serve him, he recounts all he has done for them — sovereign election ('I took Abraham'), redemption ('I brought you out'), provision ('I gave you a land you did not labor for'). Eighteen times in this rehearsal God says 'I.' The whole history of salvation is God's doing from first to last. Only after this recital of grace does Joshua issue the call to covenant faithfulness: 'Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness' (v. 14).

Then comes the most famous verse in the book, the great call to decision: 'Choose this day whom you will serve... But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (v. 15). Joshua sets before Israel the inescapable choice — the gods of their fathers, the gods of the Amorites, or the LORD. There is no neutral ground; every soul must choose whom it will serve. And Joshua, the aged leader, plants his own flag without hesitation: whatever the rest may do, his house will serve the LORD. Here is the resolve of faith, the personal and familial commitment that must finally be made by every believer.

The chapter — and the book — ends with three burials and one renewed covenant. Joshua dies at 110 and is buried in his inheritance. The bones of Joseph, carried out of Egypt in faith (Gen. 50:25), are finally buried at Shechem, the promise to Joseph fulfilled after four centuries. And Eleazar the priest dies. An era closes. The generation that saw the mighty acts of God passes into the grave, leaving behind a renewed covenant and a solemn choice — a choice that echoes down to every reader: 'Choose this day whom you will serve.'

sections.title: The Rehearsal of Redemptive History: Grace Before Demand
sections.commentary:
Joshua gathers all Israel to Shechem and presents the covenant not with a list of demands but with a recital of grace. Speaking in the voice of God, he sweeps across the whole history of redemption: 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates... and they served other gods. Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many' (vv. 2–3). Note where the history begins — with Abraham an idolater 'beyond the River,' worshiping other gods, until God sovereignly took him. Israel's entire existence as a people begins with God's free, unmerited election. They did not seek God; God sought them.

The recital continues through the whole story: Isaac and Jacob, the descent into Egypt, the plagues, the exodus, the Red Sea, the wilderness, the defeat of the Amorite kings, the failed curse of Balaam turned to blessing, the crossing of the Jordan, and the conquest of the land. And it climaxes in a stunning summary of grace: 'I gave you a land on which you had not labored, and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant' (v. 13). Everything Israel has, they received as a gift. They labored for none of it; God gave it all.

Eighteen times in this rehearsal, God says 'I' — 'I took... I gave... I sent... I brought... I gave.' The whole history of salvation is God's doing from first to last. This is the gospel pattern, the very structure of grace: God recounts what he has done before he calls for any response. The indicative precedes the imperative; grace precedes demand. So in the New Testament, the great doctrinal recitals of God's saving work (Rom. 1–11; Eph. 1–3) always precede the calls to obedience (Rom. 12; Eph. 4). Sproul observed that the covenant is grounded entirely in God's prior, sovereign grace; Israel's obedience is to be the response of gratitude, never the basis of acceptance. Keller often pressed this very point: the gospel says 'I have done this for you; therefore...' — never 'do this, and I will accept you.' Joshua's recital of redemptive history is a sermon on sovereign grace, the foundation on which the call to serve the LORD will rest.

sections.title: Choose This Day Whom You Will Serve
sections.commentary:
Only now, after the recital of grace, does Joshua issue the call: 'Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD' (v. 14). The response to grace is wholehearted, sincere, exclusive devotion — putting away every idol and serving the LORD alone. And then comes the most famous verse in the book, the great call to decision: 'And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve... But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (v. 15).

Joshua sets before Israel an inescapable choice. There are only three options — the gods of their fathers beyond the River, the gods of the Amorites in whose land they now dwell, or the LORD. But there is no fourth option of neutrality, no possibility of serving no one. Every soul serves something; the only question is what. Bob Dylan caught the biblical truth: 'you're gonna have to serve somebody.' The call 'choose this day' confronts every heart with the necessity of decision; to refuse to choose the LORD is, by default, to choose the idols.

And Joshua, the aged leader at the end of his life, plants his flag without hesitation or qualification: 'But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' Whatever the rest of the nation may do, his decision is made and his household is committed. Here is the resolve of mature faith — personal, unwavering, and extending to his whole family. Joshua does not merely commit himself; he commits his house, exercising the spiritual headship that leads a household to serve God. Begg observed that Joshua's declaration is the model of the believing parent and leader: not 'I hope my family will choose well,' but 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' — a settled, declared commitment to lead one's household in the worship of God. This verse has been inscribed over countless thresholds and engraved on countless hearts, for it captures the essence of decisive faith: in a world of competing gods, the believer chooses, and declares, and leads his house to serve the LORD alone. The choice confronts every reader still: whom will you serve?

sections.title: The Covenant Sealed and the Witness Stone
sections.commentary:
The people respond with enthusiasm: 'Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods... we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God' (vv. 16–18). But Joshua, far from accepting their easy profession, responds with startling severity: 'You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins' (v. 19). This is no discouragement of faith but a sobering of presumption. Joshua will not let Israel make a glib, self-confident vow. He confronts them with the holiness of God and the weight of the commitment, so that their covenant will not be shallow words but a considered, sober resolve.

There is profound pastoral wisdom here. Joshua knows the human heart's tendency to make easy promises it cannot keep, and he knows — prophetically — that Israel will indeed turn away (as the book of Judges would soon record). His words 'you are not able to serve the LORD' expose the truth that, in their own strength, sinful people cannot keep covenant with a holy God. This drives us, in the end, beyond Israel's broken resolve to the only One who could keep covenant perfectly — the greater Joshua, who alone served the LORD with flawless faithfulness, and who keeps the covenant on behalf of his people. Ferguson observed that Joshua's severe word unmasks the inadequacy of human resolve and points, by its very starkness, to the need for a faithfulness greater than our own.

The people insist, 'No, but we will serve the LORD' (v. 21), and Joshua holds them to it: 'You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD' (v. 22). The covenant is sealed; statutes and rules are recorded in the Book of the Law of God; and Joshua sets up a great stone under the oak at Shechem as a witness: 'it has heard all the words of the LORD... it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God' (v. 27). The stone, like the altar of chapter 22, stands as a silent, enduring testimony. Calvin noted that Joshua's insistence on sober, witnessed commitment was meant to leave Israel without excuse. The covenant is made; the witness stone is raised; the people are bound by their own confession. And the whole solemn scene reminds us that covenant with God is no light thing — it is a binding, sacred commitment to a holy and jealous God, to be entered not glibly but with the deepest seriousness, and kept only by the grace of the faithful God himself.

sections.title: Three Burials and the Closing of an Era
sections.commentary:
The book closes with three burials, and they are heavy with meaning. First, 'Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old' (v. 29). He receives at last the title that crowned Moses — 'the servant of the LORD' — the highest honorific in Scripture. The great leader, who fought every battle, divided the land, and renewed the covenant, is buried in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah. And the narrator adds a precious epitaph for the whole generation: 'Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua' (v. 31). The covenant held for one generation — but the ominous implication hangs in the air: what of the generation to come? The book of Judges would supply the tragic answer.

Second, 'the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem' (v. 32). Here is a burial four centuries in the making. Joseph, dying in Egypt, had made the people swear to carry his bones to the promised land: 'God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here' (Gen. 50:25; Heb. 11:22). For 400 years, through slavery and exodus and wilderness, those bones were carried in faith, awaiting the fulfillment of the promise. Now, at last, in the land God gave, Joseph is laid to rest at Shechem — the very plot Jacob had purchased generations before. The faith of Joseph, who believed God's promise though he would not see its fulfillment in his lifetime, is vindicated. The bones that traveled in hope finally rest in the land of promise — a testimony that God keeps his word across centuries, and that those who die in faith will surely inherit the promise (Heb. 11:13, 39–40).

Third, Eleazar the priest, son of Aaron, dies and is buried. The priestly generation passes with the leadership generation. An era closes; the conquest generation goes to its rest. The book of Joshua ends, then, with graves — but they are graves of hope, not despair. Joshua, the servant of the LORD, rests in his inheritance. Joseph's bones rest in the promised land, his faith fulfilled. And the renewed covenant, the witness stone, and the choice — 'choose this day whom you will serve' — remain as the legacy of the conquest generation to all who come after. The greater Joshua would one day come, bearing the same name, to lead his people into a better inheritance and an eternal rest. And the choice Joshua set before Israel echoes still to every reader of this book: 'As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' Whom will you serve?

24.theology:
Grace Before Demand. Joshua's covenant begins with a recital of God's saving acts — eighteen times God says 'I' (vv. 2–13) — before any call to obedience. This is the gospel pattern: indicative before imperative, grace before demand. Israel's obedience is the response of gratitude, never the basis of acceptance. 'I have done this for you; therefore serve me' — never the reverse.

The Inescapable Choice. 'Choose this day whom you will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (v. 15). There is no neutral ground; every soul serves something. Joshua models decisive, declared, household-leading faith. Yet his sobering word 'you are not able to serve the LORD' (v. 19) exposes our inability and points beyond our broken resolve to the greater Joshua, who keeps the covenant perfectly on our behalf.

God Keeps His Word Across the Centuries. Joseph's bones, carried in faith for 400 years (Gen. 50:25; Heb. 11:22), are finally buried in the promised land. The faith of those who die without seeing the promise fulfilled is vindicated; God keeps his word across generations, and all who die in faith will surely inherit (Heb. 11:13, 39–40).
24.examples:
Then: At Shechem, Joshua rehearsed all that God had done — sovereign election, redemption, the gift of a land they did not labor for — and only then called Israel to choose whom they would serve, planting his own flag: 'As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' The covenant was sealed, the witness stone raised, and the conquest generation laid to rest, with Joseph's bones finally buried in the land after four centuries of hope.

Now: The gospel always comes in this order: grace before demand, what God has done before what we must do. And it sets before every soul the same inescapable choice Joshua set before Israel — for there is no neutral ground; we will all serve somebody. Joshua's word 'you are not able' drives us to the greater Joshua, who alone kept the covenant and keeps it for us. Resolved by his grace, we declare with the aged leader: 'As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' Whom will you serve?
